articles.title: Yemen war heats up further as Hormuz stalemate persists
articles.body:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi heads to China to meet his counterpart Wang Yi as Beijing is exceedingly trying to mediate an end to the US-Israeli war
The Houthi Foreign Ministry says that navigation remains safe in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and blames Saudi Arabia for trying to "mislead the international community". Meanwhile, fighting continues with reports of a Houthi drone downed near Mecca, and Houthis claiming that they shot down a Saudi fighter jet
US officials met representatives of Yemen's Houthis in Oman over the weekend, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic stretch of the Red Sea coast in a sweeping offensive that routed Saudi-backed forces
The Trump administration is preparing to approve a $2.8bn arms package for Israel that includes 40,000 heavy bombs. At the same time, Israeli attacks are continuing on Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
And so we continue our live coverage...
Images show heavy damage from Iran strikes on US bases
A destroyed aircraft, shredded tents, trailers that have been ripped apart: images taken by US troops show significant damage from Iranian strikes targeting American military assets in the Middle East, CBS News reported.
The undated images -- taken at a base in Saudi Arabia and two facilities in Kuwait -- were provided to CBS by American personnel on condition of anonymity due to US military restrictions, the outlet said late Tuesday.
"This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public," CBS quoted one US service member as saying.
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face," the service member added.
The Pentagon's inspector general released a report earlier this week that said the military's Central Command (CENTCOM) -- which is responsible for US forces in the Middle East -- had reported widespread damage to American facilities and equipment.
CENTCOM said Iranian strikes "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan," the report said.
"In addition, dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged" during the war, the report said.
Hundreds of oil tanker trucks were stranded in northeastern Syria's Kurdish region Wednesday after demonstrators blocked a major highway near the town of Tal Tamr in protest over rising fuel prices.
It was the latest evidence of rising discontent in the Kurdish region in the midst of a push to integrate a once-powerful Kurd-led force into Syria’s army and bring formerly autonomous institutions under the control of the central government.
The integration agreement with the Syrian Democratic Forces has been widely regarded as a victory for the government of interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa.
But in recent weeks, a series of issues have sparked discontent among Kurdish communities in formerly SDF-controlled areas, testing al-Sharaa's ability to consolidate his rule and bring unity to a country emerging from 14 years of conflict.
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming a locally made munition was used to target the warplane.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military mobilisations in the airspace of Marib province," the Houthis' military spokesman said.
In the statement posted to social media the spokesman, Yahya Saree, accused Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes in the the last week.
He added the jet had been targeted "using a locally made surface-to-air missile".
Saree also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy city of Mecca this week.
"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said.
Later, the Iran-backed group released footage of what it said was the targeting and downing of the jet.
In the video posted on social media, the burning wreckage of an aircraft could be seen in the desert and fighters posed with a part of the plane that appeared to show a Saudi flag.
Yemen's civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between the Houthis and the internationally recognised government forces reignited in July.
The Houthis have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and have been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The strait has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
How billionaire Robert Kraft derailed Ed Sheeran's tour
Billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft has come under renewed scrutiny after confirming that he pressured Ed Sheeran over rapper Macklemore’s participation in his US tour following the artist’s outspoken support for Palestine.
Kraft owns Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, one of the venues where Macklemore was due to perform as an opening act for Sheeran’s tour.
The creation of a US-secured corridor in the Strait of Hormuz has significantly boosted the flow of oil through the strategic waterway, an AFP analysis of industry data showed.
US President Donald Trump said in mid-August that a "tremendous amount of oil" was being shipped out of the vital waterway, although data from shipping trackers Kpler and Lloyd's List Intelligence show that volumes are still around half the levels seen before the war.
White House officials also told Axios that the US has controlled the corridor hugging the Omani coast since around mid-June, when a peace memo was agreed.
The US military has escorted convoys of vessels since fighting resumed on July 8 and Iran once again threatened to attack ships using the route.
Approximately 330 million barrels of oil aboard vessels assessed by AFP, using Lloyd's criteria, as not linked to Iran have exited Hormuz since 8 July, equivalent to around 4.9 million bpd.
But that figure rose steadily through August and September, reaching an average of almost 8 million bpd during the seven days to 7 September.
More than 14 million barrels were shipped out on 7 September alone.
By comparison, around 18 million bpd crossed during peacetime, 1.4 million bpd during the first phase of the war when restrictions were first imposed, and 9.4 million bpd during talks when restrictions were lifted.
Vessels waiting in the Strait of Hormuz. [Getty]
Sweden expels Iran embassy employee, summons ambassador
Sweden said Wednesday it had expelled an Iranian embassy employee and summoned the country's ambassador, accusing Tehran of making threats against Jewish and Israeli interests in Sweden.
"We know that Iran, over a long period of time, has conducted activities that threaten security in and against Sweden, targeting both individuals who oppose the Iranian regime and various Jewish and Israeli interests in our country. This has, among other things, been done by making use of criminal networks," Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer said in a statement to AFP.
Arab League chief condemns alleged Houthi attack on Mecca
Arab League Secretary General Nabil Fahmy condemned on Wednesday an alleged attempted attack by Yemen's Houthis targeting Mecca in Saudi Arabia.
"Compromising the security of Mecca and the sanctity of Islamic holy sites is a matter of extreme gravity," he said in a statement, applauding the Saudi air force's thwarting of the attack.
He warned that Houthi attacks on Saudi territory "threaten the region's security and stability".
Yemen's Houthis say targeted Saudi oil facility, air base
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they targeted an Aramco facility in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu as well as an air base in southern Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi airstrikes.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched more than 450 air strikes this week, and that in response, the Iran-backed group "targeted the Aramco facility in Yanbu with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" causing fires, as well as "the Khamis Mushait air base".
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi rejected on Wednesday any plans for Palestinian displacement, hours after Israel's defence minister said the army would "finish the job" in Gaza and remove Palestinians.
During a visit by Palestinian president Mahmud Abbas, Sisi "reiterated Egypt's firm stance against the displacement of the Palestinian people or any attempt to annihilate the Palestinian cause".
Egypt shares the only land border with the Gaza Strip that is not controlled by Israel, and has since 2023 rejected plans to displace the territory's more than two million people into the Sinai peninsula.
Last year, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo had turned down multiple offers to forgive parts of its massive foreign debt bill in exchange for allowing mass displacement into its territory.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday said it was only a matter of time before Israel resumes full-scale war in Gaza, "to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan".
Since May 2024, Israel has controlled Gaza completely after its military occupied the Philadelphi Corridor, the buffer zone along the Gaza-Egypt border. Egypt cannot evacuate any Palestinians from Gaza or send essential supplies into the Strip without Israel’s permission.
US officials met Iran-backed Houthis in Oman: Reuters
US officials met representatives of Yemen's Houthis in Oman over the weekend, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic stretch of the Red Sea coast in a sweeping offensive that routed Saudi-backed forces.
The meeting, which has not been made public, was held at the US Embassy in Muscat, three of the sources said on the condition of anonymity. Two sources said that Oman's government, a longtime regional mediator, helped organise the meeting.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis a "foreign terrorist organisation" in March 2025, criminalising support for the group. But Washington has negotiated with them since, reaching a ceasefire in May last year after bombing the group for two months to halt a campaign of attacks on Red Sea shipping.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the Houthis had phoned his administration asking the United States to keep out of the Yemen war. Vice President JD Vance said on Monday the United States was in direct contact with the group, without giving details.
In the meeting, which one source said took place on Sunday, the Houthis told US officials that they had no intention of attacking US vessels and that they were committed to the 2025 ceasefire with the S, two sources said.
One of the sources, a Yemeni, said the militia group also said they would not attack Israeli ships or any commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
According to two of the sources, the US side was represented by embassy personnel.
One of those sources said the Houthi delegation included a senior official based in Muscat who is under US sanctions, Mohammad Abdulsalam. Another source confirmed Abdulsalam's presence along with that of another senior Houthi official, Abdelmalik al-Ajiri.
After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on UK
As the UK sanctions occupied West Bank settlements, Israeli politicians and the lobby are weaponising antisemitism to defend the occupation and evade accountability, writes Richard Silverstein.
Deputy Commander of the Revolutionary Guard Naval Forces for Political Affairs, Ali Mohammadi, said that no ship in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is outside the scope of monitoring by Iran, indicating that any ship can be targeted at any point if necessary.
He said, according to what was reported by Fars agency: "The Americans believe that they can impose surrender on us by destroying a few bridges or roads, while we were present in the most difficult weather conditions, even in places like Farsi Island, whose area is no larger than a few football fields, and our connection to the motherland was never severed."
What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Mideast
Greece is buying more than an air-defence system from Israel. It is deepening a strategic relationship, with implications for the wider Middle East, writes Giorgio Cafiero.
At least 20 people, including five children, died, and dozens remained missing on Wednesday after a apartment building in Gaza collapsed from damage sustained in earlier Israeli strikes, the territory's civil defence agency said, giving an updated toll.
The bodies of "20 martyrs have been recovered from the rubble of a building that collapsed... Among the dead are five infants, while dozens of people remain trapped beneath the debris," said Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesperson for the civil defence agency.
Since May 2024, Israel has controlled Gaza completely after its military occupied the Philadelphi Corridor, the buffer zone along the Gaza-Egypt border. Egypt cannot evacuate any Palestinians from Gaza or send essential supplies into the Strip without Israel’s permission.
China FM says willing to 'safeguard' Iran's rights
China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Beijing was willing to "safeguard" Iran's rights during talks with his counterpart Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday, as Beijing seeks to mediate in Tehran's war with the United States.
China is "willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran, and safeguard Iran's legitimate rights and interests", Wang told Araghchi as they met in the Chinese capital.
"We encourage Iran and the US to stay rational and restrained," he added.
The talks come one week before an expected trip by Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington, where he will meet US President Donald Trump.
China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict in the Middle East, which has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.
"We do not wish to see regional tensions spilling over into Yemen and the Red Sea," Wang said.
Saudi Arabia calls an attempted Mecca attack a 'red line'
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels overnight of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city, prompting condemnation from countries in the region but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key US ally, declared Mecca a "red line" as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad.
Lebanon wants Israel security deal, Hezbollah disarmament
Speaking ahead of his departure to France on Wednesday, President Joseph Aoun told AFP Lebanon wanted a new force, European or otherwise, to prevent a security vacuum after UN peacekeepers leave south Lebanon when their mandate expires at the end of the year.
He called on the United States, European Union and Arab countries to support Lebanon's military as it deploys across the south.
In Paris, Aoun will attend a meeting hosted by President Emmanuel Macron and attended by King Abdullah II of Jordan to build international support for Lebanese troops as they deploy across the country.
"What matters is that there is no vacuum," Aoun told AFP on Tuesday. He added that any new force for Lebanon's south, part of which is occupied by Israel, would be "temporary until the (Lebanese) army can deploy".
"Whatever the nature of this force, that poses no problem for me: European, non-European, American, another United Nations force, Asian, or even a mix of European, Arab and Asian forces," Aoun said.
"The best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate," he added.
Aoun also said he wants a security agreement with Israel "primarily to end the state of hostility and the deployment of the army on the border. This could be a prelude to a later peace agreement, but we cannot jump directly to a peace agreement".
"We have no choice but negotiations, because the alternative is war, which would be very costly for us," Aoun added.
Aoun reiterated Lebanon was determined to disarm the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, saying the decision was "neither negotiable nor open to discussion".
However, he said, "the objective is not a confrontation... We are determined to resolve this issue peacefully. "This is not about building a state at the cost of a bloody conflict... or a new civil war."
"The best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate," Aoun added. [Getty]
Washington fired 70 missiles to repel Iran attack on Jordan
The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US and regional officials, that the US military fired up to 70 or more of its advanced interceptor missiles for air defense last week in response to the Iranian rocket attack on Jordan, noting that this massive expenditure is evidence of Iran’s improved ability to target US forces and challenge its air defenses.
Some officials said US forces fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptor missiles to counter the attack, including about 20 ballistic missiles. The Americans also fired more than 12 THAAD interceptor missiles, according to one official. Another official explained that this expenditure is roughly equivalent to what the United States has spent in an entire week during other periods of the war.
War-damaged Gaza building collapses killing 12 people
Gaza rescuers on Wednesday combed through the wreckage of a bombed-out apartment building that collapsed overnight, killing at least 12 Palestinians, including five children, and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
The incident highlights the ongoing danger for tens of thousands of Palestinians who live in an estimated 2,000 damaged buildings due to Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.
Rescue workers from the civil defense said at least 12 people, including five children, were killed and 14 others injured when the seven-storey building collapsed.
Nearly 100 more people were believed to be trapped under the rubble, around 50 are believed to be children.
The United States hammered home a message touting its energy dominance at Tuesday's meeting of G20 energy ministers in Houston, while brushing past the consequences of Washington's war in Iran and environmental concerns.
The meeting's slogan to "Unleash the full potential of American energy" has been repeated by US officials tirelessly in Texas since the gathering kicked off Monday.
Members of US President Donald Trump's cabinet say his policies are a reversal of his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, with Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) chief Lee Zeldin accusing Biden of participating in "climate alarmism" by promoting renewable energies.
"The whole idea was to produce enough energy for prosperity at home, but to be able to provide secure, affordable, reliable energy for all of our allies," Interior Secretary Doug Bergum said.
To help meet the growing demand for electricity, driven by the needs of the artificial intelligence industry, the EPA announced a reduction in limits on pollution from gas- and coal-fired power plants, sparking outcry from environmentalists.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned on Wednesday "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous" attack on Mecca, which a Saudi-led coalition blamed on Yemen's Houthis.
"The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he said on X.
The Houthis have denied attacking Islam's holy city.
Israel will 'finish job' in Gaza and 'remove Palestinians'
Israel's defence minister said Wednesday it was only a matter of time before the country resumes full-scale war in Gaza and moves to force out its two million Palestinians—a war crime.
Israel Katz, who is known for xenophobic and horrific remarks, was responding to criticism from another right-wing contender ahead of 27 October elections.
Katz said 70 percent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population by the Israeli war.
He said that an October 2025 ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump had "supreme value for all Israelis" by leading to the return of remaining hostages and ensuring "a commitment by the United States" to disarming Hamas.
"We all understand that this is not going to happen—and the IDF is prepared, once given the directive to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan," Katz said in a statement, referring to the Israeli military.
He said earlier this month that Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the two million people would go.
Nearly all of Gaza's population has been internally displaced and most of the territory lies in rubble after the war.
Forcibly displacing a population under occupation is consider a war crime and crime against humanity.
The war with Iran cost the US military around $38 billion as of August 1, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday, with billions more potentially added to the price tag each month the conflict wears on.
"As of August 1, 2026, the armed conflict with Iran has cost (the Department of Defense) approximately $38 billion," said the CBO in a report, referring to the war that started after US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran from late February.
It added that depending on the intensity of violence, costs per month could range between $2-$3 billion or more if the conflict continued.
The overall figures reflect the cost of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle and increased fuel costs for the military, among other factors, the report said.
The price of replacing munitions used through August 1 was estimated at $21.7 billion, with CBO noting that such replacements have been the largest single component of costs incurred by the Defense Department in the conflict.
The "main opportunity cost" for the department meanwhile has been the depletion of missile defense interceptors, leaving the United States with reduced inventory for several years.
Comparing the reported expenditures of missile defense interceptors with total numbers the department has bought suggests the United States "has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025," the CBO warned.
For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president's desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it's time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming a locally made munition was used to target the warplane.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military mobilisations in the airspace of Marib province," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes.
He said the jet had been targeted "using a locally made air-to-air missile".
The spokesman also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy city of Mecca this week.
"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July.
The group have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and have been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The strait has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: Germany’s rearmament push runs through America
articles.body:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth stands alongside German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius during an honor cordon welcome ceremony at the Pentagon in Washington on Sept. 15, 2026. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
WASHINGTON — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius came to the Pentagon on Wednesday with a dilemma: Berlin wants a stronger, more self-reliant European military, but much of what it needs comes from the United States.
Pistorius is in the U.S. this week after earlier being rebuffed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Berlin is seeking direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.
"Germany is strengthening its defense capabilities and acts as a driving force in Europe," Pistorius said at the Pentagon alongside Hegseth. "We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the U.S. and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe over time."
Advertisement
He said Germany has increased its defense spending to $147 billion this year — up by 25% compared to 2025 — and has almost tripled it over the last decade.
The two signed a statement of intent on defense-industrial cooperation covering joint production, licensed manufacturing, maintenance hubs and supply-chain resilience. What the document did not contain were concrete projects, timelines or investment commitments.
Despite efforts by Germany and other European countries to build up their defense industries and reduce dependence on the U.S. in areas such as long-range missiles and satellites, much of the new defense spending is ending up with American companies.
On Friday, Pistorius will travel to Fort Worth, Texas, for the rollout of Germany’s first Lockheed Martin F-35A fighter jet, arguably the most significant weapon in the Bundeswehr’s modernization drive. Berlin has ordered 35 aircraft, with pilot training beginning next year in Arkansas and deliveries scheduled through 2029. Officials are already discussing a potential follow-on order of 15 more jets.
The F-35 is more than another procurement program. It secures Germany’s role in NATO nuclear sharing, unlocks new operational capabilities and ties the Luftwaffe into the alliance’s rapidly growing community of F-35 operators.
And it is only one example of reliance on U.S. arms-makers.
Advertisement
Germany’s rearmament increasingly runs through American production lines: CH-47F Chinook transport helicopters, P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, Patriot air-defense systems and key technologies for the future F127 air-defense frigate.
Hegseth praised Germany's higher defense spending and said it was a key step toward what he calls "NATO 3.0" — the idea that European allies will bear more of the burden of defending the continent while the U.S. pivots to other areas of the world.
“Europe must assume primary responsibility for its conventional defense,” he argued.
Transatlantic divide
But the views of Berlin and Washington are diverging.
Pistorius underlined that the major danger facing the continent is Russia, calling it “the greatest threat to the alliance, the West, and our way of life since the height of the Cold War.” He also cited challenges from Iran, North Korea and China.
The German minister stressed Berlin's continued support for Ukraine. The Trump administration has halted almost all new military aid to Kyiv since taking office.
Advertisement
Hegseth identified no specific threats and underlined that President Donald Trump's main mission was "American manufacturing, American made, American jobs."
For now, Germany's rearmament drive dovetails with that vision. Pistorius said: "Germany is investing and buying in the U.S., adding up to about $50 billion, creating growth and jobs in the United States of America."
But Germany is using its own resources and teaming up with other European countries on defense projects. Berlin is also increasingly frustrated that the U.S. is favoring its own needs — boosting production of Tomahawk missiles to rebuild its own stocks depleted by the war against Iran — which is delaying potential deliveries to Germany.
Berlin sees the Typhon launcher system and Tomahawk cruise missiles as essential for deterrence against Russia. The acquisition would give Germany something it has never possessed: the ability to strike targets deep behind enemy lines with conventional land-based precision weapons. The problem is that the capability Germany wants depends entirely on American production.
“I made it very clear that the timelines previously discussed are too slow from our perspective,” Pistorius said after raising the issue with Hegseth. The Americans, he added, had “taken note of this positively.”
Hegseth is leading a rethink of U.S. force posture in Europe, and the Trump administration has already pulled troops out of Germany. Asked after their meeting whether he had gained greater clarity about future U.S. deployments, Pistorius was blunt: “No, not yet.”
Advertisement
Pistorius insisted that buying more U.S. weapons would not undermine Germany's effort to boost its own capabilities.
Instead, Berlin wants German firms integrated into American supply chains, maintenance networks and licensed-production arrangements. Throughout the visit, Pistorius emphasized that German industry could help relieve production bottlenecks and expand capacity on both sides of the Atlantic.
"NATO needs to become more European in order to stay transatlantic," he said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calling it a 'red line'
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca, calls it a 'red line'
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Houthis on Wednesday of launching an attack on the holy city of Mecca, which the Iran-backed rebels denied. Saudi Arabia, a US ally which has been the target of large-scale Houthi strikes since early September, declared Mecca a “red line” as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city, as the region responded with condemnation Wednesday but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key US ally, declared Mecca a “red line” as slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
With the world’s biggest oil exporter under fire from the rebels backed by the Saudis' regional adversary, the kingdom needs a safe outlet for its crude as well as military assistance. There's no clear path to either.
A crucial Saudi pipeline has been shut down, reportedly for weeks, after an attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Houthis have been targeting infrastructure in the kingdom and its shipping on the Red Sea, where they have seized several islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices remain above $100 a barrel.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometres (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Mohammed.
The attacks are the first test of a new defence pact among Saudi Arabia, NATO member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan. But officials from Turkey and Pakistan told The Associated Press they have not received a Saudi request for support in response to the Houthis' escalation.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Turkish official said efforts to “institutionalize” the alliance need to be completed before the pact becomes operational. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.
Amid the condemnation of the attempted attack on Mecca, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said his country and the Saudis stand “unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder”. Turkey's foreign minister expressed solidarity and said no country can “remain indifferent”, state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
Criticism also came from the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, representing over 57 Muslim states, which said the attempt violates the “sanctity of holy sites”.
This was the second attempted attack by the Houthis against Mecca after the rebels fired a ballistic missile toward the city in 2017, according to Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the rebels.
Saudi Arabia has been in talks with allies in hopes of replenishing its stock of interceptors, which has been depleted because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, according to two regional officials.
Read moreSaudi crown prince seeks neighbours' backing as Houthi attacks rattle Red Sea oil routes
The officials said the Saudis have asked allies, including France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt, to deploy air-defence teams to help defend against missiles and drones.
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media.
One of the officials said the Saudis turned to European and regional allies because the United States has seen its own stock of interceptors depleted.
A second official said Saudi Arabia is also seeking to rally its regional and international allies to launch a collective response against the Houthis. “But the decision now is to give diplomacy a chance,” he said, noting the roles of Oman and Egypt in the process.
The United States has sold billions of dollars in weapons to Saudi Arabia and has committed to other support, but top US officials have indicated a lack of desire to get involved in the conflict.
US Vice President JD Vance on Monday said Washington had been in “constant contact” with the Saudis and had “engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis.”
When asked whether Saudi Arabia had requested intervention, a US official said the US military’s Central Command has a task force in place for “enhancing intelligence sharing and planning support with Saudi forces”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
CENTCOM last week hosted senior military leaders from eight countries at a conference in Germany to discuss “opportunities for enhancing security cooperation in the Middle East”, the official also said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The official did not confirm which countries attended.
On the ground, forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government have said they are regrouping to combat the Houthis after fleeing the rebels' advance. But those forces are a collection of armed groups with varying aims.
Later Wednesday, the rebels claimed, without offering evidence, that they shot down an F-15 fighter jet operated by the Saudi-led coalition over Yemen’s central province of Marib.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree didn’t say when it occurred, and the AP could not independently verify the claim. The rebels at times take days to claim attacks.
Spokespeople for the Saudi-led coalition and the Saudi government didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
While Saudi Arabia appeared to face the choice of pursuing diplomacy or taking the fight to the Houthis, the top diplomat for rival Iran was in China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi called on the US and Iran to exercise restraint and reopen the Strait of Hormuz as soon as possible, and expressed China’s concern about the spread of the fighting to Yemen and the Red Sea, according to China’s foreign ministry.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a statement after the meeting that Tehran seeks “the restoration of calm to the region and friendly and peaceful relations with our neighbors”.
“In this regard we have begun dialogue with the countries of the region,” he added.
China has avoided direct involvement in the war, but President Xi Jinping at the BRICS summit in New Delhi over the weekend again offered Beijing's help in ending it.
Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered somewhat as tankers risk using a route near Oman on the other side of the waterway, with guidance from US forces. Estimates vary because ships can turn off location systems but range from 5 million to 7 million barrels per day on average.
That's less than half the amount before the war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Lithuanian MEP: Europe must stop being afraid to respond – opinion
articles.body:
Russia’s hybrid war against Europe did not begin with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, nor in recent years. The Kremlin intelligence services have been conducting hostile operations across Europe since Vladimir Putin came to power.
For too long, Europe has failed to respond adequately. Some worried that a stronger response would provoke Moscow. But the opposite has happened. The Kremlin interprets hesitation and fear of escalation as weakness, inviting further aggression. Every weak response teaches the Kremlin that it can test the next boundary, create more disruption and chaos inside our societies without facing consequences serious enough to change its behaviour. Putin goes as far as he is allowed to go. Fear of escalation has not prevented escalation: it has further encouraged it.
Europe is a target of Russian hybrid warfare that is becoming increasingly less hybrid. It combines military and non-military tools often designed to remain below the threshold of open armed conflict, including cyber operations, disinformation, economic coercion, sabotage and weaponising migration. The line between hybrid and conventional warfare has blurred. We hear daily about acts of sabotage and sabotage attempts on our infrastructure and drones violating our airspace and even being laden with explosives, like in Leipzig. Around elections, Russian cyberattacks, and disinformation campaigns intensify. GPS jamming and spoofing are everyday occurrences in Europe’s eastern border regions.
Russia remains the primary threat to Europe’s democratic integrity. It targets us through information manipulation and hybrid interference. By deploying hundreds of thousands of fake social media accounts, particularly around elections, it seeks to influence people’s minds, portray Russia as strong and invincible, and amplify narratives and candidates favourable to the Kremlin.
Russia does not act alone: it has partners in authoritarian states such as Belarus, China, Iran and North Korea. Belarus, for example, has weaponised migration at the EU’s borders, with over 36,000 coordinated crossing attempts recorded in 2024. In the Baltic Sea, Chinese-linked vessels have been involved in incidents damaging critical data and electricity cables.
Russia, its allies and its proxies must face real consequences, not just condemnation. We need a common threat picture, stronger tools, greater preparedness, real operational capacity and the will to use them. Any violation of a member state’s sovereignty must be met with effective retaliatory measures.
EU member states have yet to develop a coordinated response to hybrid warfare nationally, at European level and, where relevant, with NATO.
Europe’s eastern flank is its first line of defence, and we need faster implementation of the Eastern Flank Watch, an EU initiative intended to strengthen surveillance and defence along the bloc’s borders with Russia and Belarus.
We must also introduce tougher rules for Russian passport holders entering the EU. The minimum is to ban entry for anyone serving in Russian security and intelligence organisations, including former members who have fought in Ukraine.
The EU must use its economic and diplomatic power to stop the de facto Russian fleet from operating and bypassing sanctions. The owners and operators of these ships must be penalised. Furthermore, the consequences for damaging critical underwater infrastructure (CUI) must be significantly increased to serve as an effective deterrent.
We need better intelligence-sharing, more resources to counter disinformation and stronger protection of our critical infrastructure. But most of all we need sanctions that hit Russia’s economy at the heart.
Since the beginning of Russia’s attack on Ukraine, the EPP Group demanded decisive sanctions, but the Council’s step-by-step approach was slow, and the Russian economy had time to adapt. Kremlin propaganda claims sanctions do not work. This is false. Sanctions do work but require stronger enforcement and bolder measures.
In July, EU adopted 21st package of sanctions against Russia. By the end of the year, Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) will be banned from the EU and pipeline gas imports will be phased out by 30 September 2027. The European parliament strengthened the European Commission’s initial proposal towards a ban on oil and its products, ending long-term contracts sooner than originally proposed.
These are welcome decisions, but more must be done. The European Parliament’s proposals are set out in the report that the plenary adopted on 16 September. Europe can be strong if it wants to. But this resolve is challenged by a huge, lying Russian propaganda machinery.
European leaders must stop fearing the measures needed to defend our security. Today, Ukraine is an example of the will to defend and to win. So are Moldova and Armenia, which have faced massive hybrid attacks using every tool in Moscow’s arsenal, and whose leaders and people have nevertheless stood firm.
Rasa Juknevičienė is an MEP from Lithuania, EP rapporteur on Hybrid warfare

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian general eliminated in occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, military says
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian general eliminated in occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, military says
Key developments on Sept. 16:
- 'In his nighttime lair' — Russian general eliminated in occupied Donetsk Oblast, military says
- Partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant producing missile components
- 40% of Ukrainians ready to relocate if conditions deteriorate 'significantly' this winter, poll reveals
- Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion
- Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense
- Ukraine hits Russian bomber in occupied Crimea, General Staff says
Russian Major General Anton Grunis, commander of Russia's 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade, was killed in a Ukrainian drone strike in the occupied part of Donetsk Oblast, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, confirmed on Sept. 16.
"The general Grunis was eliminated on Sept. 12, 2026, in his nighttime lair in the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk Oblast," "Madyar" said.
The 427th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade "Rarog" carried out the strike with their drones, Brovdi said.
Apti Alaudinov, commander of Russia's Akhmat special forces and deputy head of the Russian Armed Forces' Main Military-Political Directorate, also confirmed Grunis's death, according to Russian independent outlet Astra.
In July, Grunis personally briefed Russian President Vladimir Putin on Moscow's claimed capture of Kostiantynivka, one of Ukraine's fortress cities in Donetsk Oblast. Ukraine's General Staff and President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected the claim, saying Russian forces had not captured the city.
Brovdi said Grunis was the seventh Russian commander at brigade, division, or army level whose death had been confirmed following strikes by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
read also
Partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant producing missile components
An agent of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh sabotaged the power supply to an electronics plant in the Russian city of Voronezh, the group said on Sept. 16.
The facility produces components used in Kh-101 and Iskander-K missiles, as well as Pantsir-S1 air defense systems, according to Atesh.
"Our agent, after a long study of the facility, detailed planning, and searching for weak points, managed to infiltrate an electrical substation near the VZPP-Sborka plant," Atesh said. "After bypassing security, he destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the enterprise and safely left the city."
The sabotage caused a voltage surge and cut power to the plant's workshops, the group said. Atesh also claimed that restoring full electricity supplies took several weeks, disrupting deliveries of key electronic components and delaying the production of Russian missiles and air defense systems.
Atesh did not disclose when the operation took place, saying it delayed publication to protect its agents.
Voronezh, a city in southwestern Russia, lies roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
VZPP-Sborka is a Russian manufacturer of semiconductors, integrated circuits, and power modules whose components are used in several Russian weapons systems, according to Ukraine's military intelligence.
40% of Ukrainians ready to relocate if conditions deteriorate 'significantly' this winter, poll reveals
Some 40% of Ukrainians are prepared to relocate this winter if conditions in the country deteriorate significantly, according to a new poll released by the Gradus agency on Sept. 16.
The survey, conducted by Gradus on Sept. 4–7, polled 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18–60 living in cities with more than 50,000 residents, excluding the occupied territories and areas with active hostilities.
In the lead-up to winter, Ukrainians are preparing for Russia to once again target the country's energy infrastructure in an attempt to make the country unlivable.
Russia has already escalated its attacks on Ukrainian businesses in recent weeks, targeting supermarket distribution centers, postal facilities, gas stations, warehouses, railway infrastructure, industrial plants, and Black Sea ports.
According to Gradus polling, safety is the main factor that would prompt Ukrainians to relocate. However, only one in five respondents said they would consider going abroad — the rest would look for temporary relocation within Ukraine.
"Most" respondents said the decision to relocate would not be prompted by a "single inconvenience" but by multiple factors, such as infrastructure disruptions, safety concerns, and lack of access to healthcare, education, and other essential public services.
"There is an important shift in how Ukrainians are approaching the coming winter: they are increasingly less likely to see resilience as the ability to endure any hardship indefinitely," sociologist Evheniia Blyzniuk, Gradus' CEO, said.
"People are not panicking about possible difficulties, but nor are they relying on the assumption that things will somehow work out. They are assessing risks and preparing backup options."
read also
Russia plans new prison complex in occupied Kherson Oblast among wider prison expansion
Russian authorities plan to build a new prison complex in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast under a program to construct seven such facilities across Russia and occupied Ukraine by 2035, The Moscow Times reported on Sept. 16, citing a Russian government program.
The new facilities will combine pretrial detention centers with penal colonies of different security levels and will have a combined capacity of more than 20,000 people, according to The Moscow Times. The capacity includes 5,380 places for pretrial detainees and 15,120 for prisoners serving sentences.
Apart from the occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Russia plans to build the complexes in Kaluga, Astrakhan, and Tyumen oblasts, Buryatia, and Zabaykalsky Krai, while the first is expected to open in Tatarstan by 2030.
Each facility is expected to cost between 13 billion and 20 billion rubles (around $154 million and $237 million), The Moscow Times reported.
Russia's Justice Ministry estimated that concentrating detention centers and penal colonies in the same complexes could reduce the cost of holding prisoners and detainees by 25-30%, allowing the projects to pay for themselves within about a decade.
Ukraine approves more than 80 companies for private air defense
Eighty-one companies are now authorized to form private air defense units amid near-constant Russian attacks on Ukraine, particularly Kyiv and the surrounding area, the Defense Ministry said on Sept. 16. 
As Russia shifts its bombardment tactics to near-hourly drone attacks throughout the day, increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure, more businesses are joining the program, bringing the number of units up by 30 since July.
The ministry said the program is designed to protect workers and facilities while reducing pressure on military air defenses, which now face increased strain beyond concentrated overnight barrages.
Established by the Cabinet of Ministers in November 2025, the private air defense program allows businesses to voluntarily form and finance air defense groups staffed by trained and certified civilian employees. Eligible companies include providers of essential services such as electricity, water, transport, and communications, alongside security firms protecting other businesses.
Companies apply to the Defense Ministry for authorization, then agree with the Air Force command on their units' operations. Under rules introduced in March, participating businesses can also temporarily receive military air defense equipment and ammunition unused by combat units, with Air Force approval.
Private air defense is just one component of Ukraine's multi-level system of airspace protection.
The first successful interceptions under the program were announced in March, when a company's unit downed Russian drones in Kharkiv Oblast. In April, the ministry reported a private group's first interception of a jet-powered Shahed-type drone.
By mid-July, private air defense had downed more than 50 Shahed and Zala drones, according to the ministry.
read also
Ukraine hits Russian bomber in occupied Crimea, General Staff says
Ukrainian forces have hit a Russian Su-24 fighter jet at Saky air base in occupied Crimea alongside other targets in strikes between Sept. 15 and Sept. 16, the General Staff said on Sept. 16.
The General Staff said the Russian Su-24 was hit, and the extent of the damage from the strike on Saky air base in occupied Crimea was still being assessed.
The Sukhoi Su-24 is a Soviet-developed twin-engine tactical bomber still in use by both Ukrainian and Russian forces.
Near the city of Donetsk, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian drone launch and storage site, according to the General Staff.
Ukrainian forces further struck three ground control stations for Russian drones in Staromlynivka and Pokrovsk in Donetsk Oblast and in Pokrovske in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the General Staff said.
Additionally, the General Staff reported hitting an ammunition depot in Luhansk Oblast, as well as fuel and lubricant storage bases in Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.

articles.title: The West has tried everything except ending the war
articles.body:
On 6 May 2022, I began using the term tsunami of ripple effects to describe the cost of not intervening in a war that threatens the security of the Alliance. That was NATO's own strategic ambition—right up until the Madrid Summit in June 2022, where it found its political will and military capabilities wanting, deterred by Russia.
The latest wave of that tsunami reached American voters this month, in the price of diesel—and the US President's response shows exactly how the refusal to end the war keeps compounding its costs.
Diesel, and the president who blamed the victim
President Trump has urged President Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel-supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel US diesel prices to a record high, according to CNBC.
"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said during an official visit to Ireland. "Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel because he's causing a shortage of diesel. This isn't done by the Middle East; this is done by what's happening with Russia and Ukraine."
The claim inverts the evidence. The latest IEA assessment is unusually clear: the US-Iran war and the disruption of Middle Eastern flows are the dominant shock, with Gulf refined-product exports down almost 60% since February.
Disruptions to Russia's refining system and the near-halt in Russian product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks, the IEA says, "have compounded these losses." The aggressor is responsible for the dominant shock; the war Trump himself helped start accounts for most of the rest; and the victim's attempt to force Russia toward peace has only reinforced the consequences of that aggression.
Yet Trump singled out Zelenskyy—not Putin for starting the war, not himself and Prime Minister Netanyahu for the war against Iran.
Ukraine has intensified the tempo of its refinery-strike campaign and improved its targeting to cause maximum pain to the Russian oil industry, striking at least 26 different Russian oil refineries since the beginning of 2026, according to ISW. The strikes have put roughly half of Russia's refining capacity offline and prompted widespread fuel shortages, with Moscow recently extending a ban on diesel exports through the end of September to stabilize domestic supplies.
The lie, the contradiction, and the lack of credibility
Trump's statement is an outright lie—the link to the US/Israel war on Iran is clear for anyone to see—and it is in direct contradiction with US and European policy.
As late as early July, Trump noted that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were an escalation capable of bringing the war to an end. The reversal appears driven primarily by the fuel-price shock and its political consequences—not by any change in his assessment of the strikes' military value. US consumers have seen a roughly 20% increase in diesel prices in a matter of weeks, midterms are seven weeks away, and the Republican Party is struggling in the polls.
And Ukraine's strikes aim at the exact effect Western sanctions were designed to achieve: ensuring Russia cannot afford to continue the war by undermining its economy. Neither the US nor Europe is supposed to import Russian crude or refined products—the EU banned them, cutting Russia's share of EU oil imports from 25.8% in 2021 to 2.2% in 2025, and the US prohibited them in March 2022.
"The United States is taking sweeping action against Russia's key source of revenue for funding its brutal and illegal war against Ukraine," Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said in January 2025. That is exactly what Ukraine is doing—with the difference that when Ukraine does it, Trump calls it "hurting the world."
The tsunami of ripple effects
Diesel is only the latest wave. During the year after Madrid, I watched the West take the role of bystander to a war that is all about us—a Russian ever-escalating hybrid war against European NATO members—seemingly accepting the global consequences.
I say seemingly because it makes no sense to sit idle while the tsunami grows to the point where it causes political, economic, and geopolitical chain reactions impossible to predict and difficult to control.
Inaction is not neutral. It is also a choice, and it carries the consequences of engagement with one crucial difference: inaction makes us react to the strategic environment, whereas action lets us shape it.
Aid without an endpoint is not a policy for ending the war; it is a policy for enduring it.
Enduring it is what produced the tsunami: the reverberations that raise the cost of living, undermine food and energy security, and spread famine, recession, inflation, and rising interest rates—increasing the risk of social unrest, extremism, and, ultimately, the fall of governments. Europe is living through the biggest refugee crisis since the Second World War.
he international security architecture is being dismantled, the institutions meant to unite us are discredited, and NATO no longer deters Russia—raising the risk of direct conflict between Russia and Europe.
In June 2023, I argued this would likely change the political landscape in the US and Europe—as in the 1930s—as political forces sought to exploit voters' frustration over the war's global effects. It produced President Trump and a rising tide of right-wing forces across Europe—the leading edge of what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called, at Davos, a rupture the world hasn't yet reckoned with: "We understand that this rupture calls for more than adaptation. It calls for honesty about the world as it is... We know the old order is not coming back." Its consequences for Europe have not yet dawned on us.
How to end it
The only way to end the tsunami of ripple effects is to end the war. Waiting only lets it reach the scale where it produces chain reactions impossible to control.
Since 2014, the West has tried to stop Russia's war through diplomacy, negotiations and ceasefires; sanctions and economic pressure; diplomatic isolation; military aid, training and intelligence; NATO deterrence and reinforcement; and humanitarian and financial assistance. More than 200 negotiations were held to stop the war from happening.
They were all futile, because Russia was never negotiating in good faith—it sees negotiation as a means to defeat its opponents. Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.
For a negotiation to succeed, it must solve the cause of the war: Russia's Great Power ambitions, its pursuit of strategic parity with the US and China at the expense of its neighbours. Until that is checked, there will be no peace—and those ambitions are not negotiable. They can only be denied through military power.
The West has done everything short of military intervention. It is time to employ military power, because the cost of continuing the present path is far too high. If Europe wants to turn the tide, it must become proactive. Instead of waiting for the war more intelligence services are warning about, Europe—or rather a Coalition of Like-Minded European countries—must help shift Russia's appraisal of the strategic environment. We need to intervene militarily to end the war, and the tsunami of ripple effects with it.
Editor's note. The opinions expressed in our Opinion section belong to their authors. Euromaidan Press' editorial team may or may not share them.

articles.title: A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
A crisis on two fronts: Saudi Arabia's mounting security dilemma
A drone attack launched from Iraqi territory last week against Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline to the Red Sea has revived the prospect of a two-front confrontation for Riyadh.
As the situation in Yemen spirals further out of anyone’s control, Saudi Arabia’s options for managing both fronts are narrowing.
The Houthis have completed their takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing Mocha and the islands of Perim, Zuqar, and Hanish, which command the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
While the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive has since shifted toward Marib and Jawf, the front lines remain fluid.
A second front opens
On Thursday, several drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline south of Medina, causing injuries and damage and forcing Riyadh to shut the pipeline as a precaution.
The Saudi foreign ministry said the drones had been launched from Iraq and would not retaliate “at this stage,” at the request of Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
Baghdad dismissed the commander who led operations in Missan province after an investigation traced the drones to launch platforms near al-Shib, on the Iranian border, and closed three crossings, Shalamsheh, al-Shib and al-Mandali, to stop the attackers fleeing into Iran.
Al-Zaidi has accepted an Iranian request for a joint investigation. No group has claimed the strike, and an alliance of Iran-backed factions has denied hitting the pipeline.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq called it “an honour that we do not claim”. Shalamsheh and al-Shib reopened to passenger traffic on Sunday, though not yet to trade, with a full reopening due by Thursday.
It is not the first time Riyadh has traced an attack on its oil infrastructure to Iraq. On 29 July, US and Saudi forces struck Iran-aligned Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) factions accused of hitting Saudi facilities in the Eastern Province. Twenty PMF fighters and five Iranian advisers were reportedly killed. Riyadh called it self-defence.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq initially threatened retaliation over the July strikes before backing down under pressure from Iraqi figures, including Hadi al-Amiri. Diplomatic efforts through August did not stop last Thursday’s attack.
The Shia Coordination Framework in Baghdad remains divided over how to disarm Iran-backed factions ahead of a 30 September deadline. Part of the problem is that some factions are deeply embedded in Iraq’s security apparatus and maintain close ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
That disarmament push may not even solve the underlying problem. Tamer Badawi, an Iraq analyst and associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab that the Islamic Resistance in Iraq’s denial, if it “proves accurate,” could mean Iran’s Quds Force “may be conducting attacks via new groupings”.
Even if known factions like Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada disarm, “other new and unknown groups can launch transborder attacks from Iraqi territories”.
Baghdad, Badawi added, lacks “consistent control over the Iran-aligned groups” and the “ground-to-air capabilities” needed to stop such strikes.
“It’s most certainly the case that there is coordination between Tehran, armed networks in Iraq, and Ansarallah,” he told The New Arab, though it is “taking much less of a public and celebrated appearance” than when Iraqi factions and Ansarullah synchronised attacks against Israel after 7 October.
The Institute for the Study of War described the strike as part of “a coordinated effort with other Axis of Resistance members to coerce Saudi Arabia to meet Houthi demands by attacking Saudi energy infrastructure”.
The same assessment linked the attack to the Houthi campaign around Bab al-Mandeb, saying the Houthis are “setting conditions to establish” the strait “as an Axis of Resistance-controlled body of water,” which it called “unacceptable for US national security and economic interests”.
Saudi strategy under pressure
The latest Houthi offensive began on 3 September across Taiz and Hodeidah, producing Yemen’s biggest territorial changes since a 2022 truce halted the civil war. It also undoes years of Saudi effort to reduce exposure.
Riyadh led a coalition against the Houthis from 2015, scaled back after a costly air campaign, and pursued a peace roadmap from 2023.
Direct hostilities resumed in July, after Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport and the Houthis blockaded Red Sea ports. Last Tuesday, Houthi missiles and drones hit four southern Saudi cities, injuring at least 73 people. Riyadh has relied on tens of thousands of Yemeni troops rather than deploy its own.
The Houthis claimed a fresh strike of their own on Sunday, saying they hit weapons depots and command centres at the Sharurah military base in southern Saudi Arabia. An Iranian commercial vessel was struck the same day in the Strait of Hormuz, a reminder that Riyadh’s other maritime exit remains unsettled too.
Those forces have struggled for familiar reasons. Coordination between units has been patchy, reinforcement mechanisms weak, and Saudi air support limited. Someone still has to fight on the ground, and the units expected to do that are the ones already exposed as weakest.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG), said the Houthis’ hold on Bab al-Mandeb has already changed their leverage.
“It’s clear that the Houthis now have a greater influence over the Bab al-Mandab,” he told The New Arab. “It also gives them room to expand toward the other side of Yemen and further weaken the government forces that Saudi Arabia is supporting.”
Nagi said Riyadh has few good options left. “I don’t think the Saudis have many good options to contain the situation now,” he said.
“Things have basically gone from bad to worse. If they want to contain it, they’ll probably have to make some concessions, because the Houthis are now negotiating from a much stronger position.”
That bind predates last week’s advance. Reversing the Houthi gains risks pulling Saudi Arabia back into the ground war it spent a decade trying to leave. Leaving them unanswered risks losing the coastline and the pipeline’s approach to Yanbu for good.
Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the risk advisory firm Basha Report, said that “the situation on Yemen’s West Coast remains fluid”.
The coalition, he told The New Arab, “appears to have resumed limited airstrikes against Houthi positions,” while the Southern Giants Brigades and National Shield Forces “have stabilised a new defensive line south of the strait,” with units withdrawn from the coast regrouping elsewhere.
Houthi casualties from the offensive that ended 9 September are “heavy,” though unconfirmed.
Washington stops short
The Houthi advance has already pushed Riyadh to seek military help it said only two months ago it did not need. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called President Donald Trump twice on Thursday as Saudi-backed forces retreated, asking in the second call for the US to authorise strikes against the Houthis. Trump declined.
Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM chief, travelled to Saudi Arabia on Thursday, and around 200 US personnel are now in the kingdom, with more than 100 focused on intelligence and targeting, according to reports.
In practice, Riyadh is managing the war largely alone, with indirect support, limited airstrikes, stronger air defences, and a parallel push for Oman-mediated talks.
That mix of escalation and diplomacy is not necessarily a contradiction. It reflects a Saudi calculation that military pressure and a negotiated off-ramp serve the same goal, keeping the Houthis from consolidating gains without a return to the costly ground war Riyadh spent years trying to exit.
Saudi oil route comes under pressure
The pipeline gives Saudi Arabia only a partial way around Hormuz. It lets crude bypass the strait and reach Yanbu, but tankers carrying those exports south still have to cross the Red Sea toward Bab al-Mandeb. Bypass capacity, in practice, is not secure supply.
Markets are already registering some of that risk. Saudi Arabia’s benchmark stock index fell 1.3% on Sunday, and Aramco shares 1.6%, as investors weighed the pipeline’s precautionary shutdown. Reuters put the exposure at roughly 4% of global oil supply.
The Houthis say their blockade targets only Saudi vessels. Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels a day in August to 6 million bpd, its lowest level in three decades, according to the International Energy Agency, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab al-Mandeb.
Nagi sees a deliberate logic behind the timing. Iran, he argued, has a clear interest in pressuring Saudi Arabia while Hormuz is already disrupted, and in hitting Saudi energy exports via the Yanbu reroute now within Houthi reach.
It also challenges the regional order Washington has been building ahead of the midterms.
“That obviously benefits Iran at this moment,” he said, “because it gives Tehran another way to put pressure on its regional adversaries and the global economy.”
Regional test
The escalation is also testing the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement Saudi Arabia signed with Pakistan and Turkey in August, committing each to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Whether it extends to an Iraq-origin attack is untested.
The East-West Pipeline was built to solve one problem, Saudi Arabia’s exposure at Hormuz. It is now exposed from both directions. Drones from Iraq can hit the infrastructure carrying crude to Yanbu, while Houthi forces at Bab al-Mandeb can threaten the ships carrying it onward.
That vulnerability-reduction strategy has instead multiplied where Riyadh can be tested.
But the coordination of strikes looks strategic more than operational. Tehran does not need to order a specific attack for it to serve the same purpose as the Houthi campaign at Bab al-Mandeb.
Confirmation of an operational link between the two fronts would turn this from two crises into one campaign against the infrastructure Saudi Arabia built to feel safe from either.
For now, Riyadh is reinforcing Yemeni forces, working with Baghdad to trace last week’s drone attackers, and leaning on Oman’s channel with the Houthis.
It is, for the moment, a strategy of management rather than resolution.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors
Follow him on X: @frencio_schiavi
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Russia’s Lavrov Threatens Europe With a ‘Very Short’ War
articles.body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said a war between Russia and Europe would be “very short” if European countries attacked Russia.
“If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short,” Lavrov said on Wednesday, according to Russia’s state-run TASS news agency.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian foreign minister insisted that Moscow was neither preparing for nor interested in a military confrontation with Western countries. His remarks came as European governments have increasingly discussed strengthening their defenses against potential Russian aggression.
Lavrov also repeated Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning that Moscow would view the deployment of foreign military forces to Ukraine as a declaration of war.
Several of Ukraine’s European allies have discussed a possible international contingent as part of future security guarantees.
Lavrov said any settlement of the war in Ukraine would require fulfilling what Moscow calls the original objectives of its “special military operation,” the Kremlin’s term for Russia’s full-scale invasion launched in February 2022.
Russia has repeatedly used shifting and broadly defined objectives to justify the invasion. Lavrov again blamed Western policies for the war, despite Russia having sent its troops across Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders.
He also accused President Volodymyr Zelensky of seeking to eliminate Russian language and culture from Ukraine. However, Kyiv rejects such allegations and says Moscow uses claims about protecting Russian speakers to justify its aggression.
Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant Faces Falling Water Levels, Blackout Risk, Ukraine Says
Lavrov additionally accused Western countries of attempting to interfere in Russia’s State Duma elections, both inside the country and abroad. He presented no evidence to support the allegation.
Poland and NATO against Russia
On Tuesday, Kremlin aide Nikolai Patrushev claimed Polish statehood would cease to exist within “two or three days” if Warsaw entered a military conflict with Russia.
“If Poland enters into military action against Russia, our country will use the entire arsenal of forces and means at its disposal, and Warsaw will cease to exist within two or three days,” Patrushev said.
Russia possesses one of the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles, but Patrushev did not explicitly refer to nuclear weapons in the quoted remarks.
His comments came in response to Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who said during the annual Yalta European Strategy conference in Kyiv on Sept. 12-13, that NATO would defeat Russia “quite quickly” if Moscow attacked the alliance.
“If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly,” Sikorski said.
The Polish minister pointed to NATO’s air power, estimating that European members of the alliance have about 2,500 military aircraft and describing their advantage over Russia as overwhelming.
Patrushev accused Sikorski of assessing Russia’s military capabilities in an “amateurish” way. He also claimed that Russian forces were not using their full potential in Moscow’s war against Ukraine, which the Kremlin continues to describe as a “special military operation.”
