articles.title: Leaked photos and munition depletion expose devastating toll of Iranian strikes on US bases
articles.body:
Leaked photos and munition depletion expose devastating toll of Iranian strikes on US bases
TEHRAN – A mounting body of leaked evidence and admissions from within the American defense establishment has shattered the Pentagon’s carefully curated narrative of invulnerability, revealing unprecedented devastation across US military installations in West Asia resulting from precision Iranian missile and drone strikes.
Photographic evidence obtained by CBS News and leaked directly by active-duty American personnel—deliberately bypassing rigid military censorship—provides the first conclusive visual documentation of flattened hangars, obliterated command infrastructure, and hollowed-out barracks across several regional bases.
At Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, photographic evidence confirms a catastrophic direct hit on a Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control (AWACS) aircraft, its tail severed and its radar-carrying fuselage gutted by flames. Similar scenes of ruin were documented at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a primary desert staging hub for US ground forces and armored units. The imagery starkly illustrates that conventional US blast fortifications, such as concrete “T-walls,” have proven utterly useless against the kinetic force of modern Iranian aerial operations.
The visual disclosures substantiate a damning report released by the US Department of War Inspector General, which disclosed military equipment losses amounting to $3.7 billion—including the destruction or heavy damage of nearly 60 aircraft. In its mandatory briefing to Congress, the watchdog confirmed that US Central Command (CENTCOM) sustained direct strikes across eight countries: Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan.
The disclosures have laid bare severe morale degradation and disillusionment within American ranks. Rebutting US War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s previous dismissal of Iranian projectiles as mere “squirters” breaching base perimeters, one deployed soldier admitted: “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face… We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”
Compounding Washington’s operational crisis is the unsustainable attrition of its high-end air defense umbrella. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, American forces burned through an unprecedented volume of critical munitions during a recent Iranian salvo targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. US batteries fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptors alongside more than a dozen THAAD systems to counter an attack of approximately 20 ballistic missiles—an expenditure equivalent to an entire week’s inventory in earlier phases of the conflict.
Despite launching over 70 multi-million-dollar interceptors, the layered defense failed to avert catastrophic failure. Iranian missiles equipped with warheads that separate into multiple sub-munitions penetrated the defensive net, scoring direct hits on US fighter jets and support aircraft stationed on the Jordanian tarmac.
Experts note that the air-defense math has decisively turned against Washington. While Pentagon officials publicly insist stockpiles remain adequate, the Inspector General’s report conceded that the conflict has induced “strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.” With manufacturer Lockheed Martin producing only 620 Patriot interceptors in 2025 against an annual target of 2,000, US interceptor stockpiles are being depleted at a rate Washington cannot sustain.
As Iran’s missile forces continue to demonstrate operational adaptation—employing maneuverable warheads, varied trajectories, and precise targeting—the combination of scorched hangars on the ground and dwindling stockpiles in US arsenals confirms that the era of Western military deterrence in the region has reached an irreversible tipping point.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Calls Mecca a ‘Red Line’ After Alleged Houthi Drone Attack
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia on Wednesday accused the Iran-backed Houthis of an attempted attack on Mecca, the holiest city in Islam and a site of pilgrimage for Muslims worldwide.
Colonel Turki Al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen, said that the Houthis launched a drone toward Mecca on Tuesday evening, but it was shot down by the Saudi Air Defense Forces before entering the city’s restricted airspace.
“The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line,” said Al-Malki, who warned that the Saudi-led coalition “will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures” against the Houthis.
Riyadh referenced a previous similar incident from July 2017, in which it accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca. The Houthis acknowledged launching a missile from Yemen, but said that it was aiming for the King Fahd air base in Taif.
The Yemeni militia group has denied the allegation, accusing Riyadh of spreading “false accusations” on Wednesday.
“There is no threat from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, and are far from the holy sites,” said Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree via Telegram.
The allegation comes amid a widening regional crisis. Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast are threatening shipping and energy supplies—already disrupted by the conflict in Iran— while drawing growing concern from the U.S. and other Saudi Arabia allies.
The religious stakes: Why Mecca is a ‘red line’
The past month’s escalation is only the latest development amid the wider civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemen government, which has been ongoing since 2014. But a confirmed attack on Mecca would undoubtedly be a turning point.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, whose country signed a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey last month, called on all parties to exercise restraint. He warned that the conflict was on the “brink of further escalation” and that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only sustainable path to peace.”
At the same time, he condemned the alleged attack.
“There are no words sufficient to express the depth of pain and sorrow we feel toward this unforgivable and shameful deed,” he said Wednesday.
Fawaz Gerges, a professor in international relations at the London School of Economics, questions what the Houthis would have to gain from such an attack. Over 1.7 million Muslims this year performed Hajj, their pilgrimage to Mecca, according to the Saudi government.
“For the Houthis, as a religiously dominant organization, this would be catastrophic for them—to target Mecca,” he tells TIME. “It’s a lose-lose for them.”
Gerges does, however, offer another explanation: “The Houthis are using drones and homemade missiles, so there is a real possibility that the Houthi drone basically misfired.”
In light of Riyadh’s allegation, Gerges assesses that “[Saudi Arabia] is trying to say that the Houthis are not just waging a political and geo-economic war against them, they are trying to target the most sacred religious site in Islam, and that resonates deeply.”
“Both sides are now engaged not only in military hostilities, but also for the hearts and minds of Arabs and Muslims,” he adds.
Houthi advances deepen the Red Sea oil crisis
The Houthis claimed that Saudi aircraft had carried out more than 450 airstrikes this week. The group also claimed, without providing evidence, that it had shot down a Saudi-led coalition F-15 over Yemen.
Houthi strikes, meanwhile, have been largely concentrated along the Yemeni border in the south. They have also made advances in the Red Sea, seizing key sites like Perim Island and the port of Mokha. The captures strengthen their control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—a pivotal shipping lane that could affect global trade and oil prices at a time when they are already under strain.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit lane, remains largely restricted amid continued strikes between the U.S. and Iran. Most recently, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said a vessel was struck by an unknown projectile on Monday.
Amid these regional developments, the price of Brent crude, the global standard for oil, climbed above $100 per barrel earlier this week. The price fell about 3% on Wednesday but remained above $105 a barrel. Experts warn that more strikes between the Saudis and Houthis will only drive up prices further.
“Pressure on global energy is already there, and I think it's just going to get worse,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa program, tells TIME.
Continued fighting this week “is going to start making the West bleed more efficiently over the next few weeks,” he says. “With winter, there will be a lot of need for energy and for heating.”
Pressure grows in Congress to end the Iran war
Amid precarious energy developments in the Middle East, sentiments about ending the Iran conflict seem to be shifting in the U.S. House of Representatives.
In what was its third vote on the matter this summer, three Republican Representatives changed their votes to align with Democrats in favor of a War Powers Resolution to end U.S. military action against Tehran. With a total of seven Republicans voting in favor, the resolution was approved with 220 votes, beating 204 against.
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Rep. Zach Nunn of Iowa, and Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina switched their votes in this latest round of considerations. Nunn said that Iran “must be held accountable” but that “with the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization.”
Nunn added: “I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran, and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.”
It is likely the last time the House will bring the matter to a vote ahead of midterm elections this November. But the vote is largely a symbolic gesture, as Trump would likely veto the resolution once it reached his desk.
As pressure builds in Washington to end the war with Iran, the Houthi escalation in Yemen is creating a new regional flashpoint for the U.S.
U.S. warns government personnel away from the Yemeni border
In response to growing security risks, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh prohibited American officials in Saudi Arabia from traveling near the Yemeni border as of Wednesday.
U.S. government employees are not permitted to travel within 20 miles of the border with Yemen, and they require special authorization from the embassy to travel to the regions of Jizan, Asir, and Najran in southern Saudi Arabia.
The embassy also published a travel advisory Tuesday, urging Americans to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia, citing armed conflict, Iranian missile and drone attacks, and renewed threats from the Houthis. Tehran has targeted multiple Gulf states housing U.S. military bases through the conflict, and has threatened U.S. energy assets in the region.
“Armed groups in Yemen have attacked Saudi border towns and other sites in Saudi Arabia with armed drones, missiles, and rockets. People near the border with Yemen are at increased risk. Do not travel to this area for any reason,” the embassy said in its advisory.
TIME has reached out to the White House and State Department regarding the recent developments.
Asked Monday if the Trump Administration was concerned about the recent Houthi advance and capture of Perim Island, Vice President J.D. Vance told reporters: “Concerned, certainly.”
“We’ve been in constant contact with the Emiratis, the Saudis, and others affected in the region. It’s something that the United States Administration is very much on top of,” he continued.
The Vice President added that there has also been direct communication with the Houthis. “We’re going to keep on monitoring it and making sure that America’s best interests are represented,” he said.
President Donald Trump claimed over the weekend that he had spoken with the Iran-backed militia. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with, and we’ll get that straightened out,” he told reporters during a visit to Ireland.
Following a threat from the Houthis to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in July, the U.S. President said, “If something like that happens, we take care of it.”
On Monday, a Houthi spokesperson said that the Strait “is free for navigation for all countries except for Saudi Arabia.”
Could the conflict widen?
Tuesday’s alleged drone attack toward Mecca has prompted international concern over regional escalation.
In light of the joint defense agreement signed between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, Al-Muslimi says that Ankara and Islamabad have greater political latitude to support Riyadh following the contested incident.
“Defending Mecca is going to create legitimacy domestically in their countries if they engage with the Saudis in a war against the Houthis,” says Al-Muslimi.
But Gerges suggests that support from Turkey and Pakistan would be largely ineffective, and therefore unlikely.
“The problem is how could Pakistan and Turkey really provide support since the armies are not integrated,” he says. “The key challenge facing Saudi Arabia is ground forces.”
Gerges notes that Riyadh’s aerial capabilities alone are not enough to inflict necessary damage on the Houthis.
Therefore, diplomacy could be the most viable option.
Gerges says that “the Houthis have proved to be very resilient, very dynamic, very resourceful, very nimble,” throughout the conflict, maintaining significant control in Yemen.
“Taking on the Houthis again in an all-out war, I doubt very much whether there is a viable military option,” he says.

articles.title: Kremlin-Favored Russian General Awarded Medal for Fake City Capture Dies in Action
articles.body:
Russian Major General Anton Feliksovich Grunis, a senior officer actively profiled in Kremlin media as a brilliant tactician and battle winner in Ukraine, has died in a reported drone strike, Ukrainian official military and independent news sources reported on Tuesday.
Grunis, 46, was a native of the central Russian region of Tatarstan. His combat service included the 2nd Chechen War, the 2008 Russo-Georgian War, Russia’s invasion and takeover of Ukraine’s Crimea region in 2014, Russian military operations in Syria in 2015, and Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine begun in 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Early reports of Grunis’ death surfaced in an encrypted Russian officer social channel called Surovovskoe Bratstvo on the messaging app Telegram. A death notice identified him as a graduate of the elite Kazan Suvorov Military Academy class of 1996, and comment by fellow students implied he died in combat.
Ukrainian information platforms led by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) General Staff rebroadcast the death notice and confirmed it. The Independent reports and official Ukrainian sources did not state when or how Grunis died. Official Russian information platforms by Wednesday had not mentioned Grunis’ alleged death at all.
Drone footage published by Ukrainian army sources on Wednesday identified 427th Unmanned Systems Forces Brigade “Rarog” as responsible for killing Grunis in strikes near the village Kindrativka, Donetsk region, on Sept. 12. Imagery showed kamikaze drones boring in and detonating inside buildings geo-located to that place and substantial fires, however, that content showed no conclusive evidence Grunis or any other Russian service member had been hit.
Russian Strikes Kill 6, Wound At Least 17 Across Ukraine
Promotional footage released by Russia’s Ministry of Defense on Aug. 28 showed a live Grunis being awarded Russia’s highest medal for bravery “Hero of the Russian Federation” for success in battle, and stating to interviewers that he was honored and confident in Russian victory in Ukraine.
Grunis’ reported demise follows a rash of deaths in the Russian army’s upper ranks, including Lt. Gen. Damir Davydov’s assassination in a June 9 car bombing, Maj. Gen. Valery Plokhotnyuk’s death in an Aug. 1 Moscow restaurant bombing, and the killing of Lt. Gen. Sergey Milchakov, commander of Russia’s 51st Combined Arms Army, in a Ukrainian six-missile precision strike hitting his command post in the Donetsk sector on Aug. 26.
More senior officers, including generals, may have lost their lives in the restaurant bombing and the headquarters attack, because dozens had gathered at both places, Ukrainian military intelligence spokesmen said.
Grunis had been a high-profile officer in Russia thanks to his appearances in state-run media profiling him as a tough, frontline fighter with the call sign “The Terrible,” and the man responsible for the capture of the major Ukrainian fortress city Kostyantynivka, in the east of the country.
Grunis’ command, the 4th Motor Rifle, in parallel content produced by Russia’s Defense Ministry and aired nationally, depicted the unit as an elite formation made up of Russia’s best soldiers, whose attacks with Grunis at the helm were unstoppable.
Grunis, in the June interview, praised his troops’ alleged skill in overcoming Ukrainian defenses with a hidden flanking movement through forests and swamps. The Ukrainian unit attacked by the Russians, the 156th Mechanized Infantry Brigade, was broken by infiltrating Russian foot soldiers supported by massed artillery and drone strikes that allowed a daring river crossing inside the city, Grunis claimed.
“All our units very quickly and successfully started operating on the left bank side of the city and exploited the success. As it worked out, we cut the city into pieces like a pie,” Grunis said. “Our great advantage was the Russian soldier. It is the dream of any commander, because no other army in the world has such soldiers as we do.”
Russian state television on July 3 aired video of Russian President Vladimir Putin receiving a formal report from his top general, Valery Gerasimov, that Kostiantynivka had fallen fully under the control of Russian forces thanks to Grunis’ 4th Brigade’s victory. Lower-ranking generals stood in the background were described in official media as a “command center near the front lines.”In fact, based on all other sources including official Ukrainian army statements, independent Ukrainian media, OSINT research groups, Western think tanks including the US-based Institute for the Study of War and six Ukrainian combat unit internal chat groups monitored by Kyiv Post and known to be deployed in the Kostiantynivka sector, Russian forces never came close to capturing the city and three months later it remains roughly under Ukrainian control.
The closest Russian forces came to pushing Ukrainian troops out of the city, per those sources, was with massed infiltration attacks in early July that sometimes isolated Ukrainian outposts in the center of the city for days before strike drones and assault infantry teams were able to locate the infiltrators and destroy them.Russian forces currently hold the southern districts of Kostiantynivka, Ukrainian forces’ fortifications in the north, and the center of the city is mostly a no-man’s-land out of the control of either side, those sources say. Reporting over the past week pointed to continuing Russian attempts to infiltrate foot soldiers into Konstantynivka’s Druzhivka suburb, with Ukrainian drone units operating in the vicinity claiming good results in attacking them.
Ukraine’s General Staff in a Wednesday situation update reported continuing Russian attacks in the Kostiantynivka sector with all assaults repelled. Unit information feeds for formations in that sector reported Ukrainian defenses within the city holding.
Ukrainian volunteer groups tracking Russian combat units and their members have, contrasting sharply with Kremlin messaging, long identified Grunis’ 4th Brigade as a troubled unit with soldiers complaining of officers’ extorting money in exchange for not being ordered on assault missions and soldiers’ unwilling to pay bribes or accept orders to make an assault, being locked in open-air pits until they change their mind. In a video, a man identifying himself as Sergei Moshchenko, a 4th Brigade rifleman, said that unit commanders ordered him and his mates to attack across open ground covered by Ukrainian drone swarms in an effective suicide mission, and that he and his buddies were new recruits with less than two weeks of training. During comments on Aug. 28, following the “Hero of the Russian Federation” awards ceremony, Grunis said he was “honored” to command “the best soldiers in the world.”

articles.title: Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month: CBO
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month: CBO
The six-month-old-and-counting US-Israeli war on Iran has cost $38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by $3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totaled expenses through 1 August.
The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.
The cost was close to the $37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on 21 July.
The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish US stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the US had used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the war.
The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly described President Donald Trump's attacks on Iran as "decisive action" to prevent Tehran from harming US personnel or interests. She said in a statement that the US military has "more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond.”
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell disputed the report's findings of munitions shortages and said, "We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing."
The cost inquiry was conducted at the request of the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.
“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded," Boyle said in a statement.
"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."
The report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on US military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.
Impact on US readiness
The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the US defense posture and the domestic economy.
The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving China and Taiwan, CBO said.
At the July hearing in the Senate, Hegseth pleaded for nearly $90 billion in emergency funding to restock munitions supplies.
“Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth said.
The Pentagon’s inspector general reported this week that Iran had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings on US bases in the Middle East as well as aircraft including fighter jets, refueling planes and drones.
It put the war cost through June 19 at $33.4 billion, saying the amount included about $184 million in damages to US diplomatic facilities from Iranian strikes.
Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz—the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war—and on energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices for consumers and global producers.
The rising cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating US fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed $40 trillion in August.
Trump regularly contrasts the Iran war with the illegal US invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the 11 September 2001 attacks.
The eight-year US war in Iraq, which involved more than 100,000 ground troops at its peak, cost $2 trillion, Reuters reported. The two-decade-long US conflict in Afghanistan, which also involved more than 100,000 troops at its most intense, cost $2.3 trillion, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.

articles.title: Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'We want our land back and to stop the genocide': Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
It was in mid-July when hundreds of activists gathered on the road leading up to the secretive military base in the heart of Australia.
They had arrived in the sleepy town of Alice Springs (Mparntwe) from across the country to demand the closure of a facility that has contributed to the historic dispossession of Indigenous Australians and is feared to be enabling the current displacement of Palestinians.
The US-led Pine Gap spy base has long been controversial in Australia. Since its establishment more than five decades ago, the facility has witnessed recurrent protests by activists opposed to the US military's presence and its occupation of land belonging to the Aboriginal Arrernte people.
But its presence has taken on a new significance since October 2023, when Israel began its genocidal assault on the Gaza Strip. Its activities remain shrouded in mystery, but it is believed to have played an important role in aiding the Israeli military in its destruction of the Palestinian enclave.
The three-day convergence, which took place on the 60th anniversary of the signing of the Pine Gap treaty, brought more than 600 pro-Palestine and anti-war activists, academics and politicians together with the Hayes family, the traditional custodians of the sacred land of Kuyunba.
The gathering culminated in hundreds marching to the base, chanting "From Arrernte to Gaza, Globalise the Intifada" and "Always was, always will be, Aboriginal land". At the gates, Arrernte Elder Felicity Hayes handed a letter to the local police chief asking for the land to be returned to its owners.
"We have every right to say we don't want this base here," Aunty Felicity told the inspector, before describing how her grandfather was taken advantage of to hand over the land without his consent.
Also among her requests was compensation for Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel has killed and injured almost a quarter of a million people since it began its assault in October 2023.
"Close the base because what it's doing is destroying other people's countries," she said. "We want our land back and to stop the genocide."
Nathalie Farah, a spokesperson for the convergence, said the protest was the largest at the facility since 1987. Farah, a Syrian-Palestinian activist in the Anti-Militarism Action Network, was among 100 people who had driven for four days from Melbourne to attend the gathering.
"We're very conscious of the fact that we can't stop what's happening in Palestine from Australia, but Australia plays a significant role in the system and if it can be stopped that system won't be as effective," she told The New Arab.
July's convergence was the third major protest to be held on the road to the base since October 2023, and it is unlikely to be the last.
Anti-war groups, trade unions and pro-Palestine activists are planning to hold rallies and events in cities and towns across the country on 20 September to protest the US military alliance, Israel's war on Gaza, and Australia's participation in AUKUS, the security partnership with the US and UK.
"What needs to happen is we need to build a proper anti-war movement here similar to what happened on this continent during the Vietnam war," Farah said.
From Australia to Israel
Australia's strategic position close to the Indo-Pacific has made the country an important location for US overseas military operations. In all, the US military controls 17 facilities in the country and has access to 75 more Australian-owned installations, according to recent research by the Nautilus Institute, an Australian think tank.
Northern Australia is of particular focus to the Pentagon. The US has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into building new military infrastructure in the area since 2024, making it the top overseas location for Air Force and Navy construction spending.
Pine Gap has attracted particular scrutiny because of the lack of oversight afforded to Australia's elected officials and its status as one of the most important American intelligence facilities outside the US.
The base, known officially as the Joint Defence Space Research Facility, is jointly operated by Australia's military and several American spy agencies, but Australian authorities are largely kept in the dark about the US's intelligence activities.
Classified US documents leaked by whistleblower Edward Snowden in 2013 revealed that the US National Security Agency (NSA) uses the facility to collect massive amounts of electronic signals and communication data. Intelligence is often used to identify military targets, including for drone strikes across the Middle East and Afghanistan.
Many suspect that Pine Gap has played a major role in the US's ongoing war on Iran, but the Australian government has remained tight-lipped.
The Snowden leaks also confirmed that Israel routinely receives intelligence from the NSA, with which it has eight intelligence-sharing agreements.
In 2023, investigative news site Declassified Australia published testimony from a former NSA employee who said that the base collects intelligence on Gaza.
"We know that signals intelligence data, captured by Pine Gap-controlled Orion satellites, has been historically made available to Israel," said Professor Richard Tanter, a senior research associate at the Nautilus Institute who is widely regarded as the country's leading expert on the base.
"Unless the Australian direct and indirect military relationship to Israeli activities in the Gaza Strip are closely reviewed by the Inspector General of Intelligence and Security, it is not possible for the Australian government to assure the parliament and the Australian public that Australia is not complicit in acts of genocide," he added.
"The base's intelligence-sharing with the Israeli military has been one of the key ways that Australia has failed to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention," Jorgan Doyle, a spokesperson for the convergence, told The New Arab.
Doyle is an organiser for Mparntwe for Falastin, a local pro-Palestine group set up after 7 October 2023 that has staged fortnightly rallies on the road to the base and held frequent events and vigils in the town.
He described the Australian government's approach to the US military relationship as "don't ask, don't tell", which he says is particularly problematic given expectations that the country will soon host nuclear-capable American bombers.
The Tindal air base, located 1,000 kilometres north of Pine Gap, is being expanded by the US to host up to six B-52 bombers, which are expected to arrive by the end of the year.
Political backing
The campaign has attracted support from the Australian Greens, whose senators have called on the government to rethink its military alliance with Washington. Lawmakers in the left-wing party have been staunch critics of the Israeli military's actions in Gaza and have called for cutting trade ties with Israel and sanctions on ministers in the government.
The Greens, while still a minor party, are currently polling in fourth with around 15-16% of the vote and hold 10 seats in the 72-seat Senate.
"We don't want to be a part of the United States's forever wars," Senator David Shoebridge told The New Arab.
The New South Wales senator attended the convergence and plans to submit the Hayes family's letter for a debate in parliament later this year. Among the family's demands are the closure of the base, the return of the land to its traditional owners, and the payment of compensation to the dispossessed Arrernte people and families in Gaza.
"First Nations owners of the land on which Pine Gap sits have never given consent to the US presence, they don’t want their land contributing to US wars and the killing we can all see in places like Iran, Palestine and Venezuela," Shoebridge said.
"Australians are watching as the US becomes an agent of chaos, causing instability and violence in the world… For the first time since the Iraq war, we have a mass movement of people in Australia taking a clear stance against US war and our government's role in them."
The campaign against Pine Gap comes as polls show falling support for the US among the broader public amid the chaos of the Trump administration.
Successive surveys have shown that, while the military relationship remains popular, Australian voters are increasingly supportive of a more independent foreign policy and are less willing to trust the alliance with the US.
A poll by the Lowy Institute in June found that just 21% of Australians have confidence in the US president. Meanwhile, the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre found that a third of the public believe that the second Trump administration has been very bad for Australia, while almost four in 10 see the US as mostly harmful for Asia.
Doyle, of Mparntwe for Falastin, said the convergence happened at a "really interesting geopolitical moment" amid shifting public opinion.
"We increasingly hear ordinary Australians becoming uneasy about the US alliance and Australia's place in the world," he said.

articles.title: A drone came down beside a Bundeswehr air base, weeks after Berlin blamed Moscow for the Leipzig airport attack
articles.body:
A large-scale police operation is underway after a drone of unknown origin crashed 1 kilometer from a Bundeswehr base, German media outlet Bild reported on 15 September.
Drones have repeatedly flown over German military bases, and German prosecutors are already treating one August find near Ukraine-bound cargo as attempted sabotage. Germany's military counterintelligence has tied repeated sabotage on German soil to Russia, with high probability. Neither the owner nor the origin of this drone is known. Russia has denied involvement in earlier incidents, some of which Germany has officially attributed to it.
Discovery near airbase triggers large-scale search
Parts of the drone were found east of Lake Steinhude, the media outlet said. The crash site is one kilometer from the Bundeswehr's Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, the German military confirmed to the outlet. The drone crashed in an open, uninhabited area, the state criminal police office said. After the debris was discovered, authorities launched a large-scale search operation in the area to find additional parts of the UAV, according to Bild.
Investigators do not yet know who owns the drone
The search continues, and the state criminal police office says there are so far no indications of a danger to the public. Investigators learned about the discovery on Monday and want to analyze any other drone parts they find to determine its origin, the media outlet reported. Only then could more be said about the circumstances of the crash, it added.
Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
Drones have been spotted over Bundeswehr bases many times
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the number of reports of drone sightings has "increased significantly" and become "more consistent," a spokesperson for the Bundeswehr Operations Command told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) in August.
"Overall, several hundred suspected drone overflights have been reported in the area of the German Armed Forces in recent years," the command spokesperson told RND.
What came before this crash
Germany is the busiest front in Russia's covert campaign in Europe. A Semtex-laden drone turned up beside a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, and investigators this month named a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal. Berlin blamed Moscow and ordered Russia's Bonn consulate closed.
Two Bulgarians were arrested over a September arson at a Munich building site between two defense-tech headquarters, a day after two attempts to sabotage the power grid that Germany has not attributed. Germany suspects a planned assassination of a Bavarian drone maker's boss, watched by agents hired for single jobs.
The throwaway agents Moscow sent after a Bavarian drone boss arming Ukraine—and how Germany stopped them
Not every strand leads to Moscow. German military counterintelligence this week attributed part of the drone activity over Bundeswehr sites to Chinese intelligence.
Elsewhere the tempo holds: Polish prosecutors have opened more than a hundred espionage cases in 20 months, and in the Netherlands a former commander of US Army forces in Europe said Russian saboteurs attacked the rail network and tried to kill him, which Dutch Railways said they knew nothing about.

articles.title: Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow
articles.body:
Ukraine's air defense forces have put another Western-supplied system to work as the country prepares for a fifth winter of Russian aerial strikes on its energy grid, Militarnyi reported. The 38th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment released the first public footage of the Italian-Swiss Skyguard/Aspide on combat duty.
Ukraine enters the 2026-2027 heating season with an interceptor gap that keeps widening. Patriot deliveries fell from 675 in 2023 to 364 last year and 264 projected for 2026, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. F-16 pilots have resorted to gun-only sorties when missiles run out. Every additional short-range system that covers drones and cruise missiles frees scarce high-end interceptors for the ballistic threats Russia keeps sending.
Ukraine just showed the system in action
The Ukrainian unit posted a video of crews loading missiles onto the launcher and the system standing watch.
The system arrived through two European pipelines. Spain delivered the first batch in November 2022, then-Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov confirmed. A month earlier, 19 Ukrainian troops had trained on the system at Spain's Zaragoza base. Madrid also asked Switzerland for re-export permission, Texty reported, since the Swiss firm Oerlikon Contraves — now Rheinmetall Air Defense — built the Skyguard fire control unit the missiles are paired with.
Italy pledged additional Skyguard units in February 2023. The Italian launchers differ from the Spanish ones. They carry a target-illumination radar and a TV tracking unit mounted directly on the launcher.
A Cold War-era missile in a drone war
Skyguard/Aspide, a related variant of Italy's Spada, is a short-range air defense system built to guard military sites and critical infrastructure from aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. It pairs a Swiss fire control unit with Italian Aspide missiles derived from the American AIM-7 Sparrow, a radar-guided weapon the US Navy developed starting in the late 1940s to shoot down jet bombers during the Cold War. The system can engage targets at distances up to 12–25 km and altitudes from 15 m to 6,000 meters.

articles.title: ‘Weeks’ Without Power: Partisans Claim Sabotage Hit Russian Missile Components Plant
articles.body:
The Atesh partisan movement said it carried out a sabotage operation at an electrical substation serving the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Assembly (the VZPP-Sborka plant) in Voronezh, Russia, which produces electronic components for Russian missiles and air defense systems.
According to Atesh, a partisan agent spent an extended period reconnoitering the site, planning the operation, and identifying security vulnerabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He eventually infiltrated the substation near the plant and damaged the main distribution cabinet supplying power to the facility before leaving the city.
The partisans said the statement was published with a delay to protect the safety of Atesh agents.
The sabotage caused a major voltage surge and power outage across the plant’s workshops. According to the partisans, restoring full power to the facility took weeks, during which delivery deadlines for key components were missed, delaying production of the missiles and air defense systems.
The claims could not be independently verified.
The Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Assembly is a key manufacturer of electronic components for Russian military systems.
The plant produces integrated circuits, power switches, and power supply units for the onboard computers and navigation systems of Kh-101 missiles; automation components and control units for Iskander-K missiles; and semiconductors for the radars and fire-control systems of the Pantsir-S1 air defense missile-gun complex.
CARTOON: Ukraine Continues to Hold Firm Despite the Pressure From Both Ends
“Putin does not plan to stop the war, despite massive losses, and is preparing for a broad mobilization. The Russian army and Putin’s regime must be stopped for the greater good,” the report added.
Plant previously targeted in Ukrainian missile strike
The reported sabotage follows a June 22 Ukrainian strike on a Voronezh facility producing electronic components for Russian precision-guided weapons.
Ukraine’s General Staff said that Air Force units had struck a facility that was part of Russia’s defense-industrial base and produced components for missile guidance systems, onboard computers, and air defense equipment.
Russian independent outlet Astra, citing OSINT analysts, identified the likely target as the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Assembly, a claim later confirmed by the Ukrainian military.
Ukraine said the strike was intended to reduce Russia’s ability to manufacture precision-guided weapons used against Ukrainian targets.
The General Staff said high-precision air-launched cruise missiles were used in the attack but did not specify the type. Some Russian pro-war Telegram channels claimed Storm Shadow missiles may have been used, although Kyiv has not confirmed these claims.
Russian regional authorities confirmed an attack on Voronezh, saying air defenses had intercepted multiple aerial targets.
Russian pro-war blogger ZAPISKI VERANA (Veteran Notes) claimed the strike caused fatalities, although this was not confirmed.
“Their number is being determined, but judging by the fact that the strike occurred on Monday in the middle of the workday, the consequences will be dire,” he wrote.
Astra also reported that the Voronezh Regional Blood Center announced a shortage of donor blood following the strike, but about two hours later, said that additional donors were no longer needed.
