articles.title: Kiev loses some 1,300 troops along engagement line in past day — Russia’s top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 16. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost some 1,295 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 220 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, more than 210 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and over 155 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost more than 380 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 290 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and up to 40 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
Russian forces thwart Ukrainian attempt to break out of encirclement
The Russian Armed Forces thwarted a Ukrainian military group’s attempt to break out of the encirclement near Gogino in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"[Russian servicemen] destroyed enemy manpower and equipment around the settlements of Serdobino, Khripuny, and Buzovo in the Kharkov Region. [The Russian military also] thwarted a Ukrainian assault group’s attempt to break out of the encirclement near the settlement of Gogino in the Kharkov Region," the statement said.
Air defenses down 71 Ukrainian drones over Russia overnight
Air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones over Russia overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Overnight, on-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 71 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the Bryansk, Kaluga, Oryol, Rostov, Astrakhan and Krasnodar Regions, Crimea, and over the Black Sea," the statement said.
Russian forces hit Kiev facility producing vehicles for Ukrainian military
The Russian Armed Forces hit the Kiev Motor Transport Enterprise, which produced specialized vehicles for the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Last night, the Russian Armed Forces carried out drone strikes against military-industrial facilities and ports in Ukraine, as well as against naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian military. As a result of the attacks, the following targets were hit: in Kiev, an industrial enterprise (the Kiev Motor Transport Enterprise PubJSC) that manufactures specialized vehicles intended to equip the Ukrainian military <...>," the statement said.
Russian forces hit dry cargo ship in Chernomorsk port
The Russian Armed Forces struck a dry cargo ship with military supplies in the port of Chernomorsk in the Odessa Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Odessa Region, at the port of Chernomorsk, a dry cargo ship with military supplies was hit," the statement said.
Russian air defenses intercept 258 Ukrainian UAVs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 258 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past 24 hours, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 589 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 236,847 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,935 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,778 multiple rocket launchers, 36,470 field artillery guns and mortars and 72,033 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.
Russian forces hit Ukrainian fuel, energy transport sites used by military
The Russian Armed Forces struck Ukrainian fuel and energy and transport infrastructure facilities that were being used by the Ukrainian military over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The Russian Armed Forces’ operational-tactical aviation, strike drones, missile forces, and artillery hit Ukrainian fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian military, fuel depots and military equipment storage facilities, drone assembly and storage sites, as well as temporary deployment sites of Ukrainian servicemen and foreign mercenaries in 147 areas," the statement said.
Over 600 Ukrainian soldiers eliminated in Kharkov Region in September
Russian troops have eliminated more than 600 Ukrainian army personnel within an encirclement in the Kharkov Region since the beginning of the month, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In total, since the beginning of the month, over 600 Ukrainian personnel, 15 armored combat vehicles, 9 motor vehicles, 13 quad bikes, and 23 ground-based robotic systems have been destroyed within the encirclement," the news release reads.
While expanding the outer control zone, strikes were delivered against Ukrainian units near Prikolotnoye, Petropavlovka, and Novoaleksandrovka in the Kharkov Region.
Russian forces continue fighting to liberate Malaya Volchya in Kharkov Region
Units of the Russian Battlegroup North in the Kharkov Region continue tightening the encirclement of Ukrainian forces and expanding the outer control zone. Fighting for the liberation of the settlement of Malaya Volchya inside the encirclement continues, the Defense Ministry said.
"Units of the Battlegroup North in the Kharkov Region continue tightening the encirclement of enemy forces and expanding the outer control zone. Fighting for the liberation of the settlement of Malaya Volchya in the Kharkov Region continues inside the encirclement," the ministry said.
Ukraine loses up to 50 troops in Kharkov Region encirclement over past day
The Ukrainian army lost up to 50 troops in the encirclement in the Kharkov Region over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Ukrainian forces lost up to 50 troops, two Western-made armored fighting vehicles, a car, and two ground robotic systems within the encirclement over the past 24 hours," the statement reads.

articles.title: Pentagon’s Iran war costs hit $38 billion in five months – budget office
articles.body:
Pentagon’s Iran war costs hit $38 billion in five months – budget office
The US war with Iran cost the Pentagon approximately $38 billion in its first five months, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO). The bill could rise by another $2 billion to $3 billion for every additional month of fighting – and by more if hostilities intensify.
In a report released on Tuesday, the CBO estimated Defense Department expenses from the start of US combat operations on February 28 through August 1. The figure includes the estimated cost of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, as well as additional flying hours, military operations, and higher fuel costs.
The office said its estimate was “subject to considerable uncertainty” because the Pentagon did not provide the requested information, forcing analysts to rely on government databases and publicly available reports. The estimate also excludes the cost of repairing damaged US bases, military casualties, future veterans’ care, and expenses borne by other federal agencies.
Another month of conflict would cost about $2 billion if violence remains at the “low and sporadic” levels seen in May and June, the CBO estimated. If operations return to their July intensity, the monthly bill would rise to about $3 billion. Costs could be higher still if the conflict escalates further.
Billions of dollars’ worth of US weaponry has been used up in the conflict. The CBO estimates that replacing munitions used through August 1 would cost $21.7 billion, including $7.3 billion for land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for missile-defense interceptors and $1.2 billion for other weapons.
The Trump administration asked Congress in June for $87.6 billion in supplemental funding, including $67.1 billion for the Defense Department. The CBO assessed that $42.3 billion of the overall request appeared directly related to the Iran war.
The report was released as CBS News published photographs showing extensive damage caused by Iranian missile and drone strikes on US positions across the Middle East. The images were provided anonymously by active-duty service members because of military restrictions on contact with the media.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told CBS News.
The photographs showed a destroyed E-3 Sentry surveillance aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, along with damaged buildings and burned-out vehicles at US facilities in Kuwait.
The Pentagon inspector general separately reported that US forces had suffered $3.7 billion in equipment losses through late June. Nearly 60 manned and unmanned aircraft were damaged or destroyed, according to the watchdog.
Trump said last month that the conflict was costing the United States “relatively little.” His remark came as fighting continued, despite his repeated declarations of victory. Trump proclaimed “total and complete victory” in early April and has since repeatedly claimed that Washington won or was close to ending the conflict.
The war has faced mounting domestic opposition and criticism over the administration’s decision to conduct hostilities without congressional authorization. The House voted for a third time this week to limit US military involvement, approving a war-powers resolution by 220 votes to 204. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure.
Separately, International IDEA reported that key measures of US democracy have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years. The organization said the Trump administration’s actions had weakened the rule of law both domestically and internationally, while warning more broadly that democratic erosion increases the risk of conflict.

articles.title: U.S. uncovers network that plotted assassinations of Russian ‘dissidents’ in Washington and Vilnius. Among the suspects: an ex-colonel with Putin ties, his FSB officer son, and a Cuban dancer.
articles.body:
U.S. uncovers network that plotted assassinations of Russian ‘dissidents’ in Washington and Vilnius. Among the suspects: an ex-colonel with Putin ties, his FSB officer son, and a Cuban dancer.
U.S. authorities announced the discovery of a criminal network tied to Russian intelligence services, dubbed the RIS Network, that recruited operatives to assassinate Russian opposition figures and carry out sabotage attacks in countries allied with Ukraine. Five people — citizens of Russia, Cuba, and Venezuela — have been charged, the U.S. Justice Department reported.
According to the indictment, RIS Network members have organized attacks and killings in countries around the world, including the United States, since at least 2024. Washington links the group to Russian intelligence services that carry out operations abroad, including killings of Russian “dissidents” and defectors, and, more recently, sabotage attacks in countries Russia considers allies of Ukraine.
The defendants include:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63, a Russian national known as “Colonel Yuri,” a retired colonel in Russia’s security services who has boasted of working alongside Putin in his youth
- his son, Kirill Khrameev, 27, an officer with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB)
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, a Cuban national described as an “an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia”
- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, another Cuban national also known as “Viking,” who lives in Russia
- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, a Venezuelan national living in Russia.
The indictment says Durruthy handled logistics and coordinated the network’s attacks, including operations in Lithuania and the Czech Republic, while Suarez and Castro recruited operatives to surveil and kill an unnamed Russian “dissident” living in the United States.
All five face charges of conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a sentence of up to 20 years in prison. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro are also charged with conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, punishable by up to 10 years in prison. None of them has been detained.
Investigators say the group tried to organize two assassination attempts targeting opposition figures in the U.S. and Lithuania
The first case involves a “a prominent Russian dissident” living in the Washington, D.C., area whose name has not been disclosed. In the summer of 2026, recruiters enlisted a Venezuelan citizen living in the United States to surveil him; he supplied several photographs and videos of locations connected to the opposition figure. Recruiters then offered him $40,000 to carry out the killing.
Investigative journalist Christo Grozev said this marks the first fully documented assassination attempt organized by Russian intelligence on U.S. soil. ”[T]here’s always been an unwritten rule to not conduct assassinations on each other’s territory. Clearly the old rules don’t apply.,” he added.
The second case centers on an attempt to assassinate an unnamed critic of the Russian government living near Vilnius. In 2025, a U.S. citizen living in Lithuania was hired to surveil the opposition figure. Yuri and Kirill Khrameev contacted him, claiming the target was “spreading dirt” about Russia and “distorting history.” The indictment says the younger Khrameev recruited the prospective agent while his father negotiated the assignment and payment. The agent was ultimately paid $200 for surveillance, then offered about $25,000 to kill the opposition figure.
The elder Khrameev discussed specific methods of attack with the American, suggesting, among other things, “throwing a bottle of gasoline” or “sticking a knife” in him. The U.S. citizen ultimately refused to carry out the killing, and Khrameev then suggested he instead carry out sabotage attacks against countries helping Ukraine.
The indictment states that the group recruited others for sabotage as well.
Journalists at the German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle found that Durruthy organized a series of arson attacks across four European Union countries using “disposable agents.” Most of the operatives he recruited online were from Spanish-speaking countries, and the investigation discovered that some were tricked into taking part in the sabotage.
According to DW, Durruthy instructed agents in 2024 to set fire to construction material warehouses in Poland, a bus depot in the Czech Republic, a waste processing plant in Romania, and Lithuanian-made equipment intended for Ukraine. Lithuanian authorities subsequently put Durruthy on an international wanted list.
The DW investigation also determined that Durruthy has lived in Russia for at least seven years, teaching Latin American dance in Petrozavodsk. In 2022, he married a Russian woman and subsequently obtained a Russian passport. DW was unable to establish when or under what circumstances he began cooperating with Russian security services, though one theory holds that he had run into financial trouble.
The Kremlin declined to comment on the accusations from the U.S. Justice Department, stating it had “not heard or seen any coherent evidence or argumentation based on anything tangible.”
What Yuri Khrameev is known for
Anti-corruption expert Ilya Shumanov and the outlet Agentstvo studied Yuri Khrameev’s old interviews and leaked data to piece together details of the colonel’s biography. Here’s what they found:
- Khrameev was born in the Tambov region. He graduated from the Novosibirsk Higher Military Command School in 1986 and served 10 years in special units of the Internal Troops, including deployments to various “hot spots.”
- He has been described as the first commander of the Northwestern OMON (riot police) unit and head of a combined police detachment from the St. Petersburg Internal Affairs Directorate in Chechnya. The human rights group Memorial reported that in January 2001, security officers under Khrameev’s command detained Shamil Shaipov, a resident of the village of Goyty, who was later found dead.
- In interviews from the early 2000s, he complained about theft by his superiors and described awards he had received, including some presented to him personally by the president.
- Khrameev himself was removed from his post as deputy commander of the OMON in 1994 in connection with a fraud case, but continued serving in the internal affairs agencies until at least 2017. Until 2011, he was deputy battalion commander at the St. Petersburg and Leningrad region Internal Affairs Directorate.
- From September 2023 to June 2025, Khrameev worked as general director of the private security firm “Tornado.” That same year, the retired colonel said he “visits the SVO once a month.” In May 2026, he met with students at School No. 1 in Pikalyovo, in the Leningrad region, billed as “a participant in every local conflict from 1986 to the present.”
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russian military receives sniper rounds assembled with American and Finnish components
articles.body:
Russian weapons manufacturer Promtekhnologiya, which produces sniper rifles and ammunition under the ORSIS brand, has begun supplying the Russian military with domestically assembled cartridges using high-precision bullets made in the United States and Finland.
The Insider previously reported that Russian snipers were using bullets made in NATO member states — either fully assembled foreign cartridges or hand-loaded ammunition put together by snipers themselves. Now, new evidence indicates that, in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a Russian arms manufacturer is receiving enough Finnish and American bullets to assemble sniper ammunition for Russian military units.
Previous investigations found that more than 10 million bullets made in NATO countries were imported into Russia between March 2022 and February 2024. A significant share were high-precision bullets in .338 Lapua Magnum and .375 CheyTac calibers, which are designed for long-range shooting. Those quantities are small compared with the overall scale of the war, but the imported bullets are nonetheless important for Russian snipers.
Promtekhnologiya was founded by Russian oligarch Konstantin Nikolaev, who built the weapons company with the backing of two key officials: Dmitry Rogozin, then the Kremlin’s key figure overseeing the defense industry, and FSB General Sergei Beseda.
Nikolaev’s businesses produce weapons in Russia and import ammunition from the European Union and United States through sanctions-evasion channels. And yet, he has continued to develop business interests in Italy, where his Tuscan winery has not been seized and even continued receiving subsidies from the European Union during the full-scale war.
Finnish Lapua and American Hornady bullets for Russian snipers
On April 6, 2026, the pro-war Telegram channel Bolshoy Panda (lit. “Big Panda”) reported that Russian snipers had begun receiving ammunition for ORSIS rifles from the Russian Defense Ministry that had been made with American Peterson cartridge cases and American Hornady bullets.
“The cartridges are formally considered hunting ammunition because they do not have a GRAU index, but these are the rounds supplied with the ORSIS 5000 rifles as standard ammunition for our guys. The bullet is a 178-grain Hornady OTM weighing 11.53 grams, the case is Peterson, I don’t know whose powder it is, and the manufacturer is Promtekhnologiya LLC.”
After testing the rounds at a firing range, the channel’s author praised their accuracy and consistency:
“At 300 meters from my Volkodav, 10 bullets went into the head-sized gong like kids going to school, practically one on top of another. Consistency is at a high level, with minimal variation in velocity. ... In principle, these are among the few more or less factory-made cartridges that honestly deliver 0.5 MOA from my Volkodav.”
A grouping of 0.5 MOA, or half a minute of angle, means that at 300 meters the shots in a carefully aimed series landed within a circle about 4.5 centimeters, or 1.8 inches, across.
Three days later, the channel published a clarification:
“There are currently extremely few cartridges in the configuration described above. At the moment, 6V12 sniper rifles are supplied with ammunition using Scenar bullets” — made by Finnish company Lapua — “weighing 11.53 grams, Irbis 570 powder and cases marked ORSIS.”
The post indicates that because there were not enough American bullets to supply the Russian military, Promtekhnologiya turned to Finnish components to continue producing sniper ammunition.
From Austrian Glocks to Finnish bullets
The first official evidence that Promtekhnologiya was using Finnish bullets and cartridge cases dates to December 2019 — five years after the European arms embargo on Russia was imposed. At the time, journalists from Kalashnikov magazine tested a new ORSIS .308 Winchester cartridge at a shooting range. The ammunition used 12-gram Lapua Scenar HPBT precision bullets and Lapua cartridge cases, both made by the Finnish manufacturer.
The journalists noted that assembling the ammunition in Russia from foreign-made components reduced the cost:
“The ORSIS cartridge, assembled entirely from high-quality foreign components, costs an impressive 400 rubles at the Bars store in St. Petersburg — more than the vast majority of its competitors on the shelf, but less than Norma or RWS cartridges, some versions of which cost more than 500 rubles.”
Unofficial reports of Russian precision ammunition go back to 2014, when firearms forums began advertising ORSIS cartridges made with Finnish Lapua cases, Lapua Scenar bullets, and Finnish VihtaVuori powder.
Promtekhnologiya, founded in 2009, was built with extensive European and American expertise. Between 2012 and 2015, the company pursued three projects aimed at localizing foreign weapons production in Russia.
In July 2012, it signed an agreement with Austria’s Glock GmbH to assemble fourth-generation Glock 17, 34, and 35 pistols from Austrian components. The first trial batch assembled in Russia totaled more than 2,000 pistols. Although the localization project was officially terminated after Russia’s annexation of Crimea, the Podolsk plant continued receiving products from its former Austrian partner for years afterwards. The latest known shipment came in November 2023, when Promtekhnologiya imported 100 Glock 43 pistols and 100 Glock 19 Gen5 pistols.
In 2013, Promtekhnologiya announced cooperation with the American company ArmaLite. The plan was to assemble semiautomatic AR-10 and M-15 rifles in .223 and .308 calibers using American components and Russian-made barrels. Although the agreement with the U.S. company was terminated, several years later the Moscow Region plant said it had fully localized production of its own AR-10 version.
After the 2014 arms embargo on Russia was announced, the factory also began assembling Marocchi Si 12 inertia-operated shotguns in Podolsk made with components supplied from Italy. The Italian manufacturer’s loose sanctions compliance may have been influenced by the fact that one of its vice presidents was a Russian citizen, Oleg Benedichuk.
Who brings American and Finnish bullets into Russia
The Soviet defense industry, and later Russia’s, focused on mass-produced weapons and did not manufacture high-precision bullets, which are made to tighter tolerances for weight, shape, and balance than bullets made for assault rifles and machine guns. As a result, sniper bullets show less variation in trajectory from shot to shot.
They also typically have more advanced aerodynamics, including a higher ballistic coefficient, and higher-quality jackets, allowing them to retain velocity at longer ranges and reducing the effects of wind. As a result, they produce tighter shot groups and more predictable ballistics than standard military bullets, which are optimized primarily for reliability and cost rather than maximum accuracy.
The Insider has found evidence of American and Finnish bullets being used in the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine by both Wagner mercenaries and regular Russian military units.
In Russia, precision rifle bullets in .308 Winchester and .338 Lapua Magnum are produced by the Barnaul Cartridge Plant, the Novosibirsk Cartridge Plant, and Tekhkrim, among others. But both sniper-rifle manufacturers and shooters themselves say American and Finnish bullets provide better accuracy than those made in Russia.
Previous investigations by The Insider found that more than 10 million bullets made in NATO countries entered Russia between March 2022 and February 2024. A significant number were precision long-range bullets in .338 Lapua Magnum and .375 CheyTac calibers. The bullets are critically important for Russian snipers.
There are indirect signs that some shipments of American bullets reached Russia through the European Union.
For example, on June 8, 2022, the Russian company LLC IF Tetis (ООО «ИФ „Тетис“») received a Russian declaration of conformity covering a shipment of American Hornady bullets. The declaration stated that testing documents for the bullets had been issued on April 28, 2022, by Finland’s Lapua Test Shooting Lab under protocol No. 393/16.
After a series of reports by The Insider revealed the large-scale smuggling of European weapons, Russia’s Federal Accreditation Service stopped publishing declarations for a number of customs codes, making it more difficult to calculate precisely how many weapons and rounds of ammunition are imported into Russia. Numerous social media and specialized forum posts, however, indicate that new shipments are continuing.
On Jan. 28, 2026, the Orel weapons retailer announced a new shipment of Hornady ammunition on Telegram. The store is part of a group of companies controlled by arms businessman Mikhail Khubutia, a partner of Italy’s Beretta Holding.
In the Milya group for ammunition sales, seven advertisements from five users offering Hornady bullets were posted between Aug. 31 and Sept. 4 alone.
EU subsidies for an FSB-linked businessman
The technology and equipment for the weapons plant in Podolsk came from Europe despite the company receiving political backing at the highest levels of the Russian state. Until 2012, Promtekhnologiya’s deputy chief executive was Alexei Rogozin, the son of Dmitry Rogozin, who was then the deputy prime minister responsible for Russia’s defense industry and state arms procurement. (After public accusations of a conflict of interest, Alexei Rogozin left the company. He was later replaced by the deputy prime minister’s nephew, Roman Rogozin.)
A 2018 investigation by the independent outlet Novaya Gazeta linked Promtekhnologiya owner Konstantin Nikolaev to the family of FSB General Sergei Beseda. A Panama-based company linked to the general’s son, Alexei Beseda, received 187 million rubles from Nikolaev-controlled entities and a 25% stake in a joint venture producing thermal-imaging sensor arrays.
In 2013, the same year Nikolaev’s Cyprus offshore company paid more than $5 million to the son of the FSB general and Promtekhnologiya signed its rifle-assembly agreement with ArmaLite, Nikolaev bought the La Madonnina winery in Tuscany’s Bolgheri wine region.
The winery is located near the renowned Italian estates Sassicaia and Ornellaia, whose standing in the wine world can be compared with Ferrari and Lamborghini in the automotive industry. Nikolaev invested about €40 million in La Madonnina.
The winery is owned by the Cyprus company Cetrezza Trading, which until recently belonged to British Virgin Islands-based Cedar Circle Holding Limited, whose beneficial owner was Nikolaev himself.
Ownership of Cetrezza has since passed to the Magic Forest Trust, whose owners are not publicly disclosed. The Cyprus company nevertheless retained links to the oligarch even after the formal sale. Cetrezza owned an 85% stake in the Enoteca Tognoni wine boutique in Livorno, while Nikolaev himself held 5% of the company’s share capital until 2024.
While Nikolaev-linked companies manufacture weapons in Russia and bring ammunition into the country from the United States and European Union, his Tuscan winery has not only avoided seizure but continued receiving EU subsidies.
Over the past 10 years, La Madonnina received €135,600 in subsidies from European Union agricultural funds, including €107,800 paid after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In theory, EU rules require member states to identify the ultimate beneficiaries of public funding. In practice, however, inquiries to Italy’s Financial Intelligence Unit and to the National Anti-Corruption Authority found that the databases used by regulators do not contain information on the ultimate owners even of some Italian companies, let alone foreign entities.
As a result, Italian oversight agencies are effectively unable to establish the connection between the Tuscan winery and a man who has publicly described himself as its owner in multiple interviews.

articles.title: Russia ships armor to Libya despite mounting vehicle losses in Ukraine
articles.body:
After the Russian convoy docked in Tobruk, a column including armored personnel carriers, mine-resistant vehicles, and at least three Tornado-U armored trucks was seen heading west from the port in imagery published by the open-source intelligence project Russia Maritime Watch, as reported by Militarnyi.
The armor delivery comes as Russian forces have lost more than 10,000 armored and protected vehicles in Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, Britain’s defense chief said. Africa Defense Forum reported that Moscow is funding work at six Libyan air bases, some of which support the movement of weapons and personnel toward Sudan and the Sahel. Russia’s Africa Corps already supports military governments in the Sahel, including Mali’s, while a Russian-operated base in Libya has supplied Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The cargo ships Anastasiia and Yuriy Arshenevskiy carried the shipment, while the Aleksandr Shabalin, a Russian Navy landing ship capable of transporting vehicles and troops, provided an armed escort, according to Militarnyi.
All three vessels crossed the Mediterranean without broadcasting Automatic Identification System data, the signal normally used to reveal a ship’s position.
This was at least the second Russian military shipment to reach Tobruk under naval escort this year. Both cargo ships are under sanctions and have previously carried military cargo. Satellite imagery showed equipment being loaded onto them in August at Baltiysk, a naval base in Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, Militarnyi reported.
In January 2026, the sanctioned Mys Zhelaniya delivered military cargo to Tobruk under escort by a large Russian anti-submarine warship.
Tobruk lies in eastern Libya, which is controlled by forces loyal to commander Khalifa Haftar. The six bases under development host Russian personnel, air defenses, combat aircraft, and drones.
Maaten al-Sarra, one of the six bases, lies near Libya’s borders with Chad and Sudan and supports Russian operations extending toward Sudan and the Sahel, the belt of countries immediately south of the Sahara.
Russian and Libyan authorities have not said who will receive the latest cargo, so there is no confirmation that the vehicles are intended for the Africa Corps, the Russian Defense Ministry-run force that took over much of Wagner’s former role in Africa.
Africa Defense Forum reported that Moscow pivoted toward Libya after the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, having previously used Syria as a transit hub. Moving the vehicles under naval escort as Russian forces absorb continuing battlefield losses in Ukraine underscores the importance Moscow appears to place on keeping its African corridor supplied.
How Russia expands its reach across Africa
Libya is one node in Russia’s wider African system. Through the Africa Corps, Moscow supports autocracy-minded military governments and armed groups throughout the continent in exchange for political influence and access to natural resources. Human rights groups and local residents have accused Russian personnel and their partners of killings and other abuses against civilians, including in Mali.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says Kremlin-backed Russian Houses seek to cultivate young Africans with pro-Moscow views. Moscow also invests in education programs and cultural events across the continent to spread a positive image of Russia, its politics, and its culture.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said in August that nearly 500 Africans recruited into Russia’s military had died. Ukrainian drone specialists are also helping forces fighting Russian troops in Mali and operating in Sudan and Libya, CNN reported.

articles.title: EU chief proposes a European Security Council with partners including Ukraine, Canada, and the U.K. — plus a threat-alert system independent of NATO
articles.body:
EU chief proposes a European Security Council with partners including Ukraine, Canada, and the U.K. — plus a threat-alert system independent of NATO
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed creating a European Security Council that would bring together EU leaders and their counterparts from partner countries such as Canada, Norway, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom. She unveiled the proposal during her annual address to the European Parliament.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders’ format focused on the security of our continent with partners like Ukraine, the U.K., Norway, Canada and others involved,” von der Leyen said. “This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play — this is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality,” she said. “The urgency is clear.”
The European Commission president also called for Europe to create an alert mechanism independent of NATO to coordinate responses to security threats that fall short of armed aggression. Under the proposal, all 27 EU countries would be required to begin consultations if one member state activated the mechanism.
Von der Leyen said the mechanism would complement NATO’s Article 4, which allows allies to request emergency consultations over incidents that do not constitute armed conflict but may threaten their security or territory.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said, adding that there was an urgent need for consensus on how to respond to certain incidents. The number of cyberattacks, acts of sabotage and arson, and drone incursions into EU territory is increasing every day, she said, according to Deutsche Welle.
Von der Leyen also called for Canada to be granted associate membership in the European Union. The proposal drew applause in the European Parliament, according to Reuters.
“I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said, addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in the chamber.
According to DW, EU treaties do not provide for associate membership, though the possibility has been discussed more frequently in recent months. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, among others, has proposed the idea for Ukraine.
Von der Leyen said the EU would provide Ukraine with “the most extensive support” this coming winter, which she said would be the most difficult for the country since the start of the Russian invasion. Specifically, the EU will provide humanitarian aid, bolster Ukraine’s electricity and heat supplies, and strengthen its air defenses.
In recent months, concerns have grown in Europe that Russia could attack a country on NATO’s eastern flank, such as one of the Baltic states. Vladimir Putin has said Russia has no intention of threatening European countries, contrary to claims by “European elites.” He also warned European countries against deploying troops to Ukraine, saying that “this would mean war with Russia.”

articles.title: Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant supplying missiles Moscow uses to bomb Ukrainian cities
articles.body:
Pro-Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH says it sabotaged the power supply to a Russian semiconductor plant in Voronezh that produces electronic components used in Russia’s missiles and air defense systems.
Targeting such suppliers can hit Russia’s ability to sustain its missile campaign: disrupting production of critical electronic components can slow the replenishment of weapons used to strike Ukrainian cities.
In a statement published on 16 September, ATESH said one of its agents infiltrated an electrical substation near the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Sborka (VZPP-S) and destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the facility. The movement said the agent escaped the city after the operation.
VZPP-S is a Russian producer of semiconductor devices, integrated circuits and power modules. Ukraine’s military intelligence lists the company as part of Russia’s defense-industrial supply chain and says it has produced electronic components for Kh-101 cruise missiles, Iskander-K missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
ATESH claimed the sabotage caused a major voltage surge and shut down production workshops. The movement said full power was not restored for several weeks, causing delays in deliveries of components for Russian weapons and, consequently, delays in missile and air defense production.
The movement’s claims have not been independently verified.
ATESH is a pro-Ukrainian partisan movement operating in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia. It says it recruits local residents and Russian military personnel to conduct sabotage, gather intelligence and pass information to Ukraine. The movement regularly publishes claims of attacks and acts of sabotage against Russian military and defense-industrial targets, though individual operations are often difficult to independently verify.
The plant has already been targeted
The reported sabotage comes after the VZPP-S facility was struck in a Ukrainian attack in June.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says VZPP-S produces components for the Kh-101, including transistor assemblies and matrices used in the missile’s electronic systems. It also says the company supplies semiconductor components for the onboard computer of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K system, as well as components for the Pantsir-S1’s television channel.
The company itself describes VZPP-S as a major Russian producer of electronic components, with more than 900 products in serial production.
ATESH said it delayed publication of its claim to protect its agent.

articles.title: Russian war with Europe would be ‘very short’ – Lavrov
articles.body:
Russian war with Europe would be ‘very short’ – Lavrov
Russia would make short work of European nations if they decided to attack it, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Some European nations, including Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states, have increasingly claimed that Russia could target NATO territory in the next few years, urging more military spending in preparation.
Lavrov denied those claims during his appearance at the International Youth Festival in the city of Yekaterinburg in the Urals on Wednesday.
“We’ve said repeatedly that we have no intention of attacking Europe. Russian President Vladimir Putin recently addressed this issue in detail, emphasizing that we have no interest in doing so,” he said.
However, the minister warned that “if Europe, which talks daily about preparing for war against Russia, attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short.”
During the BRICS Summit in New Delhi last week, Putin said that Western governments are promoting an imaginary ‘Russian threat’ and pushing Europe closer to a direct confrontation in order to distract the public from numerous problems in their home countries.
“We are not threatening and are not going to threaten European countries. Why would we?” he said.
The president stressed that plans floated by a number of European states to deploy forces in Ukraine would also cross Moscow’s red lines.
“They are now talking about how they are considering sending troops into Ukrainian territory. This means war with Russia,” he said.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski stated during the Yalta European Strategy meeting in Kiev over the weekend that “If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly.”
Russian presidential aide Nikolay Patrushev responded to Sikorski on Tuesday, dismissing his assessment as an “amateurish view” and saying that Moscow had yet to utilize its full military potential in the Ukraine conflict.
“If Poland was to enter military action against Russia, our country would employ the full arsenal of its available forces and resources, and Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days,” Patrushev declared.
Russian officials have previously warned that a direct clash between Russia and NATO would not be a conventional one and would likely lead to nuclear weapons being deployed.

articles.title: Images reveal major damage to US bases from Iran strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Images reveal major damage to US bases from Iran strikes
A destroyed aircraft, shredded tents, trailers that have been ripped apart: images taken by US troops show significant damage from Iranian strikes targeting American military assets in the Middle East, CBS News reported.
The undated images -- taken at a base in Saudi Arabia and two facilities in Kuwait -- were provided to CBS by American personnel on condition of anonymity due to US military restrictions, the outlet said late Tuesday.
"This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public," CBS quoted one US service member as saying.
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face," the service member added.
The Pentagon's inspector general released a report earlier this week that said the military's Central Command (CENTCOM) -- which is responsible for US forces in the Middle East -- had reported widespread damage to American facilities and equipment.
CENTCOM said Iranian strikes "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan," the report said.
"In addition, dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged" during the war, the report said.
The Defense Department estimated the cost of the war at $33.4 billion as of June 29, but that figure "does not include costs for infrastructure repairs," according to the report.
The US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, with President Donald Trump saying the goal was to prevent the Islamic republic from obtaining nuclear weapons -- which Tehran denies it is seeking.
Iran retaliated with attacks across the region and blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed -- a move that has sent oil prices soaring and caused global economic fallout.

articles.title: A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
articles.body:
A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
The Telegram channel Voyna s Feykami posted an AI-generated video about ballot stuffing. It shows a six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio, soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo, and the alien from Ridley Scott’s film “Alien” dropping ballots into a ballot box. A voice-over warns that videos purporting to show election violations may have been generated using AI.
“Stay alert! In the coming days, as the election approaches, pressure on Russians will mount. Don’t believe everything you see online,” the channel says in the post accompanying the video. The channel urges readers to rely “only on official sources” for information about the election.
By the time this article was published, the video featuring DiCaprio had been viewed more than 100,000 times and shared by several other Telegram channels.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
Voyna s Feykami is run by Dialog, an autonomous nonprofit organization established by the Moscow authorities in 2019 as an online “citizen feedback” center. As Proekt reported, Dialog was actually tasked with promoting political advertising ahead of the vote on constitutional amendments. During the pandemic, Dialog was also responsible for providing information about the coronavirus. After Russia criminalized spreading false information about the virus, the organization began searching for such content.
The organization’s responsibilities expanded after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dialog employees handled communications for the Defense Ministry and also fabricated stories about Ukraine. During this period, Dialog launched the Voyna s Feykami Telegram channel and a website of the same name.
In 2023, Meduza, iStories, and The Bell published a joint investigation into Dialog’s work. We found that Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of Russia’s Presidential Administration, oversees the organization on the Kremlin’s behalf. Sources described Vladimir Tabak, who has headed Dialog since 2021, as “Surkov’s man,” whom Kiriyenko had “inherited” along with his position. According to the sources, Kiriyenko personally visited the organization’s office to celebrate their victory in the vote on the constitutional amendments.
The journalists also examined Dialog’s internal guidelines for “debunking fake news.” When there is no basis whatsoever for refuting a story, the guidelines instruct employees to discredit the source, point out that the report contains no photos or videos, or suggest who might benefit from spreading it.
Voyna s Feykami has claimed, for example, that Ukrainian air defenses caused a gas explosion — not a Russian missile strike — that killed 46 people in an apartment building in Dnipro. It also described the strike that killed 12 people at a pizzeria in Kramatorsk as an attack on “a deployment site for foreign mercenaries.”
