articles.title: Von der Leyen risks fresh EU-NATO turf war
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed the EU take on a stronger role in security and tackling hybrid threats, reigniting a long-running turf battle with NATO over Europe's defense.
Speaking at her annual policy address in Strasbourg, von der Leyen pitched a new leaders’ crisis decision-making forum together with Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the U.K. She also floated a new urgent consultation procedure for hybrid attacks modeled on NATO’s Article 4.
“Our systems were made for a different world — they are driven by well-intentioned attempts at consensus and compromise,” she said. “But we need to consider whether they are still fit for purpose.”
The pitch is already stirring unease within NATO, which has bristled at any attempt by the EU to tackle military-adjacent threats and has warned against “unnecessary duplication.”
“I have seen many initiatives at the EU level during the recent years — none of them yet are really protecting member states,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Of course, any initiative has to be assessed on its merits, but I do feel that NATO has delivered much more in concrete terms for collective security.”
The EU proposals underscore a growing sense that Europe is failing to deal with proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness,” von der Leyen said.
The security council is supposed to help the EU react more decisively. NATO itself has struggled with how to respond to Russian provocations below the threshold of direct military attack.
Advertisement
The last time Article 4 was invoked — a formal request to consult allies due to a security threat — was by Estonia last year after three Russian fighter jets violated the country's airspace. No other capital has invoked it since.
Duplication drama
There are few details on von der Leyen’s ideas. Earlier European security council proposals — which the EU has rejected — include the idea of capitals delegating some defense decision-making powers to a smaller group of leaders in a crisis.
An Emergency Security Protocol, meanwhile, would allow one capital to convene all fellow EU members in a crisis “to coordinate a European response, to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact,” von der Leyen said — almost identical to NATO’s Article 4 procedure.
Mark Carney listens to Ursula von der Leyen's State of the Union speech to Members of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France on Sept. 16, 2026. | Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
In theory, a security council could help in “coordinating quick action” between the EU, NATO and other partners in a crisis that is “flexible across institutions,” said Giuseppe Spatafora, an analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies. The emergency protocol, meanwhile, could protect non-NATO countries like Ireland, he said.
But the alliance insists it should take the lead on security. “NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the alliance.
Not all NATO allies are skeptical. On hybrid attacks, the “EU is better placed to put in place a mechanism to react, because it has more diverse tools than NATO,” said a second senior NATO diplomat.
Advertisement
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said von der Leyen's schemes were not intended to replace NATO.
“In order for Europeans to take primary responsibility for European defense, we need to have our own defense architecture,” he told POLITICO, “and we shall do that, not undermining NATO — keeping NATO structures as they are.”
But von der Leyen's ideas pose a risk of duplication, two NATO diplomats warned, adding that allies were not formally briefed by the EU on the proposals in advance.
Countries near Russia also fret that it could worsen their security situation. “It gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said MEP Riho Terras, Estonia’s former chief of defense. “It is a very bad idea … which I hope will not have a future.”
The move also risks alienating some non-EU NATO members such as the U.S. and Turkey.
“The idea of a ‘European Security Union’ not including Türkiye, a major capable ally and a pillar of stability, security and peace at NATO’s southeastern flank, would be fatally flawed from the outset,” said one Turkish official.
Advertisement
The White House did not respond to a request for comment from POLITICO.
Setting up new EU bodies and holding consultations will not fix Europe’s underlying lack of political will to confront Russia and the need to match talk with action, said Oana Lungescu, a former longtime NATO official.
“Nations … should be talking about real capabilities and trying to harness real political will to impose costs on Russia,” she said. “How can you do that by focusing political energy and some resources ... towards yet another body?”
NATO’s “Article 4 works because it sits inside [its] Article 5” mutual defense clause, added a third NATO diplomat. “An EU ‘Article 4’ without an EU ‘Article 5’ is a consultation forum with a flattering name.”

articles.title: Lockheed’s New Modular JASSM Offers Swappable Noses and Launch Options
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Lockheed Martin has unveiled its concept for a modular version of one of the Air Force’s main air-to-ground cruise missiles, opening up a range of possible upgrades and uses for the weapon.
Lockheed revealed the AGM-158 FLEX airframe, based on the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week. The airframe has a removable nose cone to let users swap in different sensors and a reconfigurable tail for different launch options.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the Air Force has contracted or ordered the FLEX or what stage of development the project is in. Lockheed did say in a release that it has invested $35 million of its own money on the idea, based on what the firm called “a demand from our customers to have increased options.”
The Air Force has shown interest in modular munitions before—in January 2025, the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center published a notice to industry seeking technology to allow for its Extended Range Attack Munition project to have modular parts for its subcomponents. The ERAM is also a standoff cruise missile, which the Air Force rercently developed as a low-cost option to bolster its stockpiles.
Indeed, the Air Force and the rest of the U.S. military are keen to build up their weapons stocks after using thousands to strike Iran during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The U.S. used 1,100 JASSMs over just the first 39 days of the conflict, according to an analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in April.
Given that high usage and demand, the Air Force plans to significantly ramp up production of JASSM and its Long-Range Anti-Ship variant—and Lockheed sees FLEX as a way to further bolster the stockpile with more options.
The concept “will allow customers to quickly integrate capabilities,” Lockheed’s release states, and allow JASSM to be configured for surface, sub-surface, and ground launch options.
The air-launched version will remain compatible with all current and future JASSM and LRASM air-launched platforms.
Size options include a 206-inch extreme range option, the same size as the existing JASSM-XR, and a 168-inch extended range version, the same size as the JASSM-ER.
Both are built to give users “significantly increased standoff attack range.”
The weapon could feature in the latest iteration of a yearslong effort known as “Rapid Dragon,” which has now shifted to become “Dragon Cart,” a project to launch cruise missiles from palletized loads dropped from the ramps of transport and cargo aircraft such as the C-130 and C-17.
“As Rapid Dragon transitions into a Dragon Cart program of record, it becomes a viable deployment platform for a variety of Air Force munitions, both in inventory and in development,” the Lockheed spokesperson wrote. “While we can’t offer specific examples today, Lockheed Martin does consider all potential launch platforms in maturing munition offerings.”

articles.title: FQ-44 Unmanned Fighter Aircraft Integrated With Bombs and Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
Anduril has integrated aerial bombs, unguided rockets and cruise missiles onto its semi-autonomous FQ-44 unmanned fighter aircraft.
Anduril Industries said the FQ-44 has already demonstrated compatibility with a wide range of munitions.
These include 500-pound (230 kg) aerial bombs, small-diameter bombs, air-launched cruise missiles, unguided rocket pods, external targeting pods and many other types of weapons.
The unmanned fighter aircraft was previously demonstrated launching AIM-120 air-to-air missiles.
The aircraft can therefore serve as either a fighter or a bomber depending on the needs of the Air Force.
The FQ-44 Fury jet-powered unmanned fighter aircraft was developed as part of the U.S. Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.
It is intended to serve as an unmanned “wingman,” operating semi-autonomously, receiving tasks from a human operator and working alongside F-35, F-22 and other aircraft.
The aircraft is approximately 6.1 meters long, has a wingspan of 5.2 meters, a top speed of about Mach 0.95 and a service ceiling of approximately 15 km, although the specifications of the production version may differ.
Another advantage of the FQ-44 Fury is its rapid development.
A little more than two years passed between the delivery of the first prototype in April 2024, the start of ground testing in April 2025, its first flight in October that year and the signing of a contract for serial production in June 2026.
The FQ-44 Fury is being developed as a relatively inexpensive and scalable unmanned aircraft that can be produced in significant quantities.
Its architecture is designed to use artificial intelligence and autonomous systems to perform complex tasks with minimal direct control by an operator.

articles.title: US charges five as alleged Kremlin assassination network reaches American soil
articles.body:
A US-based recruit was promised up to $1,500 to surveil a prominent Russian dissident before being offered $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target, the US Justice Department (DOJ) said on 15 September.
The charges connect that alleged plot to what prosecutors describe as a wider Russian assassination network operating since at least 2024 against dissidents, defectors, and countries perceived as supporting Ukraine.
A federal grand jury in Manhattan indicted five alleged members of what prosecutors call the “RIS Network”:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63: A Russian national and former colonel in the Russian intelligence services who allegedly recruited people to kill Russian dissidents.
- Kirill Khrameev, 27: Yuri Khrameev’s son and an officer in the FSB, Russia’s principal security service and a successor to the Soviet KGB.
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35: A Cuban national living in Russia who allegedly coordinated attacks and arranged travel for operatives.
- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35: A Cuban national accused of recruiting people in the US for surveillance and murder.
- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22: A Venezuelan national accused of helping Suarez recruit US residents to spy on and kill a Russian dissident.
Suarez sent the US resident two locations associated with the dissident, according to the indictment. After the resident delivered photographs and videos, prosecutors say, Suarez and Castro made the $40,000 offer. When the resident declined to carry out the killing, they allegedly asked whether he knew “someone [who] can do the work.”
In 2025, the indictment alleges, Kirill Khrameev recruited a US citizen to photograph a target in Lithuania for a promised $200. Yuri Khrameev then offered approximately $25,000 to kill the man. When the recruit refused, Khrameev allegedly proposed a “simpler job”: burning a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. He said the purpose was to target countries helping Ukraine, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors also allege that Durruthy coordinated travel and logistics for attacks in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and in Lithuania that September. The Justice Department did not specify what either attack involved.
All five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, carrying up to 20 years in prison. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro also face a murder-for-hire conspiracy charge carrying up to 10 years.
All five remain at large. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow saw no need to comment without “credible evidence,” Reuters reported. An indictment is an allegation, and the defendants are presumed innocent.
From military espionage to alleged murder plots
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, its covert campaign against Ukraine’s Western allies has combined intelligence gathering with escalating sabotage. CSIS found that suspected Russian attacks in Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024, often using locally recruited agents against infrastructure and industries supporting Ukraine.
In August 2025, US prosecutors charged active-duty soldier Taylor Adam Lee with trying to transmit Abrams tank information and deliver hardware to someone he believed represented the Russian government, allegedly in exchange for Russian citizenship. That case involved an American insider allegedly offering military secrets, not a proven Russian recruitment operation.

articles.title: Kushner’s “win-win” peace deal is impossible when Putin wants all of Ukraine — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Zelenskyy responded to the "win-win" framing in a CBC interview published on 16 September during his visit to Canada, saying the war's human losses made such an outcome impossible from the first day of the full-scale invasion.
The US and Ukraine are framing a possible end to the war differently. Washington has pushed for a negotiated settlement in which both sides could gain something, while Kyiv has rejected territorial concessions and pressed for security guarantees.
The US approach was to "think about things in the context of win-win" and "create opportunities for both sides," Jared Kushner told reporters after visiting Kyiv on 6 September alongside US special envoy Steve Witkoff, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Zelenskyy argued that Russia's aims could not be reduced to a territorial claim.
"He has the biggest territory in the world and you need, I don't know, some kilometers. For what?" Zelenskyy said. "That's why it's very strange when some partners say, look, he needs just this part of Ukraine, just these kilometers and that's all. No, it's a crazy idea."
"No, he doesn't need kilometers. He needs Ukraine. He needs Ukraine to be a part of Russia," Zelenskyy said. "I know that this person wants to occupy totally us. And he will not change his goal. Never," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready for a ceasefire "without conditions" if Russia agreed—"just ceasefire and speak"—but added that any lasting peace required security guarantees to prevent another Russian attack.
Zelenskyy said he expects to meet US President Donald Trump in the second half of September, with the UN General Assembly in New York expected to provide an opportunity for the meeting.

articles.title: Von der Leyen announces near-term aid measures for Ukraine
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced measures to assist Ukraine this winter, including providing unprecedented support, strengthening air defenses, and tightening sanctions against Russia.
“We know that the coming winter will be tough for Ukraine. But we also know that North Korean missiles and Russian drones cannot break the Ukrainian spirit of resistance. Because the people of Ukraine are fighting for something. They are fighting for the survival of their country, for their identity and for their freedom. And they are also fighting for our freedom and our self-determination. Our task remains to support Ukraine as best we can,” she stated in Strasbourg on Wednesday during the European Parliament's plenary session, as part of the annual 2026 State of the Union address.
She named providing assistance to Ukraine as “our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war.” “Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating,” the President of the European Commission explained.
As a second point, von der Leyen highlighted the strengthening of Ukraine's air defense. “Last week, for the first time, we approved the purchase of American Patriot interceptor missiles. These now need to be delivered urgently. But we must also jointly reduce our dependence on a single supplier. That is why we would like to develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system. At the heart of this collaboration is the Freya project. Here we are combining the Ukrainians' combat experience and innovativeness with Europe's technological leadership. And, of course, our substantial production capacity. But Freya is only the beginning. More is needed,” she explained.
In this regard, von der Leyen announced the launch of a new program of joint projects with Ukrainian companies, utilizing remaining funds from the SAFE fund.
The European Commission President identified the tightening of sanctions against Russia as the third element of aid to Ukraine. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she explained.

articles.title: Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on September 16 that an armed Russian drone recovered from a beach at Rusinowo carried a live warhead, neutralized on site, and preliminarily identified as a Gerbera 2.
Col. Bartosz Okoniewski, deputy district prosecutor for military affairs at the District Prosecutor's Office in Poznań, informed the agency that the recovered aircraft had been armed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"It contained a fragmentation-high-explosive warhead together with a fuze," Okoniewski stated to PAP. "We managed to separate the warhead from the aircraft itself, and then, for safety reasons, the warhead was neutralized right there on the beach."
He added that the warhead was detonated on the evening of September 15. The airframe, now stripped of its warhead, was moved to a military site for detailed inspection, where preliminary findings indicated it was a Gerbera 2 type produced and used by Russia.
The drone was located on September 14 near Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec, in Poland's West Pomeranian region. Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the recovery that day, describing the object as a Russian military unmanned aircraft.
On September 16, Poland's Military Gendarmerie reported that soldiers had extracted, examined and neutralized components that could pose a threat, then secured the drone for laboratory analysis.
The on-site inspection, as Okoniewski detailed to PAP, was led by a prosecutor from the military division of the Szczecin-Niebuszewo District Prosecutor's Office. The Military Counterintelligence Service, military and police sappers, gendarmerie officers and the fire service also took part.
The prosecutor's office has opened a case under a preliminary classification of causing an event that threatens the life or health of many people, or property of great value, through an explosion. Investigators are additionally examining the use of an aircraft to cross the state border without the required permission.
The Gerbera is a cheap Russian drone typically fielded as a decoy and a reconnaissance platform alongside heavier Shahed-type strike aircraft, though armed and reconnaissance variants also exist.
Built largely from plywood and foam, the type carries a standard range of roughly 700 kilometers, with examples recovered abroad fitted with extra nose fuel tanks to stretch that reach.
Ukrainian estimates have put the production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, enabling the drones to be launched in numbers that force defenders to expend far costlier interceptors.
According to PAP, Kosiniak-Kamysz linked the recovery to the downing of a Russian drone over Lithuania on the night of September 15. He suggested that the aircraft found in Poland might also have flown over Lithuania on September 13, where it was tracked and targeted for an attempted neutralization.
The drone then, in his account, "crossed the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region and most likely operated over the Baltic." He indicated that Poland and Lithuania would investigate jointly, with the services of both countries cooperating.
The recovery followed a run of similar incidents across the Baltic in September. On September 13, an object that crossed from Lithuania into Russia's Kaliningrad region was identified as a drone.
Around the same time, a resident near Finland's Pellinki archipelago found an unmanned aircraft assessed as a Russian-made Geoscan 701. Two weeks earlier, on August 31, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea roughly 30 kilometers north of Łeba.

articles.title: EU Proposes Creating European Security Council with Ukraine as a Member
articles.body:
The European Commission has proposed creating a European Security Council — a new format for coordinating the actions of European states and partners in response to security threats.
Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission, stated this during her annual address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
In addition to EU member states, the new format is expected to involve Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada, and other partners.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook. We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents,” von der Leyen stated.
At the same time, the European Commission proposes establishing an Emergency Security Protocol similar to Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty. If activated, an EU member state would promptly hold consultations and coordinate a joint response to the threat.
The framework would primarily address hybrid incidents, including acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, drone incursions, and other actions that do not necessarily rise to the level of direct armed aggression.
The initiative comes amid discussions in Europe about strengthening its own defense capabilities and creating security mechanisms that would complement existing NATO structures.
In March 2025, the European Union published its White Paper for European Defence, which identified Russia as a fundamental threat and set out a strategic development plan to strengthen the defense capabilities of the EU and Ukraine over the next five years.
Individual EU member states had previously supported the idea of creating a European Security Council. In January, Andrius Kubilius, European Commissioner for Defence and Space, called for the creation of a 100,000-strong European Union army for the bloc’s own defense and to replace U.S. troops in Europe if necessary.
European officials have also considered the Coalition of the Willing as a potential foundation for a new military alliance without U.S. participation, with Ukraine as a potential member.
On February 14, Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU should implement Article 42(7) of the Treaty on European Union on mutual defence.
In April, during an address to participants of the meeting of the heads of state and government of the European Union in Cyprus, Volodymyr Zelensky proposed that Europe create a comprehensive defense system capable of protecting its borders and infrastructure and countering drone threats.

articles.title: Air Force Eyes New-Build F-16s to Boost Fighter Force
articles.body:
The Air Force will consider acquiring new F-16 Fighting Falcon jets to help fill capacity shortfalls in its aging fighter fleet, multiple people familiar with the matter told Air & Space Forces Magazine. These discussions are happening as the Air Force is building its proposed fiscal 2028 budget and the five-year spending plan that goes with it.
Buying new F-16s—which would be the U.S.’s first in more than 20 years—is viewed as one way to quickly build back lost fighter capacity, as Lockheed Martin continues to operate a hot production line for the aircraft. Buying F-16s from Lockheed, which also produces the F-35 Lightning II, would have parallels to the decision to acquire F-15EX Eagle IIs from Boeing, which likewise came after a yearslong gap in USAF purchases.
The new-build F-16s, potentially dubbed “F-16G” to reflect upgrades from existing F-16C and D models, could be on the agenda for discussion when Air Force four-stars gather this fall for a Corona gathering of top service officials.
Lockheed Martin deferred questions to the Air Force: “This topic is best addressed by the U.S. government, but we stand ready to support the U.S. Air Force and its mission needs,” Lockheed said in a statement. “Our proven products are the backbone of the USAF fleet and provide the most advanced and versatile capabilities to ensure air dominance now and decades to come.”
The Air Force, in a written response to Air & Space Forces Magazine, said it is examining its options as it looks to the future.
“The Department of the Air Force is in initial phases of analyzing options for the next Future Years Defense Program,” an Air Force spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have neither defined the precise mission requirements nor the spectrum of options that could fill it.”
Lockheed currently produces F-16E and F models, single- and dual-seat variants respectively, for the United Arab Emirates. The company moved its production line for Block 70 F-16s in 2019 from Fort Worth, Texas, to Greenville, S.C.
If the Air Force decided to buy more F-16s, Lockheed would likely keep its Greenville production line going. The potential upgraded F-16 from that line is being referred to as a G model by those familiar with the discussions.
The Air Force today has 826 F-16s in its inventory, with 484 of those operated by the Active-Duty force. The jets average 34 years old, however, and the newest in the inventory have been flying since 2005.
USAF F-16s carry out a variety of critical missions, including air-to-air and air-to-ground strikes. F-16s that carry out suppression of enemy air defense missions are referred to as “Wild Weasels” and have seen heavy action in operations against Iran.
New F-16 purchases would drive other movement in the industry. Both Pratt & Whitney and GE Aerospace make engines that go on the F-16. Pratt, which is owned by RTX, announced Sept. 15 it has licensed Hermeus to manufacture its F100-PW-229 used on the F-15 and F-16, saying the agreement will strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base by creating a new source for the widely used engine.
Northrop Grumman, which is developing two major upgrades for existing F-16s, would also likely benefit. The company is working on the Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, and an upgraded large aperture targeting pod called LITENING LA.
IVEWS, also known as the AN/ALQ-257, is an advanced electronic warfare system providing radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying and locating of potential threats.
A source familiar with the issue, who asked not to be named to speak more freely, said any new F-16 would likely have IVEWS and multiple other new capabilities placing it not only beyond the legacy C and D fighters, but also the Block 70 fighters Lockheed is currently building.
“If the Air Force were to buy a new F-16, this would not be your grandfather’s F-16,” the source said. “This would be more akin to buying an F-15EX.”
The source said buying more F-16s would make sense for the Air Force, since Lockheed and Boeing are facing capacity constraints limiting how many F-35As and F-15EXs, respectively, they can build. And the service’s existing fleet of F-16s has been flown hard in the wars of recent decades, the source said.
“There’s only so many times you can do a service life extension program before you begin to lose the strength and integrity of the airframe itself,” the source said.

articles.title: A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead
articles.body:
A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead
An overnight Russian drone strike on Kyiv destroyed a warehouse storing props from the Kvartal 95 studio, the studio said.
The studio said the strike destroyed numerous sets, costumes, and other items used in Kvartal 95 concerts, television shows, films, and series over the past 20 years.
“Russian weapons can destroy property. But they cannot stop us. We will keep working, writing new jokes, and helping Ukraine’s defenders. All scheduled concerts will go ahead — with or without the props,” the studio said.
A warehouse belonging to the Olena Zelenska Foundation was also destroyed. The foundation said on social media that the warehouse burned to the ground but no one was hurt. It held humanitarian aid that the foundation had purchased or received from partners to distribute to children, families, and institutions across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said a Russian drone struck a warehouse in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district, sparking a fire and injuring one person.
Kvartal 95 is a Ukrainian studio that Volodymyr Zelensky co-founded and was part of before becoming president. The studio was established in 2003 out of the KVN comedy team 95-y Kvartal. For more than 20 years, it has produced television shows, films, series, and concert programs.

articles.title: Denmark reports Russian flares fired at its helicopter
articles.body:
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking Russian vessels in the Baltic Sea, the BBC reports.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador to provide an explanation regarding the incident, which occurred during a routine surveillance operation. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the Russian actions as reckless, stating that they were intended to sow division and intimidate. Russia has indicated it will investigate the incident but accused the Danes of performing dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships.
The incident took place on the same day that NATO fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania that had entered from Belarus.
In a statement regarding the Baltic Sea incident, the Danish Armed Forces said that flares were fired at one of their Air Force Fennec helicopters. This occurred during a routine photography operation while monitoring a Russian frigate located in international waters near Gedser. One of the two flares passed right by the helicopter.
The Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs has described the incident as completely unacceptable.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen accused Russia of gradually pushing the boundaries of acceptable behavior and stated that the Danes would not accept this.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin stated officially that Moscow would investigate the circumstances of the incident and accused the Danish helicopter pilots of provocative actions. He claimed this was not the first time Danish helicopters had performed dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships; he noted that he had complained about a similar incident last year and added that the communication issues lay with the Danish side, not the Russian ships.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen emphasized on social media that Russia’s behavior was reckless and dangerous. She added that this incident, along with a drone shot down over Lithuania, was part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocations against Europe.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters that the frigate’s crew had not attempted to establish contact with the helicopters.
Read also: NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over Lithuania

articles.title: Army to replace Watchkeeper with Ukraine-proven drone
articles.body:
The Army is to bring the Tekever AR5 into service under a contract worth up to £400 million, replacing the Watchkeeper system in use since 2014, alongside a separate £16 million deal delivering more than a thousand small drones, the Ministry of Defence stated.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, announced both at Defence Vehicle Dynamics, the biennial land warfare exhibition, on Wednesday.
The AR5 is a long-endurance surveillance aircraft able to carry up to 50kg of cameras and sensors. The deal begins with an initial order of six, rising to up to 24 by 2029, with the aircraft to be built at a new Tekever factory in Swindon. The type has already been used by Ukraine against Russia.
Mr Pollard said: “Our soldiers deserve the best technology, and that’s what we’re delivering. From small drones giving troops eyes on the enemy, to the AR5 offering commanders better intelligence over the battlefield, we’re transforming the Army’s ability to see, understand and act first.
“This is defence procurement that backs British industry, creates skilled jobs and keeps our Armed Forces ahead of our adversaries.”
According to the department, the Tekever contract will support more than 1,000 highly skilled jobs by 2030 across the company’s British sites, which include Bristol, Swindon, Lydd, London, Southampton, Edinburgh and West Wales Airport.
Karl Brew, Managing Director of Tekever UK, said: “We are proud to be delivering the AR5 to the British Army at this critical moment for national security. This investment allows us to grow our UK operations, create hundreds of skilled jobs and bring cutting-edge surveillance technology, proven on the battlefield in Ukraine, into service with British forces.”
The smaller aircraft come from three British small and medium-sized companies, with deliveries nearing completion. Evolve Dynamics of Hampshire is supplying 245 FOXE-NATO drones weighing less than 250g and fitted with infrared cameras for use at night. Marlborough Communications Limited of Surrey is providing 670 Skydio X10 INTL aircraft, which the department says can be ready to fly in under a minute and reach 45mph. A partnership between Brigantes Consulting of Exeter and Harmattan AI is delivering 110 SONORA drones, designed to help train soldiers before they use similar systems on operations.
That deal has created more than 30 new roles so far, with 18 already filled in Hampshire, Surrey and Exeter, including several veterans. The small drone contract was delivered by the National Armaments Director Group and forms part of Project Rapstone, the Army’s programme to bring new technology to soldiers faster, with the stated goal of doubling the Army’s fighting power by 2027 and moving new equipment from industry to the front line within 24 months.
Watchkeeper, the system the AR5 replaces, entered service in 2014 after a development programme that ran considerably over time and cost, and was withdrawn from service earlier this year. The Strategic Defence Review identified its replacement as part of a wider shift towards uncrewed systems, and the Defence Investment Plan commits new investment in the Army’s long-range surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities including the next generation of uncrewed aerial systems.

articles.title: China willing to ‘safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights’, official says
articles.body:
China willing to ‘safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights’, official says
China says the US-Israel war on Iran highlights flaws in the Middle East’s ‘existing security architecture’.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Beijing is “willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran, and safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights and interests”.
The foreign ministers met in Beijing on Wednesday, a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the United States, where he is set to meet his US counterpart, Donald Trump, and they are expected to discuss the war on Iran and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can China play peacemaker as Iran’s foreign minister heads to Beijing?
- list 2 of 3China does not need to replace the US in the Gulf
- list 3 of 3The Iran war reveals the limits of BRICS
“We encourage Iran and the US to stay rational and restrained,” Wang said.
“We urge all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date,” he said, adding that China “does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea”.
He also told Araghchi that Tehran and Washington should “rebuild the negotiation mechanism based on the consensus reached so far”.
“The current situation once again demonstrates that the existing security architecture in the Middle East is inadequate and needs to be reformed and strengthened,” Wang said.
China stands ready to promote peace, fairness and justice in the region, and its policy towards Iran has remained consistent and stable, he added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said the Middle East had undergone “fundamental changes” and that Tehran had started regional negotiations to end the “aggressive” US war against Iran.
In a statement posted on Araghchi’s Telegram channel, he said “We want the return of peace to the region and friendly and peaceful relations with our neighbors, and in this regard, we have started dialogue with the countries of the region.”
Earlier this week, Beijing refuted US media reports that Chinese entities supplied Tehran with satellite images of a military base housing US troops in Jordan, and Trump said in April that he wrote to Xi a letter “asking him” not to sell weapons to Iran.
China is a top economic partner of Iran and the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil.

articles.title: Russia unveils air defence system against Ukrainian long-range drones – photos
articles.body:
Russia unveils air defence system against Ukrainian long-range drones – photos
Russian defence company Kalashnikov has unveiled for the first time the Zveroboy air defence system, armed with Kraken FPV interceptor drones.
Source: press service for Kalashnikov
Details: Kalashnikov claims that Zveroboy is designed to provide round-the-clock protection of facilities against reconnaissance and strike drones.
Among the targets of the system, Russia specifically lists Ukrainian drones such as Leleka, Liutyi, Bober and Hornet-XR.
"The system consists of an automated workstation at the ground control station, an optical targeting system, three launch containers, a digital repeater, a technical compartment with a distribution panel and switching unit, a compass on a telescopic pole, and a radar system," the company said.
The system's primary means of engagement are high-speed, multirotor Kraken FPV drones with a specialised warhead. Each of the three launch containers holds three interceptors, giving the system a total of nine such drones.
The Kraken drones can be used during the day and at night. The night-time Kraken-N version is additionally equipped with a thermal imaging camera.
Zveroboy is offered in two versions: stationary and mobile. The latter is mounted on the chassis of a mass-produced pickup truck, which is intended to simplify the system's relocation and concealment.
Kalashnikov also claims that Zveroboy can be integrated with existing surveillance and perimeter security systems.
Russia has not disclosed the system's detection and engagement range, the speed of the Kraken interceptor drones, the mass of their warheads or other key specifications.
Background:
- It was previously reported that Russia had developed the Met interceptor drone, designed to counter drones at short ranges.
- In June, Russian holding company Shvabe unveiled a system for guiding interceptor drones towards strike UAVs. The system, whose name has not been disclosed, consists of a ground-based electro-optical station, interceptor drones and an operator workstation.

articles.title: The Only Air Force Fighter Pilot in Congress Wants ‘Wingmen to Come Join Me’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—When the 119th Congress took office in January 2025, it counted a record seven former Navy SEALs among its members—and just one former Air Force fighter pilot.
Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), an Air Force veteran who flew F-15 and F-22 fighters, says that needs to change so the Air Force gets the resources it needs to recapitalize its rapidly aging air fleet.
“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”
Indeed, among the 96 veterans now in Congress, just 15 are Air Force veterans: only 15.6 percent. By comparison, there are 45 Army vets, 24 Navy vets, and 12 former Marines. The Space Force isn’t seven years old yet, but no former Space Force Guardians have been elected to Congress.
Of the 15 former Airmen on Capitol Hill, Pfluger is not the only aviator—Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) flew on the EC-130H and RC-135, Rep. Troy Downing (R-Mont.) was in combat search and rescue, and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) was an airborne intelligence officer.
But there are no other USAF fighter pilots. In 2022, Pfluger started the “Mach 1” caucus with three former Navy fighter pilots. Four years and two elections later, the Mach 1 caucus has gone from four to three members: Pfluger, Rep. Jake Ellzey (R-Texas), and Rep. Scott Franklin (R-Fla.).
With such small numbers, Pfluger said, it’s harder for the Air Force to “tell its story.”
“What I have done in Congress is try to educate my colleagues on what the Department of the Air Force does and why we, as a department, are really carrying the load in each of the conflicts—whether it’s Epic Fury, Midnight Hammer, Absolute Resolve, or any of the previous conflicts, the Department of the Air Force has been there every single time,” Pfluger said.
Airpower, Pfluger said, is uniquely capable of providing strategic effects. But modernization—and the resources that go along with it—is desperately needed.
We … need the help to make the case that while we are the oldest and the smallest, it’s not too late. We can recapitalize,” Pfluger said, lamenting that budget increases cannot be split evenly among the services if the Air Force is to shoulder much of the operational load.
More Airmen in Congress would help him make the case to other lawmakers, Pfluger said. For now, he gets help from Representatives and Senators who represent key Air Force installations. But he also urged Air Force leaders to make their case to Congress.
“We need Air Force leaders to be bold,” Pfluger said. “We need you to be bold to tell the truth, to say we’re underfunded.”
Multiyear Procurement
While the Air Force needs to make its case to Congress, Congress can help the Air Force by not only providing more resources, but making those resources more consistent.
Pentagon officials frequently decry the effects of continuing resolutions and government shutdowns when lawmakers fail to pass appropriations on time.
A more “predictable environment” is important, Pfluger agreed. One way to do that is multiyear procurement authorities—letting the Pentagon award contracts for multiple years instead of being reliant on annual cycles. Congress must approve any and all programs for which Pentagon wants to use multiyear procurement.
Defense officials say multiyear procurement saves the government money by locking in lower prices and helps industry by providing a stable demand signal. In the past, lawmakers have raised concerns about oversight, but they have grown increasingly open to granting more authorities.
Congress has already implemented multiyear procurement for a range of munitions programs, but members of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees have voted to authorize it for the F-35 and F-15EX as part of the 2027 defense policy bill. That bill is still pending, but Pfluger projected confidence that expanded multiyear procurement authorities are coming.
“I’m very convinced that we’re very close to getting some of these things accomplished,” Pfluger said

articles.title: Ukrainian electronic warfare apparently knocked a Russian attack drone off course and into Lithuanian airspace, the country’s president says
articles.body:
Ukrainian electronic warfare apparently knocked a Russian attack drone off course and into Lithuanian airspace, the country’s president says
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said after a meeting of the State Defense Council that the drone shot down by NATO fighter jets over Lithuania on the night of September 15 was a Russian Gerbera drone.
Preliminary information indicates that the drone was intended to attack Ukraine but was thrown off course by Ukrainian electronic warfare systems and entered Lithuanian airspace, Nausėda said.
“Unfortunately, there may be more incidents like this in the future. The most important thing is for us to detect such drones in time — preferably while they are still over neighboring countries — so we can respond more quickly, since we really have very little time to prepare. Given our geographic position, Vilnius is not far from the border, and, of course, once such objects are detected, we could and should have the means to destroy drones or other aircraft.”
NATO fighter jets shot down the drone after it entered Lithuanian airspace on the night of September 15, marking the first time a drone had been destroyed over the country. The drone was downed between Kaunas and Kaišiadorys, about 100 kilometers (62 miles) northwest of Vilnius. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas later said the drone had been carrying an explosive device, which was rendered safe.

articles.title: Iran: Architects of crimes against humanity to suppress protests must face international justice to deter further massacres
articles.body:
- New report finds Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their bloody suppression of the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising
- In-depth investigation exposes chain of command responsible for implementing state policy of lethal force to crush protests and identifies 87 officials who should be investigated for crimes against humanity
- Iranian authorities disproportionately targeted Kurdish and Baluchi communities with lethal repression and subjected them to the crime against humanity of persecution
- UN General Assembly should create an international criminal justice mechanism to tackle impunity for repeated mass protest killings culminating in January 2026 protest massacres
- Report released amid armed hostilities since unlawful US and Israeli attacks, underscoring the need for enduring ceasefire and accountability for violations of the UN Charter and international humanitarian law
In a landmark new report marking the fourth anniversary of the start of the Woman Life Freedom uprising, Amnesty International warns that those responsible for crimes against humanity committed to brutally crush nationwide protests in 2022 continue to control Iran’s deadly state machinery of repression today.  
The report, Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising –more than 1,000 pages long – details how Iranian authorities committed the crimes against humanity of murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds in order to crush the uprising. It also documents deadly protest repression operations and command structures, identifying 87 officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
Amnesty International is calling for an international criminal justice mechanism to be established urgently by the UN General Assembly to ensure Iranian authorities responsible for crimes against humanity are held to account and to deter further atrocities such as the large-scale protest massacres committed on 8-9 January 2026.
In light of the ongoing hostilities following unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel on Iran, Amnesty International also reiterates its call for an enduring ceasefire and independent investigations into attacks committed during the conflict. The organization calls for the UN to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law, including possible war crimes.
“The extensive evidence gathered and analysed in our report leaves no doubt: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising. They waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population demanding dignity, human rights and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Our report unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“Our report also unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks. The horrifying result has been intensifying cycles of mass protest killings, culminating in the massacres of thousands of protesters within just 48 hours on 8-9 January 2026. The UN General Assembly must end the unconscionable normalization of mass protest killings in Iran and create an international criminal justice mechanism aimed at prosecuting those most implicated in crimes against humanity.
“This report is being published at a time when people in Iran are also facing the devastating consequences of unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel. Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm.
“For years, Iranian people have faced brutal repression, persecution and impunity at the hands of their own authorities. Today, many are also bearing the human cost of unlawful military action carried out by the USA and Israel. A principled response requires rejecting both impunity for crimes against humanity and unlawful use of force. The international community must pursue people-centred diplomatic strategies that place civilian protection, atrocity prevention, justice and accountability at their core. After more than six months of air strikes that have killed and injured civilians, damaged the environment, and caused significant destruction of civilian infrastructure, an enduring ceasefire is urgently needed alongside independent investigations and action by the UN General Assembly to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law and possible war crimes committed by all parties to the conflict.”
Amnesty International’s report, released four years after the death in custody of Zhina Mahsa Amini at the hands of the “morality” police sparked nationwide protests, documents how the Iranian authorities mobilized security forces armed with military-grade firearms and shotguns loaded with metal pellets and issued orders that facilitated the unlawful killing of hundreds of protesters and bystanders, including dozens of children. The crimes against humanity also included the arbitrary arrest, enforced disappearance, torture or other ill-treatment of thousands of men, women and children as well as persecution of bereaved relatives.
Alongside the report, Amnesty International is also publishing Lives Cut Brutally Short: Victims of Crimes Against Humanity During Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising, a document recording the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, 56 of them children, based on information and evidence gathered as part of the organization’s investigation into nationwide patterns of killings by the security forces. The document includes victims’ photographs and images of their grave sites where available.
In addition to calling on the UN General Assembly to create an international justice mechanism given the political deadlock at the UN Security Council, the gravity and scale of crimes committed, and high risk of recurrence, Amnesty International also urges states to call on the UN Security Council to refer the situation in Iran to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.
The organization also urges prosecution authorities around the world to initiate investigations, under universal or other forms of extraterritorial jurisdiction, against Iranian officials allegedly responsible for crimes against humanity, including the officials named in this report, and, where sufficient evidence exists, to issue arrest warrants.
Amnesty International’s years of research for this report involved interviews with 270 people, including protesters, former detainees, relatives of those killed or detained, eyewitnesses, lawyers, human rights defenders, journalists and medical workers. The organization also analysed over 2,000 videos and extensive documentary evidence, including official statements, leaked official documents, prosecution orders, court verdicts and forensic records.
Amnesty International wrote to Iran’s Supreme Leader and senior security officials to share its findings and notify the 87 officials identified in the report. At the time of publication, it has received no response.
A nationwide attack carried out pursuant to state policy
Amnesty International’s investigations into crimes against humanity committed to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising revealed that two main security forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Police Command of the Islamic Republic of Iran (known by its Persian acronym, FARAJA), led lethal protest dispersals, implementing the state policy devised through the Supreme National Security Council, State Security Council and provincial and county security councils.
FARAJA and IRGC agents repeatedly fired into crowds, using military-grade assault rifles, handguns and shotguns loaded with metal pellets. In addition to firing into crowds, they chased fleeing protesters and bystanders, closing in on unarmed victims who posed no threat to the security forces or others and fatally shooting them at close range.
Among the FARAJA branches involved were the Prevention Police, including its Assistance Cohorts, and the Special Cohorts. The IRGC branches involved included the operational divisions, the provincial Security Cohorts and various Basij battalions, such as the Imam Ali Battalions and the Beit Al-Moghaddas Battalions. These IRGC branches operated under the relevant IRGC provincial corps, overseen in turn by a regional IRGC headquarters.
Official statements and leaked documents analysed in the report reveal the state policy as reflected in strategy meetings, binding orders, deployment plans, allocations of money and weapons, and instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.
Witnesses repeatedly described streets resembling battlefields as a result of relentless gunfire by the security forces. Mahshid, who protested in Mahabad, West Azerbaijan province, told Amnesty International: “I had never seen such scenes before… The situation was very frightening and felt like a war zone. The security forces just kept shooting.”
Most of the 377 protesters and bystanders, whose deaths Amnesty International recorded, were killed by security forces during protest dispersals between September and December 2022. Others died in custody, after release from custody or in suspicious circumstances suggesting state responsibility.
Consistent with long-standing patterns of denial and cover-up, the authorities have acknowledged only 202 deaths and falsely attributed most to non-state actors, “rioters” or “armed terrorists”, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Far from acting to stop crimes as evidence mounted, senior officials repeatedly praised security forces and instructed the continuation of operations.
Total of 87 officials identified for criminal investigation
Based on detailed documentation of the security forces involved and in-depth analysis of their command structures, Amnesty International has identified 87 Iranian officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
The list, while not exhaustive, extends from the highest levels of Iran’s security apparatus to officials operating at provincial and county level.
The list of 87 individuals comprises 62 security force commanders – including 33 commanders from the IRGC and 27 commanders from FARAJA – and 25 Ministry of Interior officials including provincial and county governors. Among them are 10 national-level officials and 77 officials at regional, provincial and county levels holding responsibilities related to the 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces on which Amnesty International conducted in-depth investigations.
Among those identified is the late Supreme Leader and commander-in-chief of all armed forces, Ali Khamenei; and the late head of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, Mohammad Bagheri, both of whom were killed in February 2026 in air strikes carried out during the US-Israeli military attack against the Islamic Republic of Iran. Amnesty International also names the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the General Commander of the IRGC, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mir Ahmadi.
This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale,” said Agnès Callamard.
“The officials named remain beyond the reach of justice in Iran. Most remain in positions from which they can unleash further deadly repression while some even climbed the chain of command after the crimes against humanity in 2022. The cost of continued impunity has been devastating. It is beyond time to establish an international criminal justice mechanism for Iran before another protest massacre.”
Devastating toll on Kurdish and Baluchi communities
Protesters from Iran’s persecuted Baluchi and Kurdish communities suffered a devastating share of the lethal repression, accounting for 62% of the total number of recorded victims while they constitute 5% and 10-15% of the country’s population, respectively.
Amnesty International recorded the unlawful killing of 106 Baluchi protesters and bystanders, including 20 children, by security forces in Sistan and Baluchistan province (33% of recorded victims). On 30 September 2022 alone, 87 were unlawfully killed as security forces opened fire following Friday prayers in Zahedan – a crackdown widely known as “Bloody Friday”.
The organization also documented the circumstances surrounding the unlawful killing of 95 Kurdish protesters and bystanders, including 13 children, in the context of protest dispersals or in militarized areas near protests that were ongoing or had recently occurred across 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces (29% of recorded victims). Most were fatally shot; others were fatally beaten, struck by tear gas canisters or deliberately run over by security force vehicles.
Iman, an eyewitness in Sanandaj, Kurdistan province, said: “The agents would shoot anyone in their sight, not caring if they were women, children, passersby or protesters.”
Amnesty International found that in the provinces of Kermanshah, Kurdistan and West Azerbaijan, security forces consistently deployed designated marksman rifles, assault rifles, sub-machine guns and heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks.
Amnesty International has concluded that acts of murder and torture were committed against Kurdish and Baluchi protesters with discriminatory intent on political and ethnic grounds, and that that the elements of the crime against humanity of persecution are met for these targeted groups.
Impunity by design
In Iran, impunity for crimes under international law and other serious human rights violations is systemic and intentional.
Iran’s constitution places the justice system under the direct control of the Supreme Leader, who is not only the commander-in-chief of the security forces, but also appoints the head of the judiciary, who in turn appoints senior judges and prosecutors. Cases involving serious human rights violations by members of the security forces are handled by military prosecution offices and courts, where judges and prosecutors can themselves come from the security forces and routinely rely on accounts from the very security bodies implicated in crimes.
Iran’s Law on the Use of Firearms by Armed Forces in Necessary Incidents allows firearms to be used to disperse protests, in blatant disregard of international law, which permits the use of firearms only as a last resort to counter an imminent threat of death or serious injury. The law also generally exempts state agents from civil and criminal liability.
“Survivors and victims’ families in Iran have been trapped in a system where the very institutions meant to deliver justice are controlled by authorities with blood on their hands. Families who seek truth and justice are persecuted,” said Agnès Callamard.
Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now. The UN General Assembly must confront the crisis of impunity that exposes people in Iran to recurring and escalating mass protest killings.”
Background
Amnesty International is launching this report while people in Iran are at risk of crimes under international law on two fronts. On one front, they are exposed to violations of international humanitarian law since the USA and Israel unlawfully attacked Iran in violation of the UN Charter on 28 February 2026.
On the other, they risk further crimes against humanity in the context of protest crackdowns. Iranian authorities have used the cover of “wartime conditions” to intensify internal repression, further militarizing public spaces, openly threatening to carry out mass killings against protesters and dissidents, and escalating politically motivated arbitrary executions.
Iran has been gripped by successive waves of anti-establishment protests since December 2017, as protesters have repeatedly taken to the streets demanding human rights, dignity, freedom, the end of the Islamic Republic system and transition to a new rights-respecting system of governance. Amnesty International’s extensive research into the authorities’ response to successive waves of protests in December 2017-January 2018, November 2019, September-December 2022 and January 2026 reveals a recurrent pattern of mass unlawful killings, torture, enforced disappearance and other crimes under international law.

articles.title: Watchdog: War with Iran has depleted US weapons reserves
articles.body:
The US Department of Defense Inspector General has reported that the war with Iran has caused a munitions shortage and a “bottleneck” in replenishing stockpiles—contradicting statements by US President Donald Trump, who regularly denies the existence of supply issues, the BBC reports.
Trump has previously claimed that US munitions reserves are virtually unlimited and that anyone saying otherwise is spreading fake news. However, the independent watchdog reported that between February and June, the US expended munitions worth over 22 billion dollars, resulting in a shortage of strategic equipment. When asked about the watchdog’s report, the White House responded that there is more than enough ammunition.
The report provides the first independent insight into typically classified information regarding US weapons stockpiles.
Previous estimates had already painted a grim picture. During the conflict, US forces expended large quantities of ammunition for long-range systems, as well as vast numbers of missiles and air-defense munitions, to repel Iranian strikes. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) concluded that stockpiles of ammunition for certain missile interception systems—such as Patriot and THAAD—had been significantly depleted, with inventories in some cases cut by as much as half.
The Inspector General’s report does not disclose the exact quantity of remaining weaponry;
however, it indicates that equipment is running low and reveals bottlenecks in the ammunition replenishment supply chain. The report adds that the Department of Defense is working to accelerate procurement processes and production capacity to address the ammunition shortage.
The White House has rejected the watchdog’s assessment; on the 15th of September, spokesperson Anna Kelly stated that the United States possesses more than enough ammunition to achieve all its strategic objectives—and then some. Trump and other US administration officials have also sought to portray reports of weapons shortages as a betrayal of the country.
In a post on X on the 4th of August, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth dismissed reports of weapons shortages as false. Meanwhile, in a lengthy post on Truth Social on the 3rd of September, Trump emphasized that the US holds virtually unlimited stockpiles of weapons and continues to build up its inventory to prepare for any contingency. When the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, Trump stated that the conflict would be over within a few weeks. In September, he said that the war in Iran would end after the midterm elections scheduled for the 3rd of November.
Polls show that the war in Iran is highly unpopular among Americans. A survey conducted in early September indicates that only 23% of Americans (and just half of Republican voters) believe the US is in a better position regarding Iran than it was at the start of the war.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Build with Ukraine has 200-plus foreign cooperation bids pending decision. Its arms industry, representing 400-plus firms, wants to help fix mechanism
articles.body:
Ukraine's largest arms-industry group says it is backing the country's drive to sell and co-produce weapons abroad, while pressing the government to fix two separate obstacles in its way. The Council of Defense Industry, which represents more than 400 companies, wants a costly new export-permit fee and a stalled joint-production program to be upgraded, it said on Facebook.
The two problems are distinct. Resolution 875, the wartime rules for shipping arms abroad, charges a 20-30 percent fee on export permits, which the industry says prices Ukrainian goods out of the market.
The export fee bites
Resolution 875, adopted in July, was intended to streamline exports, with a 30-day review period and a streamlined path for partner countries. But the fee has choked it: only about 10 small export contracts have been signed since exports began, and not one permit has been issued under the new rules, Militarnyi reports.
"Resolution 875 in its current form contains provisions that could substantially worsen the competitiveness of Ukrainian producers," the group says.
Build with Ukraine is a separate track
The program lets producers export their technology and set up joint production abroad, reaching EU markets, financing, and infrastructure, while partners fund weapons production inside Ukraine.
The program lets producers export their technology and set up joint production abroad, reaching EU markets, financing, and infrastructure, while partners fund weapons production inside Ukraine. Talks are underway with Denmark, Norway, and Germany.
President Zelenskyy has said $43 billion was raised for Ukraine's defense industry in 2025, floated a goal of partner states each spending 0.25 percent of their GDP on it, and stressed that no Ukrainian technology will reach countries tied to Russia.
The Council, whose ecosystem spans more than 360 manufacturers, 28 drone-pilot schools, and 20 defense venture funds, says it is ready to help refine the mechanism.
