articles.title: Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
articles.body:
Mearsheimer: There’s no diplomatic way out of the Ukraine war
American political scientist John Mearsheimer has claimed that the Ukraine conflict can’t be resolved diplomatically because the two sides’ goals remain irreconcilable and it will ultimately be settled on the battlefield. 
 Mearsheimer made the remarks during a visit to Moscow in an interview with Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Presidium of the Council on Foreign and Defense Policy and editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs.
 Fyodor Lukyanov: John, if a time machine brought great diplomats like Metternich and Talleyrand into the present day, what would they do to stem the bloodshed and bring today’s conflicts to an end? Would they succeed?
John Mearsheimer: Well, they were definitely skilled diplomats. And if we talk about the Ukraine-Russia war, they would go to great lengths to try to solve that. But I think that they’d be unable to do it. I don’t think that war, the Ukraine war, can be settled diplomatically. I think it’s going to be settled on the battlefield.
Now you say to yourself, why do I think it can’t be settled diplomatically? It’s because Russia’s goals are unacceptable to Ukraine, and Ukraine’s goals are unacceptable to Russia. For example, Ukraine wants the territory that Russia has annexed returned to Ukraine.
It views the Donbass, Zaporozhye, and Kherson as sacred territory. And from Ukraine’s point of view, it’s completely unacceptable that Russia be allowed to annex that territory. Furthermore, Ukraine, given what’s happened, wants a security guarantee, either from NATO or from the United States, to protect it moving forward.
This is unacceptable to the Russians. Furthermore, it’s unacceptable to the Russians to give up the territory that they’ve now annexed. So how can you have a diplomatic agreement between the two sides when there are such stark differences? Ukraine is simply unwilling to give up those four oblasts and Crimea, which Russia has annexed.
And Russia is unwilling to allow Ukraine to have that territory back. Furthermore, Ukraine wants a security guarantee from the West. It wants to be part of NATO, which is understandable from Ukraine’s point of view. But Russia certainly doesn’t want Ukraine in NATO. That was the principal cause of this war to begin with. So you see that the Russians and the Ukrainians are directly at odds on key issues where they’re unwilling to compromise.
So the question is, how do you get a diplomatic solution? And the answer is, you don’t. And this one will be fought out on the battlefield. And the final solution will be determined by who wins the war.
Fyodor Lukyanov: All right, then what would victory actually look like? Would winning the war mean eliminating Ukraine as such?
John Mearsheimer: I don’t think that the Russians are going to eliminate Ukraine. I think that’s almost impossible. I think what the Russians are going to do is they’re going to take a substantial portion of Ukrainian territory. They already have taken probably about 20%, and I think they’ll ultimately try to take considerably more territory from Ukraine. But they will not conquer all of Ukraine.
Furthermore, Ukraine will be, when this war is over, a dysfunctional rump state. And the Russians will have a vested interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state, so that it can’t join NATO, and so that it doesn’t present a threat to Russia. So I think what you’re going to get here at some point is a frozen conflict, not altogether unlike what you have in Korea.
The Ukrainians will never accept the idea that Russia has conquered all this territory. The Ukrainians and the [Western] Europeans, for that matter, will not accept the new status quo. They’ll want to go back to the borders, the pre-2014 borders.
And the Russians, of course, will want to make sure that doesn’t happen, because the Russians live in fear that Ukraine will become part of the West, and it will become a Western bulwark on Russia’s borders. So what you see is that once you get this frozen conflict, Russia will have a deep-seated interest in making sure that Ukraine remains a dysfunctional rump state.
This is one of the reasons I think the Russians are likely to try to take Odessa and to take the Black Sea coast away from Ukraine, because the Russians will see that as an important way of weakening Ukraine in the future. And again, Russia will have a vested interest in weakening Ukraine.
And from Ukraine’s point of view, it makes perfect sense to see Russia as an existential threat, to want to have help from the West to deal with Russia, and to want to get its sacred territory back. I fully understand how the Ukrainians think, but that’s unacceptable to the Russians. So if you have these two parties to a conflict, one, the Russians, and two, the Ukrainians assisted by the Europeans, who have irreconcilable differences, there’s no diplomatic way out.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Does it mean that all efforts made by the Trump administration, Kushner, Witkoff and others are just a waste of time?
John Mearsheimer: I think that’s basically correct. I mean, in the case of the Trump administration, I think that it’s important to emphasize that President Trump himself has the right instincts. He wants to settle the war, the Ukraine war, and he wants to establish good relations between the United States and Russia. There’s no question that his instincts are right on this issue.
But there are two problems. One is the structural problem that I just described to you, the fact that the warring parties have irreconcilable goals. That’s point number one. And point number two is that President Trump is an inept or poor negotiator. He views himself as somebody who is brilliant at cutting deals, and he can easily shut down the Ukraine-Russia conflict in his own mind.
But exactly the opposite is true. He’s a ham-fisted, inept diplomat, and he hasn’t even come close to shutting down this war as a result of his ineptitude.
Fyodor Lukyanov: We have just marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Looking back a quarter of a century later, how would you assess their significance from the perspective of great-power politics?
John Mearsheimer: Well, 9-11 has nothing to do with great power politics. It’s just very important to understand that. 9-11 took place during the unipolar moment, when the United States was the only great power on the planet, and there was no great power politics, because you didn’t have rival great powers that could compete with each other.
And what happened with regard to 9-11 is that a small group called Al-Qaeda, which hated US Middle East policies, found a way to attack the United States and cause serious damage, and then led the United States to launch the global war on terror, which led to a number of the forever wars that we became involved in, especially Afghanistan and Iraq. And both these wars were disasters. Our response to 9-11 was badly mistaken. There was no need to launch a global war on terror. We just got ourselves into even more trouble.
But it had nothing to do with great power politics.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Could that moment be seen as the beginning of the end of the unipolar world, as some argue?
John Mearsheimer: I think that you can make that argument. I think that the 1990s were the heyday of the unipolar moment. But Russia was in terrible shape during the 1990s. And remember, Putin comes into power in roughly 2000, right? The end of ‘99, Putin comes into power. And I believe Putin resurrects the Russians from the dead.
But during the 1990s, Russia was badly weakened. And China hadn’t grown significantly by 2001. In fact, it’s not until 2001 that China joins the WTO. And when China joins the WTO, its economic growth really takes off.
So I think you can see that throughout the 1990s, up to around 2001, 2002, the United States is an incredibly powerful country. And the unipolar moment, except for what happened on 9-11, looks like it’s going very well. But after 9-11, things tend to go downhill pretty quickly. And I think the most important event here is the 2008 financial crisis, which hurt the United States badly. And then by about 2017, the Russians had come back from the dead, and I think Putin had created a situation here in Russia where Russia was once again a great power, by about 2017. And at the same time, China was also a great power in roughly 2017. So it’s around 2017 that you transition away from unipolarity to multipolarity.
And that’s a fundamental change that has drastically altered international politics. The United States was much freer to intervene around the world during the unipolar moment because there were no great power competitors, and it was free to get itself into all sorts of trouble in places like Afghanistan and in Iraq.
But then came multipolarity, and now the United States has to worry above all else about rival great powers.
Fyodor Lukyanov: Why do you single out 2017? As far as I can see, nothing particularly significant happened that year. In 2014, there was Crimea; in 2015, Syria. So why 2017?
John Mearsheimer: Well, what I’m concerned about is the balance of power. And the question is, when you look at Russia in the 1990s and in the very early 2000s, it has hardly any meaningful military power. Its military has really been wrecked. And what you see around 2015, 2016, 2017, is that the Russian military is much more effective than it had been in the previous decade and a half.
And I think this is largely the doing of Putin. I think Putin went to great lengths to help restore the Russian economy. And as the Russian economy began to flourish, the Russians were able to translate a lot of that economic might into military might.
So, by about 2016-2017, most assessments from places like the RAND Corporation about the Russian military say that Russian military power is now quite formidable. Obviously, the Russians in 2017 were not as powerful as the Soviet Union was at any point during the Cold War.
But the Russian military by 2017, and this of course is true of the Chinese military as well, looks like a quite formidable instrument. See, my argument is if you’re going to talk about going from unipolarity to multipolarity, you’re basically asking yourself the question, when do countries like China and Russia become great powers?
And for me, a great power is a country that has sufficient military power to put up a good fight against the most powerful state in the system. And of course, this is the United States. And again, I think by 2017, most security analysts in the United States believe that the Russian military was a quite formidable instrument and was quite well positioned to put up a serious fight against the United States.
And given that military power, the restoration of military power in Russia, I think that was the basis that people used to make the case that Russia was once again a great power. And just to say one more thing on this, I think everybody understood that Russia was and still is today the weakest of the three great powers.
I think the United States remains the most powerful state on the planet. I think the Chinese are now a close second. And I think there is a danger moving forward that China could overtake the United States.
And I think the Americans or most American foreign policy elites or the American foreign policy elite is very worried about that possibility. So China, in a very important way, is the real peer competitor, not Russia.
But Russia is still a great power, I think that everyone recognizes that. And I think that’s why the United States cares so much about the Ukraine war. And I think the reason that President Trump is interested in stopping or ending the Ukraine war and having good relations between Russia and the United States is because Trump understands that Russia is a great power.
And from an American point of view, it would make much more sense for the United States to be allied with Russia against China, or at least have Russia neutral, rather than create a situation where we have, in effect, driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
I mean, if you think about living in a multipolar world where there are three great powers, if you’re the United States and this is China, you want Russia on your side of the ledger. But instead, because of our foolish policies regarding Ukraine, we’ve driven the Russians into the arms of the Chinese.
And again, I think Trump’s basic instincts about the importance of settling the Ukraine war and getting Russia on good terms with the United States is driven in good part by his insight or his belief that China is the real threat for the United States.

articles.title: Kyiv says Belarus reactivated relays that helped Russian drones strike a gas station and passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland
articles.body:
Kyiv says Belarus reactivated relays that helped Russian drones strike a gas station and passenger train near Ukraine’s border with Poland
Belarus has once again activated relays near its border that help guide Russian drones to their targets, according to Andriy Demchenko, a spokesperson for Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service.
“As of now, Belarus is actively helping Russia carry out strikes on Ukrainian territory. This includes relay transmitters that are switched on in Belarus and boost the signal for Russian ‘Shahed’ and ‘Gerbera’ drones.”
Ukraine has long maintained that Belarus hosts antennas for two-way video communication systems used by Russian long-range Geran and Gerbera drones attacking Kyiv. Like Ukraine’s military, Russia’s military uses mesh networks to maintain video links with its drones. Camera-equipped UAVs fitted with special modems serve as airborne relays for one another, allowing operators to communicate with them from tens or hundreds of kilometers away. But the initial signal comes from ground-based relays. Ukraine believes Russia’s mesh-network relays for the Kyiv area are located in Belarus.
Demchenko said drones arriving from Russia stay close to the Belarusian border so they can receive a signal before flying deeper into Ukrainian territory — particularly into the country’s western regions.
Demchenko also said the relays enabled the overnight attack on the Yahodyn border crossing with Poland on September 13. Russian forces used drones to strike a gas station near the crossing and a passenger train on the Kyiv–Warsaw rail line.
In mid-June, Volodymyr Zelensky demanded that Alexander Lukashenko remove the relays used to guide Russian drone attacks from the border with Ukraine, and issued a threat: “If he doesn’t do it, we will.” Less than a week later, the Ukrainian president said the relays had stopped working.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: He thought Ukrainian army uniform would hide what he did under occupation. It didn’t. Man who guarded Kherson’s Russian-run prison drew eight years
articles.body:
A man who guarded a Russian-run prison in occupied Kherson, where captured members of the Ukrainian resistance were held, has been sentenced to eight years. After Ukraine retook the city, the collaborator tried to disappear into a Ukrainian army unit before the Security Service of Ukraine caught him, the SBU said on Telegram.
A real prison term for a collaborator is less common than it sounds. Ukraine has opened hundreds of collaboration cases since 2022, but many have halted due to their location in occupied territories or Russia.
He guarded the occupiers' prison
After Russian forces seized Kherson in 2022, the man agreed to serve as a "junior inspector" in the administration of a Russian prison set up in the regional capital, the SBU said. In the post, he guarded the cells and the facility's perimeter, which the occupiers used to hold people from the resistance movement in south of Ukraine. Kherson's right bank was under Russian control from March until Ukraine liberated it in November. The left bank remains under occupation.
He hid inside the army
When the right bank was freed, the collaborator initially stayed put, staying in his apartment, the SBU said. He then mobilized into a Ukrainian military unit, where the service said he hoped to lie low. Instead, SBU officers detained him in March 2025 at one of the army's training centers.
A real term is the exception
The court found him guilty of collaboration under the criminal code's article on the offense and, taking his cooperation with investigators into account, sentenced him to eight years, with a ban of up to ten years on holding posts in state bodies or law enforcement.
The case was built by the SBU in Mykolaiv and Kherson oblasts in cooperation with the National Police, under the Mykolaiv specialized defense prosecutor's office.

articles.title: Yemeni forces pounded Saudi Aramco, Khamis Mushait airbase
articles.body:
The Yemeni forces carried out two military operations in retaliation for "more than 450" Saudi airstrikes this week and launched ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi Aramco facility in the western Saudi port city of Yanbu and the Khamis Mushait airbase in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
"We will continue our military operations deep inside Saudi territory, targeting Saudi troop buildups, and maintaining the equation of 'a siege for a siege' and 'an escalation for an escalation' until the aggression ceases and the blockade on our beloved country is lifted," Saree said.
The first operation targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, he said, adding, “By the grace of God, these strikes were precise and direct, causing massive fires and widespread destruction.”
In the second operation, Khamis Mushit airbase was targeted with several ballistic missiles, the spokesman underlined.
Yemen's Armed Forces on Wednesday carried out two fresh retaliatory strikes on Saudi Arabia, targeting Aramco facilities in Yanbu with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones and the Khamis Mushait airbase with ballistic missiles, Brigadier General Yahya Saree emphasized.
MNA

articles.title: U.S. Army rebuilds long-range missile stocks drained by the war on Iran
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin $1.21 billion to develop Precision Strike Missile Increment 2, adding a seeker that lets the long-range missile strike moving land and maritime targets.
- The contract follows reports that the Army's PrSM stockpile was heavily drawn down during Operation Epic Fury, the recent U.S. military campaign against Iran.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin $1.21 billion to keep developing an upgraded version of its long-range strike missile, work that comes as the Army tries to rebuild a stockpile it drained fighting Iran earlier this year.
A Department of War announcement said the contract funds early operational capability work on the Precision Strike Missile Increment 2. It is structured as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity award, so the Army will issue individual task orders against that ceiling rather than lock in a fixed number of missiles now. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is managing the deal, listed as contract number W31P4Q-26-D-A001. One company bid on the work, and Lockheed won it. The estimated completion date is Sept. 13, 2031.
The Precision Strike Missile, known as PrSM, is a ground-launched, long-range strike weapon the Army built to replace the aging Army Tactical Missile System. It fires from the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System and the M270 tracked launcher, and two PrSM rounds fit in a launch pod that used to hold a single ATACMS. Each missile costs just under $3.5 million, according to the Army’s own budget documents. The baseline version, Increment 1, reached Army units in December 2023 and hits fixed points on land out to roughly 500 km (310 miles) using GPS and inertial navigation. It has no ability to track something that moves. Australia is also buying into the program: Canberra has signed on as a full development partner and in April selected PrSM, paired with HIMARS, as its own land-based maritime strike system.
Increment 2 is meant to give the missile the moving-target ability the baseline version lacks. Lockheed is integrating a new multi-mode seeker, developed under a separate Army effort called the Land-Based Anti-Ship Missile program, that lets the missile identify and strike a target in motion, whether that is a mobile air defense radar or a ship underway. The Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation and Missile Center built the guidance package before handing it to the PrSM program office for integration. The new seeker adds this capability on top of the missile’s existing land-attack role rather than replacing it.
Lockheed flew the first Increment 2 test missile with the new seeker in March 2026, sending it about 350 km (217 miles) from a HIMARS launcher. The missile deployed protective covers over the seeker at launch and gathered performance data engineers are still reviewing. The program remains in a technology-maturation phase, with a preliminary design review underway, and Lockheed has additional flight tests planned later this year.
“With Increment 2, PrSM delivers the long-range capability the Army asked for to defeat moving land and maritime threats,” said Carolyn Orzechowski, vice president of precision fires launchers and missiles at Lockheed Martin.
The urgency behind this contract traces back to a war the Army did not expect to fight this hard with these missiles. The Defence Blog reported in March 2026 that U.S. Central Command had confirmed PrSM’s first combat use, during Operation Epic Fury, the American military campaign against Iran. The Army fired the missile at Iranian coastal radar sites, air defense positions and other targets, and the campaign consumed the stockpile far faster than planners expected. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported the Army expended “virtually all” of its ATACMS and PrSM inventory during the operation. A separate analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies put the loss at roughly 45 percent of the Army’s Precision Strike Missile stockpile in the war’s first seven weeks alone, figures Pentagon sources told CNN were consistent with classified internal data. The Army has never disclosed how many PrSMs it had before the war, and it still has not said how many remain. Independent estimates of replacement timelines run from three to five years to fully rebuild the stockpile.
This contract does not, by itself, answer that shortage. It funds Increment 2 development rather than a specific quantity of new missiles, and the Army has separately been placing production orders for the baseline Increment 1 to refill the pipeline Reuters and CNN described. The IDIQ structure gives the Army flexibility to keep ordering PrSM rounds as Lockheed’s production capacity allows, rather than commit to one large batch now.

articles.title: GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
articles.body:
GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
TEHRAN – Science, Research and Technology Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf has warned that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in data analysis could pave the way for a shift from data control to human control, potentially giving rise to what he described as “an invisible dictatorship.”
Simaei-Sarraf made the remarks while addressing the 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (GFEAI 2026), held in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from September 14 to 17, IRNA reported.
 
 Leading an Iranian delegation to the forum, the minister stressed the need to give serious consideration to the ethical implications of emerging technologies.
“Technology is not neutral, and artificial intelligence does not operate fairly on its own. Sometimes, algorithms destroy more than they build, and platforms become sources of harm rather than development,” he said.
Enhanced transparency and oversight of governments and those in power are essential. However, when the surveillance is directed at ordinary citizens, tracking their behavior, relationships, and intentions, it can turn into an invisible dictatorship, he added.
Referring to the ethical responsibility of AI platforms and developers, the science minister said, “Today, data is being used in ways that violate human rights and even lead to the death of children, thereby raising a significant question: do AI platforms accept the responsibility for how their technologies are used?”
Numerous chatbots refuse to answer questions about suicide—and rightly so—yet AI can be employed to identify and precisely target human beings with missiles, as the elementary school in Minab was targeted by US missiles, killing 168 students while they were studying.
According to Simaei-Sarraf, inequality is another fundamental challenge of the AI era. Unequal knowledge and capabilities have always created disparities. AI can widen the gap more than any other technology. Hence, the ethical framework should not be merely limited to preventing harm, but to ensuring equal access.
Developing countries should have the opportunity to develop their own AI systems tailored to their languages and cultures, and international organizations are ethically responsible to help these nations realize this goal. Technology must serve humanity, and AI should enhance human freedom, not limit it, he further noted.
In response to a question about the country’s most important measure to strengthen Iran’s capacity in responsible AI, Simaei-Sarraf said if this question was raised before June 2025, he would have definitely said targeted and sustainable investment in water and energy sectors, followed by strengthening collaborations within Iran’s AI ecosystem.
Regarding the shift in regional priorities, the science minister went on to say that “today, I think the removal of coercive measures and the establishment of peace in the region are the top priorities for Iran as well as the whole region. These sanctions are unethical, and establishing security and peace is a moral imperative.”
The Global Forum serves as a key platform to advance the implementation of the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence across all Member States of UNESCO. It supports the exchange of knowledge and experiences across regions in the development of AI policies, regulatory frameworks, and institutional capacities, to foster inclusive and sustainable social and economic development while safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Launched in 2022, the Global Forum was previously hosted by the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Thailand, with co-funding support from the European Union since 2024.
The 2026 edition of Global Forum aims to create an engaging environment with high-level ethical reflection, bridging discussions on governance with technological innovation. The science minister is scheduled to attend specialized meetings, panel discussions, and hold meetings with representatives of other countries.
Co-hosted by UNESCO and Saudi Arabia, represented by the Saudi Data and AI Authority and the International Centre for AI Research and Ethics, the event has brought together global leaders, policymakers, experts, and stakeholders to strengthen dialogue and promote practical and sustainable approaches to the ethics and governance of AI.
 
 MT/MG

articles.title: Russian general who told Putin Kostyantynivka had been captured killed in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian Major General Anton Grunis, the commander of the 4th Separate Motor Rifle Brigade (formerly the 4th Brigade of the so-called “Luhansk People’s Republic”), has been killed in the war in Ukraine, according to a report by the investigative outlet Important Stories. The death of Major General Grunis was also reported by Apti Alaudinov, commander of the Chechen Akhmat special forces unit, and by the Suvorovskoye Bratstvo (lit. “Suvorov Brotherhood”) Telegram channel, which is run by graduates of Russia’s Suvorov military schools.
The circumstances of Grunis’ death currently remain unclear. Important Stories noted that leaked records appeared to place him in Alchevsk, in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine’s Luhansk Region. On Sept. 13, a few days before the reports began appearing, Ukrainian forces struck multiple locations across the city. Ukraine said the strikes destroyed a supply depot and a location where Russian forces stored weapons and military equipment.
Around the same time, according to the Exilenova+ monitoring channel, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) attacked military equipment in the settlement of Karpaty near Alchevsk. It is not known whether Grunis’ death was connected to those strikes.
Before the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Grunis took part in Russian military campaigns in Chechnya, Georgia, and Syria. He also participated in the annexation of Crimea.
More recently, Grunis commanded a brigade advancing toward Kostyantynivka in Ukraine’s Donetsk Region. In July, the Major General reported to Vladimir Putin that the city had been captured, and a month later he was awarded the title Hero of Russia, the country’s highest honorary distinction.
Kostyantynivka, however, has still not come fully under Russian control. The open-source intelligence project Black Bird Group and the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) continue to report fighting inside the city.
The pro-war Russian Telegram channel Rybar also indicates that Ukrainian positions in the area remain, marking the territory as a contested “gray zone” that is not firmly controlled by either side.

articles.title: 12 takeaways from von der Leyen’s State of the Union
articles.body:
Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union speech to unveil a raft of proposals aimed at making Europe better prepared for a world of threats — from sweltering summers to hybrid warfare, migrant crises and social media.
What the Commission president chose to talk about in Strasbourg — and, just as importantly, what she left unsaid — will help define the rest of her term and the political legacy she leaves behind.
Here are the 12 biggest takeaways.
Advertisement
1. Canada could become the EU’s first “associate member”
Speaking directly to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was sitting in the Parliament hemicycle, von der Leyen proposed an ambitious, far-reaching new alliance spanning tech, defense, energy, critical minerals, AI, the Arctic and more.
In a message that could have been addressed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump, von der Leyen said: “This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While it remains to be seen whether EU member countries are on board with so-called associate membership — a model, it should be noted, that does not currently exist — the proposal is a striking signal of how badly Brussels wants to deepen ties with Ottawa.
2. Europe might finally get a security council
The idea of a European security executive body has been floated in various forms for years, but has taken on fresh urgency against the backdrop of Trump undermining the transatlantic security relationship and Russia’s war against Ukraine spilling over into the bloc.
Von der Leyen injected new life into the discussion by calling to create a European Security Council, saying it would bring together the EU and like-minded countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Ukraine and Norway (notably, there was no mention of the U.S.) to discuss and manage threats.
Advertisement
It would go hand-in-hand with a new “Emergency Security Protocol,” which EU countries could trigger in response to threats short of an actual attack or invasion. “In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO’s Article 4,” she said.
3. EU wants to work together on AI, but not with the U.S. or China
The Commission president is inviting the major AI labs to Brussels to discuss efforts to “pace the frontier” of AI development.
“AI comes with a balance of possibilities and risks,” she said. “Without addressing these risks, we will never be able to unlock AI’s possibilities.”
A woman uses her laptop at a metro station in Kyiv on Nov. 27, 2025. | Sergei Gapon/AFP via Getty Images
Von der Leyen called for cooperation with the United Kingdom, Canada “and others” on AI but did not mention the U.S. or China — the two countries leading the global AI race.
Von der Leyen said the remaining funds would be used for a new program involving joint projects with Ukrainian defense companies.
Advertisement
The announcement potentially turns an administrative problem — member countries such as Italy not taking up all the cheap loans available to them — into a way to integrate Ukraine's battlefield expertise and defense industry with Europe's.
5. Climate policy is becoming more about survival
Von der Leyen's climate message was notably focused on preparing for the worst rather than new emissions-cutting measures.
She defended the EU's existing climate targets but devoted much of her attention to dealing with the consequences of a hotter Europe, including a forthcoming European Heatwave Plan, a European Water Initiative and a Climate Insurance Alliance.
She said there can be “no repeat of this summer,” which was Europe’s hottest ever, causing its forests to burn and its rivers to dry up.
6. Von der Leyen wants to stop “gold-plating”
The Commission president wants EU countries to agree on a new “pact against gold-plating” — the practice of adding national requirements when implementing EU legislation.
“We are doing our best at the European level to cut red tape. But now I think it is time for the member states to step up,” she said.
Advertisement
While von der Leyen called for the overhaul of the single market to be completed by the end of 2027, she otherwise glossed over simplification and competitiveness in her speech.
7. Admitting defeat on Israel
Von der Leyen acknowledged the “deep suffering” in Gaza and condemned “unchecked settler violence” in the West Bank, while saying Europe must keep the two-state solution alive.
But she also openly acknowledged the EU's inability to agree on some of the measures she promised last year, with member countries unable to agree on action.
Destroyed buildings are seen in Gaza on June 10, 2026. | Ahmed Al Arini/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
The failure to secure majorities for sanctions against Israeli settlers and ministers, she said, was “painful for many Europeans.”
“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she added.
8. Surprisingly little to say about finance
For a Commission that has spent much of the past year talking about making Europe a more attractive place to invest and scale up, financial policy was largely absent from the address.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen's main new financial announcement was a Banking Package focused on simplification and tackling fragmentation — a proposal the Commission had already announced in July.
There was little new on the broader ambition to turn Europe into a major investment hub.
“To be very clear, our budget is about our future. And any modern budget needs new own resources,” she said, referring to the term for EU taxes.
The Commission’s proposal to generate over €60 billion through new levies has been met with resistance in national capitals.
10. China got an ominous mention
One of the questions looming over the speech was how hard von der Leyen would go in on China.
Advertisement
On Wednesday, she slammed the EU's trade deficit with Beijing — “one billion a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she said — and highlighted “dangerous dependencies” on China for critical raw materials.
But on trade, she stopped short of calling for any dramatic measures — something she did in her 2023 speech — when she launched an anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles. “We will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship,” she said this year, in an apparent reference to the EU's still-under-construction diversification instrument, but did not go further.
11. Getting tough on migration
In the wake of the Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen called for a European Emergency Response Framework, which would give EU countries in similar scenarios “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.” Translation: returning migrants faster without worrying about granting asylum.
She also wants the bloc to strengthen Frontex, its border agency, but did not mention raising staff numbers, as she has called for previously.
12. Banning kids from social media
Von der Leyen took aim at social media, which she said was stealing childhoods, and vowed tougher action to protect kids online, including keeping some minors off popular platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she said, adding platforms would also have to introduce “safe design” for under-18s.

articles.title: Saudis seek allies’ help as missile defences run low in fight with Houthis
articles.body:
Saudis seek allies’ help as missile defences run low in fight with Houthis
The kingdom’s main ally and arms supplier, the US, has seen its own stock of interceptors dwindle because of the war with Iran
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for help as its stand-off with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on, two regional officials said on Wednesday.
The officials said the Saudis have asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air-defence support to the region to help defend against missiles and drones fired by Houthis and other Iran-backed groups.
The outreach was initiated because Saudi Arabia’s main ally and arms supplier, the United States, has seen its own stock of interceptors dwindle over the course of a six-month war with Iran, one official said. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media.
Saudi officials did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

articles.title: 130 lawyers say UK Israel settlement sanctions 'fall far short'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK sanctions on Israeli settlements ‘fall far short’, lawyers warn
More than 130 legal experts, including lawyers and legal academics, have called on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce wider UK sanctions on Israeli settlements, arguing that recently announced measures “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under a 2024 International Court of Justice (ICJ) advisory opinion that found Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory unlawful.
The six-page letter was sent to Burnham on Tuesday, following Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement of a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The measures prompted a scathing response from Israel.
"We note the Foreign Secretary’s statement that the sanctions regime targets illegal settlements and settlement expansion, and not Israel. The obligations identified by the ICJ in the 2024 Advisory Opinion, and the subsequent General Assembly resolution endorsing it, however, attach to the occupation as a whole, and the Government has itself found that ethnic cleansing is taking place," the letter read.
"It is notable, by contrast to the improperly narrow approach to the sanctions regime adopted towards Israel, the UK’s Russia sanctions are not confined to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory," it added.
"They extend to Russian banks, energy companies, state-linked enterprises, shipping networks, exports, imports, investment activity, financial services and other sectors of the Russian economy because those structures are viewed as enabling, financing or benefiting from Russia's aggression against Ukraine."
The lawyers also referred to Article 6(3) of the Arms Trade Treaty, which prohibits arms transfers where a state knows the items would be used to commit genocide, crimes against humanity or grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions.
The letter also called on the government to ensure that money raised by UK-registered charities is not used to support settlement activities.
Labour MP Melanie Ward previously said Israeli settlements had received at least £28 million in donations from 32 charities in England and Wales, as the Charity Commission announced a fact-finding inquiry into charities operating in settlements in August.
Ralph Wilde, a UCL professor of international law who has acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in proceedings before the ICJ, told The New Arab that the illegality of the way the occupation is conducted, including the establishment of settlements, should be distinguished from what he described as the more fundamental illegality of the occupation itself.
"Yes, the settlements are illegal. Yes, genocide is illegal. But even if there weren't settlements, and even if there wasn't a genocide, Israel would still be acting illegally because it doesn't even have a legal right to be there in the first place," Wilde told The New Arab.
"And that's a more fundamental illegality, because it goes to the very presence itself."
Wilde said the UK had previously argued that it was neither possible nor advisable to determine whether the occupation itself was illegal, maintaining that it could continue lawfully until a peace agreement was reached.
But he described Britain's acknowledgement last week that the occupation is illegal as a significant, albeit limited, shift.
"The big shift from last week is that the UK is now saying that the occupation is illegal," he said.
However, Wilde said Britain had essentially "just acknowledged reality" without following the ICJ's reasoning to its conclusion.
"They haven't followed through and said what the court said, which was that because the occupation is illegal, it should end."
Wilde argued that further action should be taken in response to the ICJ's findings on Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory, including sanctions against Israel and individual Israelis whom he said support the occupation, including political leaders.
"There needs to be a complete end of any form of assistance given to Israel-military assistance, intelligence, or other assistance-because there's no way to be sure that that assistance is not, in one way or another, assisting the illegal occupation, and the UK is under a legal obligation not to provide assistance," he told TNA.
Meanwhile, another signatory to Tuesday's letter, SOAS professor of law Nimer Sultany, emphasised in a statement that "the elephant in the room is that the occupation is not a bug, it’s a feature."
“Israel’s political consensus opposes Palestinian statehood. Thus, ending Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territories, as determined by the International Court of Justice, requires immediate, effective and comprehensive actions by the UK government, not a piece-meal approach.”
The latest remarks follow international outcry over escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement, east of Jerusalem.
The developments prompted Britain to announce a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, alongside targeted measures against settlements and those facilitating or profiting from them.
11 other countries, including France and Canada, subsequently announced similar measures.
Meanwhile, Israeli rights group B'Tselem said on Monday that Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank form part of a wider project aimed at making it impossible for Palestinians to exist collectively as a people.
It identified five interconnected tactics and policies in the West Bank: "violence, ethnic cleansing, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction".

articles.title: Russian general who briefed Putin on capture of Kostiantynivka killed in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian general who briefed Putin on capture of Kostiantynivka killed in Ukraine
Russian Major General Anton Grunis, commander of the 4th Motorized Rifle Brigade of the Southern Group of Forces, has been killed, Lieutenant General Apti Alaudinov confirmed after Ukrainian and Russian sources had already reported his death. Alaudinov is deputy head of the Main Military-Political Directorate of Russia’s Armed Forces and commander of the Akhmat unit.
Alaudinov offered no further details. In a post on the Max messenger cited by Russia’s state news agency TASS, he said only that Grunis “died a hero, having fulfilled his sacred duty to the end.”
Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces who goes by the callsign “Madyar,” said Grunis was killed on September 12, 2026, in the Donetsk region in a Ukrainian drone strike.
According to Brovdi, Grunis was the officer who reported to the Russian president in July on the capture of Kostiantynivka, though Russian forces still do not fully control the city. At the time, Putin described Grunis as “a man with a Lithuanian surname, born in Kazan, who fights brilliantly.”
Brovdi said Grunis is the seventh senior Russian military officer killed in strikes by Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces.
In late August, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that Defense Minister Andrei Belousov had presented Grunis with the Gold Star medal of Hero of Russia “for courage and heroism shown in the performance of military duty.”

articles.title: Medvedev stated that without "greatness," Russia would simply cease to exist — such are the "laws of history"
articles.body:
Medvedev stated that without "greatness," Russia would simply cease to exist — such are the "laws of history"
Kyiv • UNN
Dmitry Medvedev stated that Russia cannot exist without the status of a great power. He also regularly threatens the West with nuclear weapons.
Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev said that Russia allegedly cannot exist without the status of a "great power." He made the statement during a meeting with the secretaries of the regional branches of United Russia, The Moscow Times reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Our country can either be a great power, or it will not exist at all. Such are the laws of history
He has made similar statements about Russia’s "greatness" before. In particular, after Kherson was liberated by Ukrainian forces in 2022, Medvedev called for reminding Russia’s opponents of the "greatness and boundlessness of the Russian world."
Medvedev regularly threatens the West
After the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Medvedev repeatedly issued threats against Western countries, including mentioning the possibility of using nuclear weapons.
At the beginning of September, he also called for strikes on Berlin and German military enterprises after Russia was accused of being involved in the attack on Leipzig Airport.

articles.title: For first time, foreign government is funding Ukrainian drone school: Canada picks foundation that has already bought Ukraine nearly $50M in drones
articles.body:
For the first time, a foreign government is paying to build a Ukrainian drone-training program. Under its Military Training and Cooperation Program, Canada has funded a 24-month course for FPV and fixed-wing drone operators at the training center of the Serhii Prytula Foundation, one of Ukraine's largest charities, the foundation said.
The money buys a system. Canada is paying to build a training cycle that can be scaled and copied, the instructors, methods, standards, and infrastructure behind the courses, so it can keep pace with a technology that changes by the month.
The arrangement runs both ways: Canada, which was slow to adopt the FPV drones now dominating the battlefield, gains access to the combat experience of the country that leads the world in drone warfare.
Canada buys a training system
The deal recognizes what Ukraine's front-line schools have built.
"This is recognition not only of our experience but of the quality and standards of our training," said Andrii Shuvalov, CEO of the Serhii Prytula Foundation.
Both sides gain from the deal
Canada's military attaché framed it as an exchange, not simply aid.
"This is a mutually beneficial partnership. Ukrainian service members will train with leading instructors, and Canada will benefit from Ukraine's deep combat and training experience," said Colonel Eric Andresen.
The problem the program targets is one every modern army now faces: technology evolves so fast that training has to keep pace, or fall behind.
The foundation brings the scale
The problem the program targets is one every modern army now faces: technology evolves so fast that training has to keep pace, or fall behind.
The Prytula Foundation, founded by the volunteer and public figure Serhii Prytula, is a credible partner given its track record. It has bought roughly $39 million in strike drones and $10 million in reconnaissance drones for Ukraine's forces, along with about $8.6 million in vehicles and some $1.9 million each in optics and communications gear, spending that has put it among the country's biggest private suppliers of the war.

articles.title: US Congress passes Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
US Congress passes Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill
The US House of Representatives has passed a bill authorizing President Donald Trump to slap tariffs on countries purchasing Russian energy and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
The lower chamber approved the legislation on Wednesday by a vote of 262-159. According to The Hill, 203 Republicans and 58 Democrats voted in favor, while seven Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed it. The bill passed the US Senate last month.
The bill, which also grants Trump the authority to impose additional sanctions on Iran, is named in honor of hawkish Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who unexpectedly passed away last month. A major Trump ally and vocal supporter of Ukraine, Graham traveled to Kiev ten times after 2022 and co-wrote the original version of the legislation, calling for “bone-crushing” sanctions against Russia.
The version adopted by Congress allows Trump to impose additional tariffs of up to 100% on countries importing or reselling Russian oil and gas. The bill is aimed at “the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion,” with China and India expected to be among those targeted.
Many Democrats argued that the bill would grant Trump additional powers amid his ongoing trade war with much of the world. “What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said.
The legislation championed by Graham remained stalled for months as Trump favored diplomacy to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine while refusing to exclusively blame Moscow for the conflict. Trump’s envoys discussed ways to normalize economic ties in talks with their Russian counterparts.
Negotiations on Ukraine, however, largely paused after Trump launched a war against Iran in late February. After a period of inactivity, Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev in September.
The bill was passed amid an ongoing energy crisis exacerbated by disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran war. Trump recently blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices and urged Kiev to stop striking Russian refineries. On Monday, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy sites, but both sides quickly denied that such a truce was in place.
Speaking during a trip to India last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin said the country had successfully adapted its economy to mitigate the impact of the “illegal” restrictions. “More than 30,000 sanctions have been imposed on Russia – almost twice as many as on all other countries in the world combined,” he said.

articles.title: Aircraft carrier arrives at on the Clyde in Scotland
articles.body:
HMS Queen Elizabeth has arrived in Scotland, sailing up the Firth of Clyde and into Loch Long to the jetty at Glenmallan, the Royal Navy has confirmed to the UK Defence Journal.
Commander Adrian Visram, a Royal Navy spokesperson, told us: “HMS Queen Elizabeth is currently in Glenmallan completing a short logistics and engagement stop before continuing on operations.”
The 65,000-tonne carrier sailed from Portsmouth earlier this month for three months of training and operations around the United Kingdom and northern Europe, in her role as NATO’s command ship for the Allied Response Force, a role she assumed in July and one neither Queen Elizabeth-class ship had performed before.
Glenmallan sits on the western shore of Loch Long in Argyll, and its jetty is the only facility on the west coast able to take a ship of the carriers’ size alongside, which is why both Queen Elizabeth-class vessels have called there repeatedly since it was rebuilt.
The jetty itself underwent a £67 million upgrade under a contract awarded to VolkerStevin in 2019, with Jacobs as managing agent and Arch Henderson as designer. It had last been upgraded in the 1970s and had reached the end of its economic life. Around £20 million of that work went to local suppliers and small and medium-sized enterprises in Scotland, and the project extended the jetty’s life by an estimated fifty years while making it accessible to the carriers.
The work involved installing four new navigational aids to allow safe passage through the confined waterway, two modular fender spacer units that move with the tide to keep the flight deck clear of the jetty, and dolphin mooring points to hold a ship of that size securely.
As we reported at the end of April, the last Queen Elizabeth-class carrier to make the trip was HMS Prince of Wales, which called at Glenmallan ahead of Operation Firecrest. That deployment, announced by the Prime Minister at the Munich Security Conference in February, took the carrier strike group across the North Atlantic and the High North, with Prince of Wales leading the force.
Firecrest was designed to deter Russian aggression, protect critical undersea infrastructure and demonstrate the ability to project force at scale within a NATO framework, against a background of a 30 per cent increase in Russian naval vessels threatening British waters over the preceding two years. It included activity under NATO’s Arctic Sentry mission and exercises alongside Standing NATO Maritime Group One, which Britain has led throughout 2026.
Queen Elizabeth’s own programme runs on a different track from her sister’s, and she will undertake advanced training under Flag Officer Sea Training, exercising across the spectrum of modern naval warfare, and will rehearse how an allied naval force would operate together in a crisis. The programme continues into next year with participation in major NATO exercises, preparing her to take over from Prince of Wales as fleet flagship and high readiness strike carrier in late 2027.
The Royal Navy has linked the deployment to the £240 million committed in the Defence Investment Plan towards developing drones for a Hybrid Carrier Air Wing, including jet-powered types intended to operate alongside the F-35B.
The first visit by a Queen Elizabeth-class ship to the upgraded jetty came in March 2021, when Queen Elizabeth called there during final preparations for her maiden operational deployment, the first time she had visited western Scotland after becoming a familiar sight on the Forth during her assembly at Rosyth.
On the way up the Clyde the ship paused over the wreck of HMS Dasher, the escort carrier lost on 27 March 1943 with 379 of her company, and laid a wreath. The ship posted afterwards that “the lessons from the tragedy improved the safety of carrier aviation. We still benefit from those lessons.”
Dasher was a converted merchant hull operating in the Firth of Clyde when an internal explosion sank her within minutes, and the inquiry that followed changed how aviation fuel was stored and handled aboard carriers.

articles.title: In April, 24 Ukrainian companies ran their own air defense. By mid-September, 81 do — about one new firm per day
articles.body:
Ukraine has authorized 81 private companies to run their own air defense against Russian drones, letting the factories and infrastructure sites that Moscow hits daily shoot back, Ukraine's Defense Ministry says. The firms have been provided "authorized" status under an experimental program, a count that has climbed from 51 in mid-July, according to ArmyInform.
The idea is to let the targets defend themselves. Russian drones strike Ukrainian factories, warehouses, and power sites so relentlessly that the state cannot shield everyone, so the Defense Ministry is enlisting the companies being hit to form their own drone-defense teams.
Ninety-two firms have already applied, among them operators of critical infrastructure and businesses from across the country's industries and regions. The teams are not freelancers: they fold into Ukraine's layered air defense under the command of the Air Force, so they do not fire into a shared sky blind.
The count climbs fast
The program has grown quickly since it began in late 2025, from 24 companies in April to 30 in June, 51 in July, and 81 by mid-September. The units are made of trained, certified civilian staff, some running mobile fire teams with heavy machine guns, others flying interceptor drones.
By June, they had already shot down more than 20 Russian attack and reconnaissance drones, the ministry said, including one jet-powered Geran, the faster variant that has strained Ukraine's defenses.
Russia's drones drive the demand
The Defense Ministry launched the project at the end of 2025 to add a layer of protection for workers and production sites that had become routine targets.
The goal the ministry set for the wider effort is stark: detect every aerial threat and destroy 95 percent of them. The steady climb in members, roughly one company added per day since July, suggests that demand is not slowing.

articles.title: Zelenskyy explains steps Ukraine is prepared to take towards energy ceasefire
articles.body:
Zelenskyy explains steps Ukraine is prepared to take towards energy ceasefire
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said there is currently no formal agreement on an energy ceasefire with Russia, although Ukraine remains willing to agree to one provided Russia stops its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with CBS, cited by his press service
Quote: "When Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were here, they proposed thinking about refineries and other energy. I told them we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but you need to know what that means for Ukraine. For Putin, energy is selling oil and gas. For us, energy is having electricity and gas supplies for our people. My message was: If the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, it means no strikes of any kind with any type of weapon...
If they say, 'We don't attack these facilities,' they have to put a list of their facilities on the table – the ones they don't want us to attack. Even during the war, you can find some moments to de-escalate. If you negotiate, that means you are showing your goodwill, or political will, to end the war."
Background:
- On 14 September, US President Donald Trump claimed that Ukraine has agreed not to strike Russian energy facilities.
- In his evening address on 14 September, Zelenskyy commented on a US proposal regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure. "If this can become the first de-escalatory step – a step towards ending Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation," he noted.
- The Financial Times, citing sources familiar with the matter, reported that negotiations on a halt to attacks on energy facilities have been underway for some time, but Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin does not want to reach an agreement before winter.
- Zelenskyy has stressed that Russia continues to attack Ukraine's energy facilities, while the defence forces continue to respond with strikes on businesses that support the aggressor state's military-industrial complex.

articles.title: Russian agents plotted assassinations in U.S. and Europe in first documented Russian intelligence attempt to kill on U.S. soil
articles.body:
The United States has charged two Russian nationals, two Cubans, and one Venezuelan with working for Russian intelligence to prepare assassination attempts in America and Europe, including the murder of Russian dissidents, the U.S. Department of Justice stated in a press release. As The Insider notes, this marks the first documented attempt by Russian intelligence to kill on U.S. soil. Besides the planned killings, for which operatives were offered up to $40,000, the agents recruited people to carry out sabotage in “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.”
The U.S. Department of Justice unsealed charges against five individuals whom investigators believe worked for Russian intelligence. They are Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services; his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, an FSB officer; Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35; Cuban Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, known as Viking; and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22. Commenting on the case, Attorney General Todd Blanche said:
“It is our job to stop America’s adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil.”
According to Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg, the perpetrators attempted to “recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin.” Over the summer, the network recruited a U.S. resident to surveil a well-known Russian dissident, identified in the published documents as “Victim-1.” Suarez promised the recruit between $1,000 and $1,500 to take photographs and video of locations associated with the potential victim. After the assignment was completed, the recruit was offered $40,000 to kill the dissident. When the U.S. resident declined to carry out the killing himself, he was asked to recommend “someone [who] can do the work.”
As The Insider found, Russian intelligence deliberately used Cubans and Venezuelans living in Russia to recruit a Venezuelan living in the United States. Angel Eduardo Castro, who had previously played baseball in Venezuela, served as the go-between.
In late July, Castro contacted a fellow countryman living in the U.S. and instructed him to surveil a Russian dissident in Washington. They communicated in code: the surveillance assignment referred to the need to “measure the plot of land and provide the measurements,” while the killing itself was called “construction.”
The same network, the U.S. Department of Justice notes, recruited a U.S. citizen in 2025 to surveil another Russian dissident — “Victim-2,” who lived in Lithuania. In that episode, the father and son Khrameev played the leading role. The younger Khrameev asked the recruit to take photographs at the potential victim’s address, and the elder Khrameev offered him $25,000 to carry out the murder. The Justice Department’s statement describes:
“Yuri Khrameev further told U.S. Citizen-1 that they wanted Victim-2 dead because he was ‘spreading dirt about my country’ and ‘distorting history.’ Yuri Khrameev then sent U.S. Citizen-1 a photograph of Victim-2 and described that he could be murdered by ‘throwing a bottle of gasoline’ or ‘sticking a knife’ in him. After U.S. Citizen-1 declined to carry out the murder, Yuri Khrameev offered to give him a ‘simpler job’ which could include ‘set[ting] fire to a warehouse of property or food’ or ‘throw[ing] a bottle of gasoline at an electrical substation.’ Yuri Khrameev made clear to U.S. Citizen-1 that the purpose was to target ‘all the countries that are helping Ukraine’ and that he was offering ‘serious money for serious work.’ Finally, Yuri Khrameev confirmed that he was a ‘colonel of Russian intelligence agencies.’”
The Justice Department notes that the network likely recruited other individuals to carry out acts of sabotage in Europe. According to the department, Cuban national Durruthy coordinated an attack in Czechia in June 2024 and another in Lithuania in September 2024.
All five individuals have been charged with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro are also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire. The first charge carries a maximum penalty of up to 20 years in prison, the second up to 10 years. All of them remain at large.

articles.title: Bloomberg: Germany is preparing hospitals for a possible Russian attack on NATO. Its military says as many as 1,000 wounded troops could need care each day.
articles.body:
Bloomberg: Germany is preparing hospitals for a possible Russian attack on NATO. Its military says as many as 1,000 wounded troops could need care each day.
Government agencies across Germany are inspecting the country’s infrastructure and health care system to assess how well they could function under martial law, according to Bloomberg.
In a report modeling possible scenarios for a Russian attack on NATO, the Bundeswehr estimated that Germany could receive as many as 1,000 wounded service members a day. The country’s five military hospitals would quickly become overwhelmed. Civilian hospitals are required to provide wartime care, putting the health care system under unprecedented strain, Bloomberg notes.
The government’s challenges reportedly include finding enough hospital beds, strengthening medical supply chains, and improving coordination between military and civilian hospitals.
Training enough medical personnel is another pressing challenge. Only a few hundred doctors in Germany have experience treating combat trauma and gunshot wounds. Civilian surgeons are now being offered specialized courses.
Private companies in the health care sector are concerned that their employees could be called up as reservists or volunteer for military service — affecting as many as 20% of their workers in some regions. The companies are also considering how to maintain uninterrupted production of critical medicines if demand surges and assessing whether adequate physical security measures are available.
Germany has seen a surge in hybrid attacks since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg. One of the latest incidents involved the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane. Germany blamed Russia for the sabotage and responded by closing the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russia responded by closing the Goethe-Institut.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has said Russia could start a war with NATO in 2029, though some analysts believe it could happen even sooner. In that event, Germany would be obligated to defend the alliance and, because of its geographic location, would likely become a key transit hub for military personnel, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title: Israeli groups oppose calls to revoke NAZA directors citizenship
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli rights groups oppose calls to revoke NAZA directors’ citizenship
43 Israeli human rights groups and NGOs have backed Oscar-winning NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor amid threats against them and calls to revoke their citizenship.
A statement issued on Tuesday by the organisations called on Israeli authorities to stop the threats and reject calls to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship or prosecute them and their sources, amid fierce backlash from Israeli politicians following the documentary’s Special Jury Award win at the Venice Film Festival.
“The institutional response to the film and the threats against its creators are characteristic of dictatorial regimes,” the statement said.
“Citizenship is not a prize granted by the regime or the government, but a fundamental right belonging to each and every one of us,” it added.
The statement came after Culture and Sports Minister Miki Zohar described the film as “horrifying” and an “act of treason against the state”.
Zohar said in a post on X over the weekend that he would take immediate action to revoke the citizenship of NAZA’s creators.
The groups stressed that freedom of expression and freedom of the press are fundamental to democracy, warning that persecution and attempts to silence dissent can extend beyond an individual or a single issue.
The statement acknowledged that most representatives of the organisations had not seen the film, as it has yet to receive a full release.
However, it said the allegations at the heart of the controversy surrounding NAZA warranted an investigation.
It also highlighted the escalating death toll in Gaza, calling for the allegations raised in the film to be thoroughly investigated and for independent journalists to be granted access to report from the devastated territory.
The latest statement follows a separate petition signed by more than 1,000 Israeli filmmakers in support of the NAZA directors amid pro-Israelbacklash over the film’s claims.
The petition said: “We filmmakers and creators call on everyone who is still fighting for freedom of expression and artistic freedom to join us in expressing support and solidarity with Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, the creators of the film NAZA.”
The filmmakers also warned that the continuing backlash and hostility could threaten the physical safety of the directors, as they stressed the importance of independent journalism in Israel.
“The central role of art and journalism is to hold up a mirror to the society in which they exist and to generate discourse and debate without giving anyone a pass, even when the reality is difficult.”
What is NAZA about?
NAZA is based on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel, most of whom spoke anonymously, and examines systems and practices used during Israel’s war in Gaza.
The filmmakers say the documentary builds on investigations previously published by +972 Magazine, Local Call and The Guardian.
The film takes its name from a military acronym reportedly used to indicate the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike on Gaza.
After receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the 80-minute documentary won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.

articles.title: Trump administration plans $2.8 billion weapons sale to Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump administration plans to send powerful bombs to Israel in $2.8 billion weapons sale
The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns over mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration temporarily paused their delivery two years ago.
The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 of the bombs, made up of 20,000 Mk84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to two US officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss the package, which is not yet final.
Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing—in which US taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.
The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israeli’s military capacity. The Israel's genocide of Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and has decimated the enclave.
The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its genocide.
The sale signals that some strains in the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, especially since the two countries launched the war against Iran in February, are not impeding the closeness of the US-Israeli alliance. Trump has had a hot-and-cold history with Netanyahu over the years and expressed some frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House.
In 2024, the Biden administration held off on one shipment of the bombs, but Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.
Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January.
The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants, with some designed to penetrate deep, underground targets while others detonate above ground and cause widespread damage.
Though the Israeli military has offered few details about what bombs and artillery it has used in Gaza, experts analyzing strike footage and blast fragments found on-site believe the US-made bombs have been used there, killing several people in densely populated areas.
While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the fragile ceasefire took hold in October, Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the territory, including some overnight and into Tuesday that killed several people. That is even after Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a key Mideast negotiator, met with Netanyahu last month in an effort to push the ceasefire deal forward and asked Israel to reduce its attacks.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 73,264 Palestinians, including those killed since the ceasefire.
